articles.title: Racist abuse of French judo star Teddy Riner investigated after he spoke about rise of far right
articles.summary:
Paris public prosecutor opens investigation into online harassment of Riner, one of France’s most popular sportspeople

Paris’s public prosecutor has opened an investigation into the racist…

blocks.text: Paris’s public prosecutor has opened an investigation into the racist abuse and online harassment of the French judo star Teddy Riner after he expressed concern about the rise of the far right.

Riner, who has often been voted France’s most popular sportsperson and is one of the most successful judo competitors of all time, told a TV sports show this month that he felt “anxiety” about the rise of the far right in France. Numerous racist insults and hate messages were subsequently directed at him online, the prosecutor’s office said.
The far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN) party politician Marine Le Pen is polling high ahead of next spring’s presidential election.
The French football team captain and Real Madrid player, Kylian Mbappé, was at the centre of a row in May when he expressed concerns that Le Pen’s party could win the presidential election.

Riner, 37, who was born on the French Caribbean island of Guadeloupe and grew up in Paris, has a massive following in France, where his ability to swiftly throw and pin his judo opponents to the ground made him a star the Paris 2024 Olympics. He is a French gold medal hope for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Riner wrote on social media on Thursday: “Debate and contradiction are legitimate. Hatred and racism are not.”

Earlier, he told the state broadcaster France 2 he would continue to speak out. “I grew up in a France where people in difficulty were close-knit and united. Today’s attempts to divide France, to create an mood of instability are unfamiliar to me. What will we leave for our kids tomorrow? The France I want is the France I grew up in where everyone knew how to live together.”

In May, Mbappé, 27, who grew up in Paris’s northern suburbs in a family with Algerian and Cameroonian heritage, was criticised by RN party figures after he told Vanity Fair: “I know what it means and what consequences it can have for my country when people like them come to power.”

Le Pen told RTL radio at the time that she found it reassuring that Mbappé did not want her party to win, because his own strategy of leaving Paris Saint-Germain in order to win at Real Madrid had not worked. “Frankly I think football fans are free enough to know who to vote for without being influenced by Mbappé,” she said.

Julien Odoul, an RN MP and party spokesperson, said that Mbappé, as the captain of the French men’s team, must represent all of France including the millions of RN voters, and should not become a “political activist”.
Riner wrote on social media: “Being a high level sportsperson does not stop you keeping your feet on the ground and having an attentive eye on your country.”

He said he shared many French people’s concerns about the “current situation” in France – describing what he called rising anger, people struggling to make ends meet, plummeting respect for institutions, the fragility of the French education system and lack of perspective for young people.
Riner wrote: “I love France deeply – I’m defending its history, its talent, its heritage, its republican values and its diversity.”

articles.title: Fossil-fuel firms in line for billions in benefits after answering Trump’s donation call
articles.summary:
Senators’ report says taxpayers face higher bills after ‘bargain’ between president and major polluters

The fossil fuel industry secured an estimated $190bn in tax breaks and subsidies over…

blocks.text: The fossil fuel industry secured an estimated $190bn in tax breaks and subsidies over the next decade after responding to Donald Trump’s pre-election call for major campaign donations, leaving American taxpayers to shoulder higher bills and public health costs associated with pollution, according to a new report.

Released on Thursday by Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, ranking member of the Senate environment and public works committee, and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, the report details what the senators describe as the fossil fuel industry’s expansive influence over the Trump administration.

Pointing to Trump’s April 2024 fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago, Florida where he reportedly asked industry executives for $1bn in campaign contributions, in exchange for tax breaks and deregulations, the report said: “Big oil delivered in the hundreds of millions.”

The senators said: “The Trump administration has delivered right back, handing polluters benefits worth hundreds of billions of dollars. That bargain came at a price, and American families are the ones paying it: higher energy bills and higher costs associated with increased damages from climate change and air and water pollution.”
The senators also cited the Trump administration’s “near-total refusal to cooperate with legitimate congressional oversight”, saying it “complicated” their investigation.

The estimate of $190bn savings for industry is calculated from existing tax breaks and subsidies over the next 10 years plus new benefits delivered by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to an analysis by Senator Bernie Sanders for legislation he proposed with Congresswoman Ilhan Omar to eliminate “handouts” for industry.

In addition to an estimated $201m investment in Trump’s re-election campaign, industry executives contributed $19m to his inaugural fund, which the report described as “the largest political investment the industry has ever made”.

In exchange, the report said Trump appointed 26 senior officials – all of whom had previously worked for fossil fuel, chemical, or other polluting industries – across various government agencies including the Environmental Protection Agency, as well as the energy and interior departments.

The report also noted that the fossil-fuel industry secured various policies that would curb competition from clean energy, increase gas and coal consumption and “force Americans to spend at least $580bn in added fuel costs alone over the next three decades”.

As part of Trump’s “big, beautiful” domestic spending bill, signed last July, the government created a $1bn direct subsidy fund for fossil fuels, using the Defense Production Act authority to “funnel taxpayer money into propping up fossil fuel projects” considered economically risky by private capital markets.
The act also provides a permanent 20% business income deduction for oil and gas companies, which the report said would cost the government an estimated $737bn overall.

blocks.caption: Trump gives a pen to a coalminer after he signed an executive order supporting coal-fired power plants in February. Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The report further accuses the Trump administration of exempting companies from pollution controls, saying Trump “abused” the Clean Air Act by exempting more than 180 polluting facilities. The senators noted that “the rules at issue were designed to limit emissions of known neurotoxin and carcinogens”.
It also highlighted that the Trump administration repealed federal vehicle greenhouse gas standards and moved to roll back emissions rules for power plants and oil and gas facilities.

While the Trump administration estimated the changes would save Americans $1.3tn, the report cites an EPA estimate of $1.5tn in additional fuel, repair and maintenance costs for consumers. Separately, the EPA estimated that the repeal would result in at least $580bn in additional fuel costs over the next three decades. The report describes the policy as potentially the “single largest payback” the Trump administration has provided the fossil fuel industry.

Moreover, the report found that the Trump administration’s attacks on fossil fuel competitors include paying companies $1.8bn in taxpayer funds to cancel wind projects across the country. As of May, more than 160 projects – all proposed on private land – had been frozen.

According to the report, the stalled projects represent approximately 30 gigawatts of generating capacity, $54bn in capital investment, and enough electricity to power more than 8.5m homes. The report also pointed to Trump’s own pledge earlier this year: “My goal is to not let any windmill be built.”

The report said: “The buyouts follow the same structure: taxpayer money is used to buy off fossil fuel’s low-cost clean energy competition – a double hit, first to the public treasury, then to the electric rates.”

In the second Trump administration, environmental enforcement has also weakened. The report found that the justice department has brought 76% fewer civil environmental enforcement cases than during Joe Biden’s first year in office, and 81% fewer than during Trump’s first term.

Highlighting the impact of the fossil fuel industry’s influence on Trump and its consequences for the American public, the report stated that Trump’s “polluter-first agenda exposed Americans to price shocks on fossil fuels, heating, food production, and electricity; increased the cost of trucking food to grocery stores; and raised fertilizer prices for farmers”.

One modeling estimate cited in the report found that average household energy bills could be $78 to $192 higher per year by 2035. Industrial energy costs, meanwhile, are projected to rise by between $7bn and $11bn over the same period.

In response to the report, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told the Guardian: “These Democrat senators should do some self-reflection on their ties to the so-called ‘green’ energy industry. They wasted billions of American taxpayer dollars in the name of the Green New Scam.
“While they are focused on a useless partisan report, the Trump administration is actively working to pass historic permitting reform to help improve energy infrastructure and lower costs.”
The administration has hailed its “energy dominance” agenda as delivering for industry, energy workers and saving the US public money in energy costs.
The report, however, said the sharpest increases could ironically fall on Republican-led states that lack state-level policies supporting renewable energy development.

In addition to rising energy costs, the report pointed to the public health costs associated with Trump’s policies, noting that fossil fuel-related air pollution and climate-related harms cost approximately $820bn annually, or roughly $2,500 per person in additional health costs each year.
“Even if Americans do not suffer from polluter-driven heart or respiratory disease, they pay more as health insurance companies spread around those costs,” the report said.

Homeowner insurance costs are also rising as climate-driven disasters become more frequent and severe. The report noted that the average American homeowner now pays “about $2,948 per year in insurance premiums, nearly 12% higher than just one year ago”.

The report also found that in 2025, fossil fuel companies paid more to shareholders than the direct damages attributable to extreme weather in the US, despite surges in hurricanes, wildfires, floods, heatwaves and droughts.
Several environmental advocacy organizations have criticized the Trump administration in response to the report.

Climate Power spokesperson Alex Glass told the Guardian: “This report lays it out in black and white. The Trump administration isn’t setting energy policy; the fossil fuel industry is writing it for them. Fossil fuel money bought access, and fossil fuel executives got the keys to the agencies meant to regulate.”

Similarly, Mahyar Sorour, the director of beyond fossil fuels policy at the Sierra Club, said: “This report elevates a troubling reality: while fossil fuel companies throw money at politicians to fulfill polluters’ wishlists, American families are left paying for an energy system that puts corporate profits ahead of public health.
“It’s time to make polluters pay.”

Meanwhile, David Arkush, director of Public Citizen’s climate program, told the Guardian: “The campaign contributions to Donald Trump by big oil have paid dividends, and have allowed the fossil fuel industry to continue to pollute our communities … Every American family struggling with high costs is suffering because of the corrupt relationship between Donald Trump and the fossil fuel industry.”

Good morning.

blocks.text: Good morning. Donald Trump has welcomed Xi Jinping to the US, greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews at the start of his state visit. Xi’s trip coincides with the UN general assembly in New York, but he is not attending the gathering.

The pageantry will continue with a formal welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events. The White House has also invited major tech leaders to a state dinner being held for Xi.

items: What will the two leaders discuss? Amy Hawkins note in this explainer that topics are likely to include the development of AI technology, frosty trade relations and Taiwan.

What developments have there been in US-China relations? The US treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, announced that the US ⁠and ​China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called Busan ⁠agreement – a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies.

Who else has been invited to the US? The US has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the G20 meeting scheduled to take place in Miami in December, in what would be the Russian leader’s first attendance at such a summit since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.”

blocks.text: In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian described the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table. But he balanced that with a willingness to talk, saying: “We are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.”

Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the country’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, at the start of the US-Israeli war. He held up photographs of the ayatollah and some of the more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict. He also insisted that Tehran had never started a war.

articles.title: Reported assaults on Britain’s railways rise to nearly 25,000 a year
articles.summary: Unions say record high figures, including assaults on rail workers as well as members of public, show need for more staff and policing

blocks.text: The number of reported assaults on Britain’s railways has risen to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year.

Unions said the “horrendous” figures showed the need for more staff and policing, as the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) revealed a sharp increase in assaults on the travelling public and on railway staff last year.

There were 13,464 reported assaults against passengers and members of the public on the mainline railway in 2025-26, up 36% on the previous year and the highest number recorded by the ORR since it started tracking the figures in 2004.
Assaults on rail staff were up 12% in a year to 11,289 reported incidents, mainly verbal abuse but including nearly 2,500 physical assaults – an average of about seven every day.
The assaults on members of the public included startling rises in cases of harassment, up 52% year on year, and common assault, up by 30%.

The figures partly reflect increased reporting and zero-tolerance campaigns on public transport, but also underline concerns flagged by unions about the ongoing threats to frontline workers as well as passengers, and the availability of transport police.

The RMT general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said the numbers were horrendous but chimed with the union’s own surveys showing two-thirds of its members had experienced some form of violence at work in the past year.

He said: “We are calling for a significant increase in staffing across public transport, including an end to lone working. We also clearly need stronger legal protections for public transport workers against assaults at work.
“British Transport Police funding cuts have also been disastrous which has undermined a proper policing presence on all public transport.”
The chief inspector of railways, the ORR’s Richard Hines, said: “The increase in reported assaults is concerning. No one on the railway should be subjected to violence, threats or abuse.
“We’re working with industry and our trade union colleagues to address work-related violence and harassment, including through recent guidance which sets out what we expect from rail employers.

“This includes understanding where the risks are, putting effective controls in place, encouraging staff to report incidents and providing appropriate support afterwards. Our inspectors will continue to check how these risks are being managed.”

blocks.caption: The RMT is calling for increased rail staffing, including an end to lone working, and stronger legal protections for public transport workers.  Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

blocks.text: A spokesperson for Network Rail and train operators said: “Violence, abuse and intimidation directed at passengers or staff are completely unacceptable. The rail industry works closely with British Transport Police to investigate incidents, support victims and bring offenders to justice.”
after newsletter promotion
They said the numbers also reflected greater intelligence sharing, improved reporting processes, and more CCTV and body-worn cameras for frontline staff.

The ORR report noted that the headline numbers of reported assaults can include multiple counts in a single incident, for example for both harassment and common assault, while workforce assaults are now recorded even if no physical injury occurs. On the London Underground, where there is single counting, the number of assaults on the workforce fell slightly last year.

The chief executive of the Rail Safety and Standards Board, Mark Phillips, said the rail industry was taking action to better protect staff, but the figures “underline the need for a change in public behaviour and greater respect for the people who keep the railway running safely every day”.

Reports in recent years have highlighted that women and girls were at particular risk, while the growing number of assaults year on year since the pandemic has coincided with pressure on British Transport Police numbers.

The abuse and intimidation faced by frontline staff on the railways has also been seen in sectors including retail and in the NHS. The British Retail Consortium warned over “endemic” violence towards shop workers earlier this year, while the number of reports of violence against NHS staff by patients surpassed 100,000 in 2025.
The Department for Transport and British Transport Police were approached for comment.

articles.title: Boy, 11, shot in the face and neck in Sydney dies from his injuries
articles.summary:
The 11-year-old died at Westmead children’s hospital three days after incident at a unit in Norwest

  • Get our

blocks.text: A young boy who was allegedly shot at a home in Sydney’s north-west earlier this week has died.
Police said that the boy, who had been in a critical condition since being found with a gunshot wound at a unit in Norwest on Monday, died in hospital at about 8pm on Thursday.
Police had been called to the unit in Fairway Drive at about 5pm on Monday after reports of a shooting.
Officers found the 11-year-old boy had sustained a gunshot wound to his face and neck.
He was treated at the scene by NSW Ambulance paramedics before being taken to at Westmead Children’s hospital in a critical condition.
Five other people who were in the home at the time of the incident were not injured.
Three men, all aged 18, were arrested. Two were taken to The Hills police station and later released pending further inquiries.
One of the men, Isaac Bechara, was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence, while two of the other men were arrested and released pending further inquiries.
He appeared at Blacktown local court on Tuesday morning , where he made no application for bail, which was refused.
Det Supt Naomi Moore told reporters on Tuesday afternoon that police were “aware” of the unit where the shooting had occurred and had “engaged with the occupants previously”.

“This shooting at this stage does not appear to be linked directly to current conflicts however a number of individuals who were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW police,” she said. “Their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators.”
Police said the investigation was continuing.

articles.title: Tropical Storm Queenie expected to stay far from Philippine landmass
articles.summary: While Tropical Storm Queenie (Surigae) won't directly affect the Philippines, its trough or extension could trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms

blocks.text: QUEENIE. Satellite image of Tropical Storm Queenie (Surigae) as of September 24, 2026, 4 pm.
PAGASA
While Tropical Storm Queenie (Surigae) won't directly affect the Philippines, its trough or extension could trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms

MANILA, Philippines – Tropical Storm Queenie (Surigae) is expected to remain far from land and will not have a direct effect on any part of the Philippines, although its trough or extension is causing some rain in portions of the country.
The tropical storm had entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) at 7 am on Thursday, September 24. It is the country’s 17th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for September.
As of 4 pm, Queenie was located 1,205 kilometers east of Northern Luzon, moving northwest at 25 kilometers per hour (km/h).

So far, it still has maximum sustained winds of 75 km/h and gustiness of up to 90 km/h. But it may intensify into a severe tropical storm on Friday, September 25, and into a typhoon by Sunday, September 27.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) expects Queenie to generally move west northwest until Friday, before turning north northeast by Sunday. Its exit from PAR could happen by Monday morning or early afternoon, September 28.

While Queenie won’t directly affect the country, its trough or extension could trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms in Mindanao, the Negros Island Region, Aklan, Iloilo, Guimaras, and Siquijor, as well as isolated rain showers or thunderstorms in the rest of the Visayas and Bicol, on Thursday evening.
Strong to gale-force gusts may also hit Davao Oriental, Davao Occidental, and Sarangani in the next two days, still due to the trough of the tropical storm.
Other parts of the country have generally fair weather, with just localized thunderstorms.

The southwest monsoon or habagat is already winding down. The transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan could start within the next couple of weeks, according to PAGASA Weather Specialist John Manalo. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Czech PM Andrej Babis reiterates importance of NATO for his country but rejects calls to increase defense spending
articles.summary: The US and NATO want Czechia to spend more on defense. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis says Prague cannot afford faster increases, despite growing warnings about the threat from Russia.

image.caption: Babis announced on Monday that the Czech state will run a deficit of 386 billion crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion) next yearImage: Michaela Rihova/CTK/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Czech Republic "must remain committed to increasing defense spending," Matthew Whitaker, the US envoy to NATO, demanded in Prague last week. "We ⁠expect our allies to step up," he said.

The call is nothing new. As warnings about the threat emanating from Russia increase, and Washington demands European allies take greater responsibility for security, NATO has raised its target for defense spending from 2% to 3.5% of GDP, and pressure on those lagging is rising.

Czechia, alongside Slovenia and Albania, has yet to meet the old target. But Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, whose government cut the defense budget for 2026 to around 1.7% of GDP when it took office late last year, pushed back against the latest barb from Washington.

While reiterating that NATO membership is crucial for Czechia, the premier bluntly stated that the government cannot afford to accelerate spending. He has pledged to hit the 2% target in 2027 but plans no further increases.

blocks.caption: US Ambassador to NATO Matthew G. Whitaker (pictured here in Iowa earlier this month) has made the US position clear to Prague: Czechia 'must remain committed to increasing defense spending'Image: Tim Evans/REUTERS

blocks.text: That leaves the populist billionaire hoping that a personal rapport with US President Donald Trump will protect the country amid the burgeoning row.
Warnings of a growing threat
Whether Trump will protect Czechia from the threat of Russian hybrid warfare targeting Central European NATO allies is another question.
A growing wave of stray drones and Russian intelligence operations — suspected bombings, sabotage and cyber warfare — have spread alarm in the neighborhood.
Germany and Poland — key Czech partners — have reported high-profile incidents and linked them to attempts to intimidate Ukrainian allies.
Czechia should understand the threat better than most, having been among the first to experience such an attack.

Czechia's Security Information Service (BIS) reported in 2021 that the bombing of a depot storing weapons linked to Ukraine seven years previously had been carried out by Russia's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Security Service (FSB).
Babis, then in his first stint as PM, responded by expelling around 100 Russian diplomats and embassy staff, freezing relations with Moscow.
The BIS remains in step with other intelligence agencies across the region in warning that the threat from Russia is growing.
However, like its predecessors, the Babis government has failed to keep pace in terms of the national defense budget, even as neighbors have leapt into action.
Prague spent just 1.86% of GDP on defense last year; Poland and the Baltic States have already met the new NATO target and will hit 5% next year.
Prague's priorities
Babis has made it clear this approach will not change. However, his claim that Czechia can't afford to boost defense spending is at odds with the 2027 budget his government approved on September 22.
The fiscal plan will expand expenditure generously and targets Czechia's second-highest deficit ever at 386 billion Czech crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion).
While finally catching up to the old NATO target will account for some of that spending, most of the increased outlay will reflect the coalition government's domestic political priorities.

The plan clearly reflects the election campaign promises of Babis's ANO party and its junior partners, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) and radical-right Motorists for Themselves party. They all say defense can't be allowed to disrupt the urgent need to spend on pensions, education, healthcare and infrastructure.

"The claim that the country cannot spend more on defense is primarily rooted in domestic politics," Ales Michal, a political scientist at Prague's Charles University, told DW. "The major priority is investment in the social system."
That will be welcomed by supporters of the governing parties, who skew older and less well off, and resent the support being given to 300,000 or so Ukrainian refugees.
"None of the governing parties promised voters higher defense spending," in campaigning for last year's election, Michal notes.
Critics, however, say that's because the government is downplaying the threat from Russia. The government's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
'We don't want World War III'
The reticence to raise defense spending also reflects political narratives around the war in Ukraine.

Two days after Whitaker's rebuke, Babis appeared in a video dressed in a T-shirt emblazoned with the words "No War" in blue and yellow letters. While he noted the threat from Russia, he called for greater efforts to find peace.
"We don't want World War III, do we?" he pronounced, repeating his claim that Europe should work harder to end the conflict.
It was a performance echoing the stance of Europe's radical right-wing, and the sort that has seen the Czech PM labelled "pro-Russian" in some international media.

The truth is more mundane. Babis is a pragmatist. The ANO electorate is populist and anti-Ukrainian, but also strongly pro-Western. Surveys show that the plan to keep defense spending at 2% of GDP precisely matches its views.

Yet Babis's divisive personality leaves the party dependent on extremist partners for enough support to govern, and so he must also try to speak the anti-system, pro-Russian language of the SPD, which, despite controlling the defense ministry, was pushing to cut spending further in the 2027 budget.

"A critical stance towards Ukraine also shapes the government's position on spending," said Michal. The pro-peace stance downplaying Russia's aggression moves ANO "closer to the European radical right," he notes, but Babis is "guided by opinion polls," and must try to find a "balance between two polarizing positions."
Strategic understanding
The opposition sees this dichotomy as the government's Achilles' heel.

Martin Kupka, leader of the center-right Civic Democrats (ODS), welcomed Babis's reiterated NATO commitment before asking the PM: "When will you get rid of the Kremlin fifth column, which you took into the government and even entrusted with the Ministry of Defense?"
However, although the ODS-led government that held office between 2021 and 2025 offered fervent support to Ukraine, like all its predecessors, it also failed to meet the NATO spending target.

"Our partners may be unhappy about the approach to spending, but it's the reality of the political situation in our country," Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.
However, he added that while weak defense spending growth "is not optimal," the biggest issue is a lack of strategic understanding regarding the military's size and role.

articles.title: 'Pope fever' takes hold as Pope Leo visits France
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV is expected to draw large crowds during his visit to France. As part of his trip to Europe, he's also set to address the continent's future and some of the challenges ahead.

image.caption: Saint-Etienne Cathedral draped with a welcome banner for Pope Leo XIVImage: Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP

blocks.text: France is gripped by "Pope fever." Since the 1905 French law on separating church and state, the country has embraced secular traditions. But over the next few days, the streets will tell a different story.

From Friday, Pope Leo XIVwill spend four days in France, visiting the capital Paris, Lourdes and Metz. All his public events have been sold out for weeks. Organizers expect around one million people to fill the streets of Paris on Saturday for a massive open-air mass at the Place de la Concorde.

"The pope is popular among both believers and nonbelievers," political scientist Olivier Roy told DW. He added that Leo XIV's conflict with US President Donald Trump in particular had lent him "a moral standing that extends far beyond the Catholic Church."
Paris gears up for influx

And massive crowds are expected. Some 600,000 people who were able to get tickets will fill the entire Champs-Elysees, going right up to the Arc de Triomphe. Many more are expected to show up without tickets. Authorities have announced that a number of metro stations will be closed. Across the city, churches have been draped with large portraits of the pope and Vatican flags. Security forces are gearing up for a major challenge.

With France's presidential elections just over six months away, the visit comes at a delicate time. The left, Roy said, "appreciates Leo's personality but is skeptical about the state's involvement in organizing the reception."

Those on the far right, he continued, welcomed the visibility of Catholicism but had objected, for example, to an interfaith meeting planned in the eastern city of Metz, which they say places Islam on an equal footing with Christianity.
Because of the separation of church and state, the president will not be able to attend the large public masses.

blocks.caption: Pope Benedict XVI celebrated an open-air mass at the Invalides in ParisImage: Osservatore Romano/ansa/epa/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Leo's visit is likely to boost the pope's profile in the country, which last saw a papal state visit in 2008, when Benedict XVI (2005-2013) traveled to Paris and Lourdes, the world-famous pilgrimage site in the southwest of the country. He drew smaller crowds than those expected for Pope Leo.

Pope Francis (2013-2025) visited Strasbourg in 2014 and Ajaccio in Corsica in 2024 on one-day trips, and in 2023 he spent a night in the Mediterranean port city of Marseille. But each time, he came for a specific occasion rather than visiting the country as a whole. In his speeches to the European Parliament and Council of Europe in Strasbourg, he criticized the migration policies of what he described as an "aged and weary" Europe.
Roy described the contrasting perspectives of recent popes. John Paul II (1978-2005), he said, viewed Christianity as "primarily European," while Francis saw it as "more shaped by the Global South."

This, Roy argued, explained Francis' "certain disregard for Europe." Leo was likely to assume the middle ground, while extending his predecessor's message, Roy said: "He affirms the universality of the Catholic Church, while also recognizing Europe's weight within that universality."
Europe's key role for the pope

For Augsburg-based church historian and papal expert Jörg Ernesti, Europe has remained "the most important political point of reference for popes since the late 19th century," despite the growing internationalism of Catholicism Ernesti pointed to the demographic shift: In 1900, more than two-thirds of all Catholics lived in Europe, he said; today, the figure is only around 20%. This internationalization had also shaped the College of Cardinals, albeit with a time lag. "While Europeans have historically always made up the majority, they now account for just 39%."

During his four-day visit, Leo is scheduled to deliver 15 speeches and homilies. Most of those in Paris will be aimed at wider French society and its political leaders, while the large masses and events in Lourdes will focus primarily on France's Catholics.

blocks.caption: In April 2026, Pope Leo received French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife, Brigitte Macron, at the VaticanImage: Vatican Media/Catholic Press Photo/ipa-agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: The most keenly awaited speech is one scheduled for the final day in Metz, which French President Emmanuel Macron will introduce. It is titled "To the roots of Europe for peace and unity."
The choice of Metz itself is symbolic. Once a center of the Carolingian Empire, the city has changed language and allegiance several times over the centuries, at times being German, at others French.

Leo will be able to invoke the name behind the Robert Schuman Convention Center. Born in Luxembourg, Robert Schuman (1886-1963) was a French statesman who had inherited his father's German citizenship at birth. In the aftermath of World War II, he was an early advocate of Franco-German reconciliation. He pushed for a new, united Europe and in 1958 became the first president of the newly established European Parliament. After his death, he was buried in a small church in Scy-Chazelles, near Metz.

blocks.caption: Robert Schuman's tombstone in a church in his hometown Scy-ChazellesImage: Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP

blocks.text: For Pope Leo, Roy said, "Europe is a real entity that must be sustained and developed beyond nationalism." That, he said, "has always been the message of the Catholic Church since World War II. It is Schuman's message."

Roy will be watching closely to see whether, and how openly, Pope Leo criticizes populism and nationalism in his call to strengthen the EU and whether he will speak about a form of nationalist Catholicism found in France. He said that defenders of the traditional Latin Mass were not infrequently "identitarian nationalists or even close to far right circles."
Leo to meet abuse survivors

It is hard to imagine a papal trip without mention of the long-running issue of abuse. When Pope Benedict visited France in 2008, he did not take the chance to meet any survivors of sexual abuse in the French Catholic Church. His successors did, though the institution has been slow to confront its past amid a spate of new scandals.

blocks.caption: This grotto is at the heart of religious life in Lourdes. According to legend, the Virgin Mary appeared several times to a young woman in 1858Image: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: This time round, a meeting with survivors is on the pope's agenda in Lourdes. But something else has changed. During the pontificates of Benedict and Francis, those who met with them were usually not named. At times, it appeared that access to the Vatican came in exchange for silence. In France, the seven survivors who will meet Leo have spoken out together ahead of the meeting, with five of them also making their names public.

"Dialogue does not mean approval," they said. "Being received does not mean giving up our demands." The issue is likely to remain a thorny challenge for the Catholic Church — in France and elsewhere for a long time to come.

articles.title: Poland says fire at Starlink station is sabotage as Denmark warns of rising Russian threat
articles.summary: The satellite station is used in part to provide internet coverage to neighbouring Ukraine, the government says.

blocks.text: A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said.

Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the fire in the Masovian Voivodeship province was "deliberately designed to disable the station... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army".
He told Polish public broadcaster TVP Info an investigation was ongoing but "many indications suggest" the attack fits into a "new Russian doctrine of attack". The Kremlin has not commented.
Meanwhile, Denmark's intelligence service issued a new threat assessment saying it expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in the coming months.
It said an attack remained "highly unlikely" but warned of "a low but growing risk" that Russia could launch a limited military attack against Nato countries.
In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.
Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary - for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation.
Proxies are often used to carry out the attacks and Russia always denies involvement, despite growing evidence to the contrary.
The fire at the state-owned Polish satellite station broke out on Wednesday night in Wola Krobowska. It remains operational.
The deputy prime minister said it transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals.

Asked about the incident at a news conference with Bulgaria's leader on Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he disliked "labelling something as sabotage versus an accident without 100% certainty, but it looks bad".
On Wednesday Poland also said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing it to scramble fighter jets.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.

Earlier this month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said it was Europe speaking about preparing for war, adding: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.
In Ukraine, Kharkiv and Kyiv experienced the worst of Russia's attacks overnight into Thursday.
In Kharkiv, six people were killed and twelve others injured in a Russian strike on a farm in the village of Stara Hnylytsia, Ukraine's state emergency services said.
It said they were agricultural workers sorting vegetables, with the head of the Kharkiv region adding that four were women.
Russian aerial attacks on Ukraine have become more devastating in recent months because of their new jet-powered drones, which are harder to shoot down.
Kyiv is racing to develop low-cost weapons that can counter them as the missiles and fighter jets it has to fight them are too expensive.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, "we need ballistic interceptors to protect lives" and called on the US to help.

He said Putin needed to be stopped from continuing the war and "spreading this evil further", adding: "Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land."
He said Ukraine would seek to target the Russian energy sector over the winter.

The Ukrainian president's comments came as Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev headed to the US to meet Trump administration officials, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Reuters reported, citing two sources.
Russia's Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday there would be no pause in the war.

articles.title: ‘Going places with panache’: Max Mara channels audacious women for Milan show
articles.summary:
Chore jackets and loose-fit trousers nod to ‘nonconformist glamour’ of Amelia Earhart and other pioneers

The Max Mara catwalk at Milan fashion week had well-cut coats, sturdy block-heeled…

blocks.text: The Max Mara catwalk at Milan fashion week had well-cut coats, sturdy block-heeled boots, crisp white shirts and capacious suede handbags. What it quite deliberately did not have was shock value. “I hope everyone watching this show can recognise something of themselves in what they see,” said Ian Griffiths, the British designer who has been at this Italian house since 1987. “I think that’s really important. Without being critical of other brands or designers, so much of fashion alienates people and makes them feel that they aren’t good enough or thin enough or young enough to wear what’s being represented.”

blocks.caption: Every piece was designed to work with everything else, and to blend into an existing wardrobe. Composite: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty Images

blocks.text: Trousers were pleated and roomy, skirts long enough to be elegant but not long enough to trip you up. In shades of sand and chalk, grey and black, every piece was designed to work with everything else, and to blend into an existing wardrobe. The styling gestures – a popped collar here, a knotted belt there – stopped short of gimmick. The models could have walked off the runway and on to the Milan street – which, Griffiths said backstage, was the point. “The catwalk show is only the prelude to what to me is the real presentation, which is when I see women walking down the street in my clothes.”

Recently, even this most adult and sensible of brands has sometimes been unable to resist the temptation to chase the youth vote. This season, Max Mara went back to doing what it does best, which is fashion for grown-ups. (Nothing here for wearing in da club.) Griffiths said: “We were founded on the simple mantra of real clothes for real women, back in the 1960s, and when we stick to that idea, we never go wrong. So more than ever, I wanted to focus on real life chic.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Max Mara has gone back to doing what it does best, which is fashion for grown-ups. Composite: Giovanni Giannoni Credit WWD/Getty Images

blocks.text: The beauty of practical clothes is that they allow you to live an exciting life. On Griffiths’s moodboard for this season were portraits of aviators Amelia Earhart and Beryl Markham, explorer Freya Stark, wildlife photographer Osa Johnson and cross-continental driver Eva Dickson, audacious women of the 1930s and 1940s whose “nonconformist glamour” Griffiths wanted to channel for the modern wardrobe. Some models wore their hair swept up and away at the temples, a tousled take on the victory roll, but nothing looked twee or retro. Griffiths said: “I’m not suggesting for a minute that women fill the pockets of their organza cargo vests with notepads and compasses and explorer’s instruments. It’s the idea of getting up in the morning and going places with a certain amount of panache.”

Chore jackets, loose-fit trousers, cross-body bags and shirting are a modern uniform in cities all over the world. This collection was a glossy, Milanese take on how many women already dress. Overshirts, with four patch pockets, took the chore jacket principle and added a dash of safari-jacket exoticism. Stretchy halter tops were cinched with D-rings; while double-breasted silhouettes made for dashing blazers.

blocks.text: Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now likely unconstitutional, judge rules in restoring temporary access
Good morning and welcome to the US politics live blog.

We start now with breaking news from the late night hours: a federal judge has temporarily restored White House access to journalists from CNN, Politico and MS Now after president Donald Trump banned them due to their coverage of his administration.
US district judge Tim Kelly issued his order in a lawsuit that the news organizations filed ‌contesting the ban that the president announced ​on 18 September, saying it was ⁠likely unconstitutional.

Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and issued a temporary restraining order that will be in effect for 14 days. Such orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo pending a closer review of the case by the court.
In other news today:

items: US president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping meet in Washington for high-stakes talks that expect to cover their competing economies, trade, artificial intelligence and Taiwan.

Benjamin Netanyahu will speak at the UN general assembly today where he is expected to attack New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, a vocal critic of the Israeli prime minister who has repeatedly described him as a war criminal. You can follow live coverage of the Israeli prime minister’s address here.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 13m agoTrump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now likely unconstitutional, judge rules in restoring temporary access

blocks.text: Donald Trump has been raging about a story first reported by MS Now on Wednesday that he is seeking to rename the Ford Theatre in Washington DC, a site infamous for the assassination of president Abraham Lincoln, after himself.
Last night he posted on Truth Social about the news item, blaming “Dumocrats” for the “ridiculous lie.”
This morning, hours after the late night ruling from the judge that temporarily reinstated CNN, Politico, and MS Now, Trump (again) said:

double quotation markThe Dumocrats make up lie after lie. The new one is that I want Ford’s Theater named after me. That’s where Abraham Lincoln was assassinated. Who would want that? I don’t! It is FAKE NEWS started by MSDNC AND CNN.

This is his first mention of the day of his lesser-favored media outlets. He has not acknowledged the judge’s ruling to restore them access to the White House – yet. We’ll bring you more lines as they come in.
Some more background information on this ongoing situation between the Trump administration and the White House press correspondents:

The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration in federal court in Washington on Monday, saying the ban violated the US constitution’s first amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. They requested a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while their legal challenge plays out. Trump had said on social media that the three outlets “shouldn’t be ⁠able to constantly write or ​report ​FICTION and LIES,” ​and justice department lawyers ​had ‌sought to ​justify ​the ban on national security grounds. A Justice Department lawyer told the judge the Trump administration provided a sufficient explanation for the revocation of the ​press passes in letters sent to the news outlets ​on Tuesday. But the judge signaled skepticism of that argument, ​noting that the letters were sent after the revocation occurred and the lawsuit was filed. In a legal filing on Tuesday, the ​Justice Department argued that access to the ‌White House is a ​privilege, not an entitlement, and that the ​president has the authority to suspend access by news organizations.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas are both expected to address members of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) on Thursday, with the issue of the Middle East writ large on the day 3 agenda.

Netanyahu, who is increasingly unpopular at home and abroad, will not meet with US officials or Arab leaders during his stay. His office cited a "tight schedule" as the reason, listing as many as nine meetings during his visit, including with the presidents of Argentina and Bolivia, the vice president of Colombia and the prime minister of Papua New Guinea.

The increasingly isolated Israeli leader's Palestinian counterpart, President Mahmoud Abbas, will also address the General Assembly. Abbas, however, will do so via video, as the US State Department refused to issue him an entry visa.

The broader subjects of Gaza's future and Palestinian statehood will also be topics of discussion. The UK will convene a meeting on Gaza's current and future status, and Saudi Arabia and Norway will host a ministerial meeting to hash out plans for the implementation of the so-called "two-state solution."

articles.title: Police arrest far-right activist Daniel Thomas after ‘dinghy slashed in Channel’
articles.summary:
Thirty-seven-year-old in custody on suspicion of crimes including criminal damage with intent to endanger life

The far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been…

blocks.text: The far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been arrested on suspicion of “criminal damage with intent to endanger life”, after he filmed himself appearing to slash the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel, while a rescuer was onboard.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said a 37-year-old man, of no fixed abode, had been arrested after a boat that had an emergency responder onboard was damaged in the Channel. The man was arrested “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety”.

He was also suspected of committing “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals”. Police said he remained in custody on Thursday.

The force had earlier said that it was looking at footage livestreamed by Thomas, in which he can reportedly be seen using a knife to stab and slash an inflatable dinghy in the middle of the Channel after asylum seekers had been helped to safety, but with a French rescue worker who had just got onboard.

Thomas’s footage appeared to show him approaching one of dinghies, which was empty, shouting: “Let’s get rid of that boat.” After the rescue worker got onboard, Thomas shouted: “Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.” His footage shows his boat speeding away before the rescue worker climbed back on the larger boat.

Thomas, who goes by the name Danny Tommo, had spent the afternoon in a boat, filming himself as he tracked two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK. The livestreamed footage was watched by more than 200,000 people.

blocks.caption: Far-right activist Daniel Thomas in London this month. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images

blocks.text: A longtime associate of fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, Thomas this summer gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella anti-immigration movement Patriot Platform. The organisation was behind marches this month in Dover and Portsmouth, when masked men in black gathered and protested over immigration and asylum policy. Thomas repeatedly told his followers they should march silently, without violence and avoid doing anything that could lead to arrests.

Thomas apparently managed to film and upload footage of his own arrest before police were able to stop him. On Wednesday night a 56-second clip was uploaded to his YouTube platform showing a police officer telling him that he was being arrested on suspicion of criminal damage “recklessly endangering someone’s life”.
Thomas said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”

His arrest came amid renewed focus on the Home Office’s handling of small-boat arrivals in the UK, after there were two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days. Most small boats carrying asylum seekers across to the UK are escorted to shore by rescue services or Border Force vessels, and no unescorted small boats had been recorded since 6 September 2025.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, said: “You can’t stop everything all of the time”, after 21 people were detained when a boat evaded Border Force to reach the beach of Samphire Hoe in Dover on Wednesday. Another dinghy made an uncontrolled landing in Folkestone on Monday morning.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, describing the failure to intercept the two boats as “not acceptable”.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Powell said: “Of course, it’s a concern. That’s why the home secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable.”

articles.title: Global bond sell-off piles new pressure on UK borrowing costs before budget
articles.summary: Rising cost of 10-year gilt to near 19-year high hikes upfront cost of government investment and limits chancellor’s room for manoeuvre

blocks.text: A global sell-off in government bonds has put fresh upward pressure on UK borrowing costs, before a tough budget for John Healey next month.
The yield – effectively the interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds, known as gilts, had risen to 5.38% by mid-morning on Thursday, approaching the 19-year high set last week.

Higher interest rates raise the upfront cost of government investment and feed through into Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts of whether the chancellor is on course to meet Labour’s fiscal rules.

Analysts believe recent increases in yields have wiped out more than half of the £24bn “headroom” against the rules that the former chancellor Rachel Reeves had built up at the time of the spring statement in March.
Healey, her successor, has repeatedly promised to meet the rules with a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly lower than £24bn.

Rebuilding it to that level would be likely to require large tax increases or spending cuts; but Treasury sources insist the budget will be “focused”, with important spending decisions postponed to a review next year.
Investors across the main markets have been ditching bonds in recent weeks in a wave of selling prompted by fears of higher inflation and interest rates as the conflict in the Middle East rumbles on.

The Bank of England chief economist, Clare Lombardelli, said in a speech on Thursday that the longer oil prices remained elevated as a result of the war, the more likely it was that UK interest rates would have to rise.

“The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response,” she told an economic conference in Warsaw, Poland.
“On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.”
Higher rates would mean increased mortgage costs for homeowners, at a time when Andy Burnham’s government has promised to offer consumers a “breathing space” against the rising cost of living.
after newsletter promotion
The Bank is also expecting an eye-watering 24% rise in the quarterly energy price cap that determines household utility bills in January, if oil prices remain high.
Lombardelli’s message echoed that of the Bank governor, Andrew Bailey, after the nine-member monetary policy committee left interest rates on hold at 3.75% last week.

She stressed that high oil prices had had less impact on other prices across the economy than the Bank had feared; but the longer they remained high, the greater the risk of inflation becoming entrenched.
As the bond sell-off continued to worsen on Thursday, yields on 30-year US Treasury bonds surged to 5.444% – the highest level since 2004.

Alongside higher inflation, investors appear to be concerned about the risks of uncontrolled US government spending. Some analysts also suggest large-scale bond issuance by AI firms is undermining demand for treasuries.

articles.title: As the EU advances free trade with Southeast Asia, why is there no ASEAN-wide deal?
articles.summary: After years of arduous negotiations, the EU is closing on a string of bilateral trade deals with countries in Southeast Asia. And yet, a bloc-to-bloc agreement between the EU and ASEAN remains a…

image.caption: The Philippines is one of the many ASEAN countries pursuing closer ties with the EUImage: Ezra Acayan/AFP

blocks.text: The EU and several Southeast Asian nations are nearing the finish line on bilateral trade deals, and if the current deadlines hold, the European bloc will have agreements in place with six out of 11 ASEAN states by the middle of next year.

Free trade agreements with Singapore and Vietnam are already in force. Negotiations with Indonesia have concluded, and Jakarta aims to sign the agreement in October, with implementation targeted for early 2027.
Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US

Talks with Thailand, relaunched in 2023, have reached nine negotiating rounds, while Malaysia resumed negotiations in early 2025 after a 13-year pause. Both are expected to be finalized by the end of the year or early 2027.
Earlier this week, the EU and the Philippines announced that they had reached "substantial agreement" on their free trade agreement, putting it on course for formal conclusion in the coming months.
Trade up by more than half in single decade
Speaking to DW, Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, described EU engagement with ASEAN on trade and investment issues as "at an all-time high."
EU-Southeast Asia goods trade reached €274.9 billion ($313.7 billion) last year, up around 6% from the previous year and more than 50% from the €177.9 billion recorded in 2016, according to EU data.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is now the EU's third-largest goods trading partner outside Europe, behind only the United States and China.
The Philippines is chair of ASEAN — these are its goals

This week, Manila hosted both the ASEAN–EU Business Summit and the 22nd meeting of ASEAN economic ministers and the EU's trade commissioner. The two blocs pledged greater cooperation to protect themselves from rising geopolitical tensions, including unilateral trade actions and regional conflicts, that "collectively threaten the rules-based international order."
Why is Southeast Asia so important for Europe?

Brussels is expanding its network of trade agreements globally as it looks to expand to new markets and form more resilient supply chains. Southeast Asia, in turn, sits at the center of supply chains for semiconductors, electronics, electric vehicles and batteries, with investment pouring into data centers, renewable energy and digital services.
EU-Mercosur free trade deal: Who gains the most?
An article published this month by the International Monetary Fund said ASEAN's 11 economies already form a $4.5 trillion bloc, growing at more than 4.5% a year.
Such economic expansion, combined with multinational firms' efforts to diversify production beyond China, has made access to Southeast Asian markets more attractive for European companies.

Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW that geopolitical and geo-economic changes are also accelerating cooperation between the two regions.

US President Donald Trump's "protectionist and erratic trade policies" have acted as a crucial catalyst, he said, while the EU's strategy of "de-risking from China" and diversifying supply chains boosted Southeast Asia's strategic importance.

A stronger partnership with European nations also plays in favor of Southeast Asia governments, who have long tried to maintain broad economic relationships with competing powers rather than becoming excessively dependent on China, the United States or any other single partner.
EU companies push for an ASEAN-wide deal

The EU-ASEAN Business Council, said Humphrey, is calling for a region-to-region economic framework with a clear pathway to an eventual region-to-region free trade deal, "something European business has consistently called for."
"This would adopt a modular approach, perhaps starting with a region-to-region Digital Trade Agreement and an Investment Protection Agreement," Humphrey told DW.

The idea is not exactly new — the EU and ASEAN launched negotiations for a region-to-region agreement in 2007, but the talks bogged down over enormous differences between ASEAN economies and disagreements over the agreement's scope.
The talks were put on ice by mutual agreement in 2009, after which Brussels switched to negotiating bilateral deals with individual ASEAN members.

The main difficulty preservers to this day, as ASEAN includes Singapore, one of the world's wealthiest economies, alongside developing and least-developed members, making it difficult to agree on common commitments acceptable to Brussels.
"In addition, meeting the EU's high social, labor and environmental standards is difficult for the less-developed ASEAN members," said Gerstl.
Is the Commission ready to up the stakes?

Yet, even without an immediate prospect of a full region-to-region agreement, completing the current bilateral deals would give the EU preferential trade arrangements with most of ASEAN's largest economies and demonstrate that Southeast Asia has moved higher up Brussels' trade agenda.
For Humphrey, however, that should be the starting point rather than the endpoint. The concern, he said, is the European Commission might not be willing to move towards region-to-region agreements.

"With 2027 marking the 50th Anniversary of EU-ASEAN relations, we remain hopeful that the Commission will take this milestone seriously and ramp up work on a region-to-region economic architecture," he told DW.
"Failing to do so will only make ASEAN think that the EU does not take the region seriously."

articles.title: Tensions between India and Bangladesh are in focus after Dhaka skipped the BRICS summit in Delhi
articles.summary: Bangladesh's absence from the BRICS summit in New Delhi has raised fresh questions about strained ties. Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina's exile in India remains a major obstacle to normalizing relations.

image.caption: Bilateral ties have improved since Rahman took office but are still far from normalizedImage: Mahmud Hossain Opu/AP Photo/picture alliance; Patrick van Katwijk/ANP/picture alliance

blocks.text: When India hosted a BRICS leaders' summit in New Delhi earlier this month, a notable absentee was Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

The Indian government says Rahman received two invitations: one to attend a BRICS outreach session as the chair of a regional group of nations around the Bay of Bengal, known as BIMSTEC, and another for a bilateral visit to India.
Invitation or snub?
But in Dhaka, these invitations were viewed as a snub, as Rahman was not formally invited to the summit proper in his capacity as prime minister, but only as the chair of BIMSTEC.
This represents a departure from Bangladesh's previous prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, who was invited as premier to previous BRICS summit events, even though Bangladesh is not a member.
The case is the latest example of the frosty ties between the two South Asian neighbors that have developed since Hasina's ouster in 2024 following huge protests and a deadly crackdown.
Hasina fled to India, and last year was sentenced to death after being convicted in absentia of crimes against humanity over the response to the protests.
Bangladesh has called on India to extradite Hasina so that she can face justice.
Hasina has rejected the verdict, calling it politically motivated.

After her ouster in 2024, bilateral relations entered their worst period in years — visa services were curtailed as disputes mounted over her presence in India as well as the management of the border and alleged forced returns without due process of undocumented, mostly Muslim, Bengali-speaking migrants — known as "push-ins."
India forces Bengali-speaking Muslims into Bangladesh

Since Rahman's Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won February's election, that drift has partly reversed. India resumed tourist visas in June and appointed Dinesh Trivedi as its new high commissioner.
But while a bilateral summit is being discussed for November, Hasina's exile in India remains a major obstacle to normalizing relations.
Former Indian diplomat Ajay Bisaria told DW that Bangladesh had "missed a trick" by staying away.
"It was a chance to engage not just with India but with other global leaders," he said. "But the lost ground is easily recovered."
Has the India-Bangladesh relationship fundamentally changed?
Both sides, he added, would need to manage the "irritant" of Hasina's presence in India. A positive bilateral summit later this year could reset ties, he added.
Humayun Kabir, a former Bangladeshi diplomat, said the relationship is not what it was before Hasina fled to India.
"Ties were one-sided before the uprising, and Dhaka is now looking for something different," Kabir told DW. "There has to be dignity and equality."

Dhaka is willing to engage, but New Delhi must create a congenial atmosphere for a Rahman visit, Kabir said, including by keeping Hasina from making "provocative" remarks and acknowledging the court verdict against her.
Zafar Sobhan, a Bangladeshi political analyst, told DW that Bangladesh will now engage only on equal terms.

"It was hoped that with the exit of the (Mohammad) Yunus-led interim government, New Delhi could mend ties with the elected BNP government," he said. "However, both sides are held hostage by hardliners, giving them limited room for maneuver."
Sobhan said the best way for India to rebuild trust with authorities in Bangladesh is "not to allow Hasina to destabilize Bangladesh with provocative statements."
"Failure to rein her in is seen as an act of unfriendliness," Sobhan explained.
Others read Rahman not taking part in the BRICS summit more sharply.
Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, founder of the Mantraya Institute, called it "clearly a snub", even though Dhaka cited procedural problems with the invitation.

She said the episode must be viewed alongside the unresolved Hasina question, stalled talks on the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty — which is set to expire in December — and Bangladesh's deepening ties with China and Pakistan.

"The BNP is clearly on its way to diversifying its relations amid China's growing overtures and India's hard postures," D'Souza told DW, describing it not as a pivot away from India but a "recalibration toward hedging and greater autonomy."
Sreeradha Datta, a Bangladesh expert at the Jindal School of International Affairs in India, offers a more cautious take.
"India will always remain an important neighbour for Bangladesh," Datta told DW, "but India holds few advantages over Dhaka, and both sides understand that."
"It's too early to suggest the two neighbours have moved apart," she said. "Delhi and Dhaka seem measured in their overtures to each other."
The China factor

That caution matters because the China relationship is not new. Beijing has spent a decade building its economic and strategic presence in Bangladesh, spanning infrastructure, energy, trade and defence, since Dhaka joined the Belt and Road Initiative in 2016.
China is now Bangladesh's largest trading partner and a major defence supplier.

Beijing also pledged support for Bangladesh's long-delayed Teesta initiative, a major river-management and infrastructure project to control floods and improve water supply on the Teesta River, which flows between India and Bangladesh.
Despite years of talks, Bangladesh and India failed to sign a Teesta water-sharing treaty.
On his June visit to Beijing, his first overseas trip in office, Rahman leaned into that relationship, securing agreements on trade, investment, infrastructure and defence.

"It is normal for a mid-sized state like Bangladesh to seek relationships with Beijing and other nations," D'Souza said, warning that heavy-handed pressure from India could push Dhaka further that way.

D'Souza advises New Delhi to separate the bilateral agenda from the Hasina question, offer Rahman a concrete package on water, trade and connectivity, and hold firm red lines on any Chinese military presence near the Siliguri corridor and the Bay of Bengal.
Shahab Enam Khan, a Bangladeshi scholar of international relations, pushed back on the idea that improving ties is only in Dhaka's interests.
"If anyone should worry about this relationship, it is New Delhi," Khan told DW, citing India's trade surplus and its dependence on Bangladeshi goodwill for its own security.
India, he said, treated the 2024 uprising "as the loss of a client rather than a neighbour's political transition," pointing to suspended visas, closed land ports and shelter for Hasina.
"Bangladeshis took it as a message that Delhi's goodwill depended on who held power in Dhaka," Khan said.
Rebuilding trust, he said, means ending Hasina's party activity in Delhi, resolving bilateral disputes, and lifting post-2024 trade restrictions.
What India still holds

Geography still complicates any clean break. Bangladesh and India share a 4,096-kilometer (2,400-mile) border, the longest either country has. Bangladesh still depends on India for trade routes, transit, electricity, fuel, medical travel and regional connectivity. The two countries also share 54 rivers.
But those dependencies are also friction points.
The 1996 Ganga Water Sharing Treaty expires in December, the Teesta dispute remains unresolved, and alleged Indian push-ins of undocumented migrants across the border remain a sore point.
Bisaria sees some balancing of its ties between India and China as "natural."
"India can live with that, as it does with its other neighbours," he said.

The real question, then, may not be whether India is losing Bangladesh outright, but whether it is losing its old ability to shape the relationship on its own terms with an increasingly assertive Dhaka.
South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere

blocks.text: Here are some of the major headlines from India on Thursday, September 24:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
September 24, 2026
CJP targets Gyanesh Kumar over SIR, alleges voter deletions benefit BJP

Cockroach Janata Party founder Abhijeet Dipke has accused India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of undermining the country's democracy and alleged that the Election Commission's voter-roll revision is being used to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, Dipke called Kumar "the biggest threat to India's democracy" and demanded his resignation.
CJP said it would launch protests across the country ‌if ⁠India's ⁠chief election officer does not resign in 48 ​hours.
Kumar overruled fellow election commissioners' concerns

Dipke's accusations came after the Indian Express published an investigation that fellow Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data, the report said.
In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

Sandhu and Joshi, along with Kumar, are responsible for overseeing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). The process is meant to remove redundancies in India's electoral rolls, but the process is accused of having gone far beyond that remit and removed millions of legal voters.

According to the Election Commission, the revision was needed to remove the names of deceased individuals, those who have permanently moved and duplicate entries — as well as avoiding the "inclusion of the names of foreign illegal immigrants."

blocks.caption: In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was 'unauthorized and illegal' [FILE: March 15, 2026]Image: Ishant Chauhan/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Kumar's actions benefit BJP'
Dipke alleged that more than 130 million names have been struck off draft electoral rolls across 30 states and union territories during the SIR process.
Dipke alleged the removals from voter registries were intended to widen the BJP's electoral advantage as voter deletions had disproportionately affected opposition strongholds.
Dipke pointed out that during the 2024 election the difference in total votes between the ruling party and the opposition coalition was 2%.

"Deleting 130 million votes means deleting approximately 13 to 14 percent of the votes," Dipke said. "So, is Gyanesh Kumar intentionally deleting them so that the two-percent gap, where it appears that the BJP could lose, becomes larger, so that they never have to leave power?"

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi also alleged earlier that the SIR process benefits the BJP. The ruling party has dismissed such claims, arguing that those removed largely involve dead voters and illegal immigrants, thereby protecting India's democracy.

articles.title: Baste Duterte to be held in contempt? Not right away -- Win Gatchalian
articles.summary: While Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte can be held in contempt if he fails to show up at the impeachment trial of his sister Vice President Sara Duterte, Senate President Sherwin "Win"…

blocks.text: VP SARA IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 24, 2026 7:23pm

While Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte can be held in contempt if he fails to show up at the impeachment trial of his sister Vice President Sara Duterte, Senate President Sherwin "Win" Gatchalian said Thursday it would depend on the reason for his absence.

The mayor was subpoenaed after GenCorp Industries Inc.— a business declared by the Vice President in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth — was able to secure contracts amounting to P30 million with the Davao City government.

“May contempt powers kami. So kung hindi siya dadating, tingnan muna natin kung anong dahilan. We have to listen, we have to... Tingnan natin kung valid ba ‘yung kanilang dahilan. Tingnan natin kung mayroon ba talagang valid reason. So, papakinggan muna natin. Hindi naman kaagad iko-contempt,” Gatchalian said in an ambush interview.

(We have contempt powers. So if he does not come, we will see what his reason is. We have to listen, we have to… we will see if his reasons are valid. We will see if he has a valid reason. So we will listen first. We will not hold him in contempt immediately.)
Gatchalian said he has yet to receive word if Baste will appear before the proceedings.
When it comes to security should the mayor appear, Gatchalian said the Senate Office of the Sergeant-at-Arms has already maintained security and monitoring for the entire impeachment trial.

Other than appearing at the Senate, the impeachment court also ordered Baste to bring certified true copies of relevant official records from the Davao City Government from 2020 to the present, including contracts with GenCorp Industries, Inc., and any entity that owns or operates a Jollibee branch or establishment.
The mayor said in a previous statement that he was unaware of his sister’s links to Gencorp Industries, Inc. —RF, GMA News
