articles.title: Opportunities abound as Philippines to become aged society by 2028 -- CPD
articles.summary: The Philippines will be classified as an “aged society” by 2028, which will be accompanied by more potential opportunities for the country's development, the Commission on Population and Development…

blocks.text: Published September 24, 2026 5:02pm

The Philippines will be classified as an “aged society” by 2028, which will be accompanied by more potential opportunities for the country's development, the Commission on Population and Development (CPD) said Thursday.

Speaking at the 2026 World Contraception Day Forum in Pasig City, CPD Deputy Executive Director III Lolito Tacardon said the proportion of the working age population is steadily outpacing the non-working population.
As of 2024, 66.2% of the country's population was 15 to 65 years old, which is considered to be the working age group.
Meanwhile, Filipinos aged 0 to 14 years old are at 27.7% of the population, and those aged 65 and above were at 6.1%. The latter two age groups are the non-working population.

"And 6.1% of our older populations, we are getting close to the estimated period where the Philippines will be experiencing or be will considered as an aged society by 2028, because by UN (United Nations) definition, a country is considered to be an aging society if the proportion of its 65 years old and above, is at 7% already," Tacardon said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Tacardon said that 16 out of the 18 regions in the Philippines experienced slower population growth rates—with Bicol even having a negative population growth rate. The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) is the only region with an increasing population growth rate.
Window for development

According to Tacardon, there is a "time-bound opportunity" for the Philippines to use this period to advance socioeconomic development. The large working age population could help develop the country.

If the government is able to provide more employment opportunities, the working population could have better income and savings, Tacardon said. This older population could then still contribute to the economy later.

"This period is very tight because… by around 2050, 'yung working age population natin will start to decrease na rin, and ang tataas ay 'yung portion of older population naman," Tacardon said, citing data from the Philippine Statistics Authority.
(This period is very tight because… by around 2050, our working age population will also decrease and then the portion of the older population will increase.)
Quality of life

Tacardon said this is a good opportunity for people to focus more on improving the quality of their lives. For example, if a household already believed that they have enough children, they could invest in other opportunities such as education.

While family planning was initially used to control population growth, it is now a chance to help prepare people for having children. Tacardon said family planning still allowed people control over their reproductive right.

"Women have to make choices between having children and being part of the labor force. Hindi sila makapag-participate sa labor force kasi mayroon silang anak to take care of. Pero hindi ba puwede pagsabayin?" Tacardon said.

(Women have to make choices between having children and being part of the labor force. They could not participate in the labor force because they have a child to take care of. But can this not happen at the same time?)
"Family planning… regardless of their conditions, they should achieve their personal aspiration," Tacardon said in a mix of English and Filipino. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Clan leader in Paris sentenced to eight years over child pickpocketing gangs
articles.summary:
Roberto Hamidovic, 48, ran network of thieves who targeted tourists in Paris Métro and Disneyland

A clan leader who sent gangs of child pickpockets to target tourists in the Paris Métro and…

blocks.text: A clan leader who sent gangs of child pickpockets to target tourists in the Paris Métro and popular attractions such as Disneyland Paris has been jailed for human trafficking.

Roberto Hamidovic, 48, likened to Fagin, Charles Dickens’s notorious criminal boss, ran a network of child thieves, mostly girls, some as young as 10, who brought in an average of €25,000 (£21,500) a day, according to police.
If the terrorised youngsters failed to hand over enough money, they would be beaten, burned or sexually abused, the Paris court heard.

While Hamidovic, the patriarch of a Roma family of Bosnian origins, and the adult family members lived a “life of luxury” – enjoying designer clothes, five-star hotels, expensive restaurants and cars, and flashing their cash at casinos – the girls were put up in budget hotels or dilapidated squats.

Seven members of what detectives called the Hamidovic clan – four men and three women – were on trial for human trafficking, organised theft, corruption of minors, money laundering and criminal association as part of what detectives say is an international pickpocket network spanning several European countries. All denied the charges.

The court sentenced Hamidovic to the maximum eight years in prison and a €500,000 (£430,000) fine; his wife, Lejla, was given a six-year prison sentence and €300,000 fine. Two of the couple’s sons, a nephew and two female relatives were given between five- and seven-year prison sentences and fines. All were told they would be extradited and banned from entering France on their release.

For detectives who have been investigating the Hamidovic network for decades there was a grim sense of deja vu. In 2010, French police arrested Roberto Hamidovic’s uncle Fehmi, 58, who already had a conviction for people trafficking in Austria, along with his two sons near Rome and a dozen other clan members in the south of France and Italy. At the time, Paris’s judicial police chief, Christian Flaesch, said: “It feels like we have broken up a completely medieval structure.”

After Fehmi Hamidovic was convicted in 2013 and sentenced to seven years in prison, his nephew Roberto took control of the clan, believed to be responsible for up to 75% of thefts in the Paris Métro. In court, however, Roberto Hamidovic claimed he was a secondhand car dealer earning between €2,000 and €5,000 a month.

Alice Guillet, the public prosector, put forward a different story. She said the Hamidovic family used minors “to ensure a kind of impunity”. The pickpockets were told to tell police they were 12 years old – a year below the age of criminal responsibility in France – forcing police to release them. She described the girls’ daily lives as particularly “challenging and painful”.
They were “children without roots, without a future, whose parents sometimes don’t even know their birth date”, she added.

A pre-trial investigation by Le Monde revealed that Hamidovic’s son Roberto Hamidovic Jr, 22, nicknamed Gony, oversaw the pickpocket gangs on behalf of his father – booking taxis to transport them to various sites around Paris.

Investigators said groups of six to nine youngsters were sent each day at Disneyland Paris, Charles de Gaulle airport and the Métro and told to target foreign tourists. At Disneyland they would mingle with crowds gathered for the evening parades.
They would also hang around bank cash machines, wait for customers to put in their pin numbers, then surround them and steal the money and their wallets.
Hamidovic and his wife are believed to have amassed an estimated €2m, much of which is reportedly hidden abroad. The couple spent part of their time in the Adriatic seaside resort of Pula in Croatia.

His son, Roberto Jr, one of 13 siblings, grew up in Rome in the care of a grandmother and moved to France at the age of 14. Like his brothers and sisters he did not attend school regularly. Most family members are unable to read or write. He and his wife, Alessandra, have a three-year-old son called Al Capone who is being raised by a nanny in Bosnia, Le Monde reported. The paper said Hamidovic Jr told detectives he did not drink but they discovered he had spent €1,420 on two bottles of champagne at a Paris nightclub to celebrate his brother Goran’s release from prison.
Guillet described the network as a grim cycle. The exploited children sent out to steal became exploiters in turn when becoming adults.

“During this trial, the issue of determinism arose, an issue that is glaringly obvious from the very first line of the case file,” Guillet said, pointing out that the seven accused had themselves been forced to steal for their parents during their childhood.

“What chance did they have of not putting the younger children to work in turn as soon as they were old enough?” Guillet added. “The chances were slim, if not nonexistent. They went from being victims to perpetrators … we have to stop this defeatism and fatalism.”

Guillet said the only way to challenge the impunity with which the Hamidovics continued to operate through three generations, in defiance of previous convictions of family members, was to impose long prison sentences followed by extradition from France.
“In the face of such a system, the only tool is severity. This sends a message,” she said.

After the sentencing, Emperatriz Aguirre, Roberto Hamidovic’s lawyer, said: “The sentences are too severe because they relate to the crime of human trafficking for which there was no tangible evidence.”

Many of the dozens of children used as pickpockets, who were not called to give evidence in order to protect their identities, disappeared after the seven were arrested or were taken by social services and placed in foster homes. Almost half of them are believed to have since run away.

articles.title: Comedy festival packed Citadel Hill, but vendors say it didn't pay the bills
articles.summary: Some food truck operators who worked at the Great Outdoors Comedy Festival in Halifax are calling for a boycott of the festival, saying they're owed thousands of dollars for their work even though…

image.caption: Thousands of people packed the side of Citadel Hill in Halifax to watch comedians including Matt Rife at the Great Outdoors Comedy Festival last month. (Submitted by Paula Yeates)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

Some food truck operators who worked at the Great Outdoors Comedy Festival in Halifax are calling for a boycott of the festival, saying they're owed thousands of dollars for their work even though the organizers are already selling tickets for next year.
Three vendors tell CBC News they're owed more than a combined $60,000

Some food truck operators who worked at the Great Outdoors Comedy Festival in Halifax are calling for a boycott of the festival, saying they're owed thousands of dollars even as organizers are already selling tickets for next year.
Thousands of people packed Citadel Hill's Garrison Grounds from Aug. 6 to 9 to watch comedians including Matt Rife, Nikki Glaser and Fortune Feimster.
Trixstar, the production company behind the festival, hosts the same event in several cities across the country.

This was Michelle Kerfoot Bernava's fourth time working at the Halifax shows, which she said are usually a highlight of her summer. She drives her food truck, Mama K's, from Moncton, N.B., to take part.
But now she's one of three food truck owners who say they're owed a combined total of more than $60,000 — money they fear they will never see.
"Basically [the company] is saying don't contact us, we'll contact you when we have any information in regards to your account," Kerfoot Bernava said in an interview with CBC News.

In early September, Trixstar abruptly cancelled the festival in Mississauga, Ont., with just three days' notice, saying the decision was made after "careful consideration" and the event would be rescheduled.
Headliner John Mulaney confirmed in a Sept. 8 Facebook post that the decision came entirely from the producers.
The cancellation sent Kerfoot Bernava into a tailspin.

"Red flags went off to me. Something's not right, something's going on," said Kerfoot Bernava, whose truck operated inside the festival's VIP area, where meal costs were included in the admission price.

Rather than collecting payment directly from customers, she said her contract called for the festival to keep 30 per cent of her sales and issue her payment for the rest within a day of receiving an invoice.

Kerfoot Bernava tracked her sales, which were nearly $29,000 over four days. But she said when her money still hadn't arrived weeks later, she told Trixstar it was in breach of contract, and she's now demanding the full amount.
"That amount of money can absolutely wipe out a small business, beyond a doubt," she said.
"We are lucky that we're in our sixth season when this happened. I can truly say if this happened in our second season that we would not be open now."
CBC News made repeated attempts to reach the Great Outdoors Comedy Festival and Trixstar.
Jonathan Norman also drove from Moncton to participate in the festival for the first time.
He owns the Serious Smoke Food Truck, and parked in the concierge area where he says people paid $500 a ticket, which included food as well.

Because he was required to use the festival's point-of-sale system, Norman also collected no money from customers. Because of that, he doesn't know his exact bill, but estimates it's at least $14,000 before tips.
"We contemplated talking to a lawyer but then the lawyer gets paid and I don't see if we're going to be able to recoup much."
Norman said he made multiple attempts to reach the festival's finance department to no avail.
He said he received a call from his point of contact on Monday, but the employee offered no payment update — asking only that he cancel his interview with CBC News.

"There's been no reassurance whatsoever that we're even getting paid," he said. "They had record attendance on the Friday night that Matt Rife was there. They said it was over 22,000 people. They had our money. People had already paid for this stuff."
A third food truck owner, who did not want to be interviewed, told CBC News he's owed more than $19,000.
Because Citadel Hill is federal land managed by Parks Canada, Norman wants the agency to release the festival's insurance information so he can file a claim.
He also wants next year's event in the city to be cancelled pending payment of vendors and is calling on people to boycott to show their support for small businesses.
"If I went to a venue and was supposed to be paying a commission and didn't pay my commission, I wouldn't be allowed back the following year, that's pretty simple."

Parks Canada said in a statement that it's up to vendors to deal with the company directly. It said while dates for the 2027 festival have been announced, licensing discussions with Trixstar are ongoing.
When CBC reached out to the festival, some emails received automated replies, including one from Trixstar's finance department.

"Due to the volume of inquiries we are receiving, we cannot provide individual updates on account balances or payment timing," the email said. "If there is an update relevant to your account, we will contact you directly."
Calls to phone numbers, including one direct line to an employee, went to the same pre-recorded message with no option to leave a voicemail.
"We're either here helping another guest, untangling festival logistics, or keeping the inbox from becoming the opening act," it said.

Kerfoot Bernava and Norman are now accepting extra bookings this year. Both said they would typically be winding down their summer businesses, but instead need to work up until the Christmas holidays to make up for the losses.

articles.title: 4 years after Fiona, N.S. family lives in garage due to unresolved insurance claim
articles.summary: For nearly four years, Alma and James Doucette have lived in a garage on their Upper Malagash, N.S., property after post-tropical storm Fiona damaged their home in September 2022. The public adjuster…

image.caption: Alma and James Doucette of Upper Malagash, N.S., have spent nearly four years living in a garage on their property due to an outstanding home insurance claim for damage caused by post-tropical storm Fiona. (Richard Woodbury/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

For nearly four years, Alma and James Doucette have lived in a garage on their Upper Malagash, N.S., property after post-tropical storm Fiona damaged their home in September 2022. The public adjuster working on their case says he continues to work on unresolved Fiona claims.
'I shouldn't have to worry every day, 'Are the kids gonna get hurt?'' says Alma Doucette
Alma Doucette gets choked up when she thinks back to her routine of walking one of her grandchildren to the morning school bus stop.
Her granddaughter, who is on the autism spectrum, struggles deeply with change — and every walk to the bus stop in recent years was a reminder of that.

"She'd look at the old house and cry because she couldn't understand why, that she couldn't live in her house 'cause we've had her since birth and to see her like that, that really got to me," said Alma.

For nearly four years, the Doucettes have lived in a garage on their Upper Malagash, N.S., property after their home was damaged in September 2022 by post-tropical storm Fiona, one of the most powerful and destructive storms in Canadian history. The public adjuster working on their case says he continues to work on a number of unresolved Fiona claims.
The garage that Alma, her husband, James, and three of their grandchildren call home has interior plywood walls and a concrete floor.
"I shouldn't have to worry every day, 'Are the kids gonna get hurt?' because we don't have a proper home," said Alma.

Fiona caused the home's roof to leak and the basement to flood, and mould soon accumulated. Because of the damage, the home was torn down in 2024, and today only a patch of weeds remains where it once stood.

Because their home was uninhabitable after the storm and their insurer, Aviva Canada, covered rental housing for only about two months, the Doucettes say they felt they had no choice but to move into the garage.

items: It's been 3½ years since Fiona, but N.S. man still fighting insurer to get home fixed
Fiona fallout: Insurance dispute has kept N.S. single mom, son out of their home for 2½ years

blocks.text: James said the insurance company didn't dispatch anyone to undertake repairs, so he went up onto the roof of the house to install some tarps. When he was coming down, he fell, hurting his hand and wrist. He then went to a hospital for treatment.

"The doctor didn't worry about my hand stuff. He thought I had dementia because I was so messed up. I didn't know if I was coming or going and I was saying just weird things to him, so he sent me for a dementia test and it was just caused by stress," James said.
He used to have a business selling oysters, but between the economic fallout of the COVID-19 pandemic and stress from the insurance ordeal, he can no longer work.

The garage was formerly used for his business, so with nowhere to turn, the family moved in there. It initially didn't have electricity and they had to run extension cords from their house to power things.
Frustrated the matter wasn't getting resolved with Aviva Canada, the family turned to a public adjuster, Francis Martin of ClearClaim Adjusters, to help them.

Unlike an independent adjuster who represents insurers, public adjusters represent property owners. They are paid either a commission out of the insured's final settlement or based on an hourly rate plus expenses.

"It's one of the most heart-wrenching cases I've seen in my entire life … it's a family that are trying to do their best," said Martin. "They don't come from means. And after the loss, they were just sort of left on their own."
In a followup email, he said the Doucettes "were made to feel as though they didn't deserve respect and decency. The handling of the file had the same flavour."
Martin has worked in the insurance industry for 13 years and started his career with Aviva.
"That's why it breaks my heart even more," said Martin.
The matter is also going before the courts, with the family suing Aviva Canada in Nova Scotia Supreme Court.

To make ends meet, the Doucettes have had to sell many of their possessions, including fishing gear, a wood splitter and all-terrain vehicles, and assets like a 22-hectare woodlot. They even sold a dishwasher they had bought but never used.

Martin said the damage their home initially sustained could have been repaired if it had been dealt with right away. However, because of delays that he attributes to the insurer, the home became unfixable.

items: A property sale would have transformed their lives, but N.S. family got an epic shock instead
Nova Scotians seek answers on what flooding damage is covered by their insurance

blocks.text: "Mould sets in and starts eating away at the home and then the nails [in] the walls start to rust and everything just starts to collapse and eventually the home didn't sustain itself after a while," said Martin.

Aviva provided the family with some money, which they used to install a wood stove in the garage and set up sleeping quarters upstairs. They chose to spend the money on the garage because it would not have gone far enough to repair the main house.
In a statement, Aviva Canada said it understands having a claim can be a difficult and stressful experience, and that it strives to settle claims as fairly and quickly as possible.
It said it has a "small number" of Fiona-related claims that are unresolved as they go through legal proceedings.

"We're also committed to treating all customers fairly, professionally and with respect," the company said. "Our expectation is that all claim decisions and customer interactions are based on the facts of each claim and conducted in line with our customer service standards."
A new start
While the insurance dispute drags on, Martin has arranged for the family to purchase a lot and mobile home in Digby County so they can resume their life.
The family expects to move before the end of the month.

items: More stories from Northern Nova Scotia

blocks.text: Alma said she can't wait to leave Upper Malagash, where there are simply too many bad memories.
"I wanna give better for the kids," she said. "They deserve better than this."

articles.title: Kayla Sanchez denied Asian Games medal anew, takes 4th in 50m freestyle
articles.summary: Kayla Sanchez falls short of ending the Philippines’ 28-year wait for an Asian Games swimming medal, finishing fourth in the women’s 50m freestyle final

blocks.text: BEST BET. Swimmer Kayla Sanchez in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Kayla Sanchez falls short of ending the Philippines’ 28-year wait for an Asian Games swimming medal, finishing fourth in the women’s 50m freestyle final
MANILA, Philippines – An Asian Games medal remained elusive for Kayla Sanchez.
Sanchez once again fell short of a podium finish as she placed fourth in the women’s 50m freestyle final at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre in Japan on Thursday, September 24.
Logging 24.75 seconds, Sanchez narrowly missed the bronze medal by a 0.29 seconds, with China’s Cheng Yujie beating the Filipina for it with a time of 24.46 seconds.

China completed a 1-3 finish as Wu Qingfeng struck gold with a new Asian Games record of 23.98 seconds, preventing Hong Kong’s Siobhan Haughey from capturing a third freestyle title in this edition of the continental showpiece.
Haughey, who ruled the 100m and 200m events, settled for silver with 24.32 seconds.

The result denied Sanchez from becoming the first Filipino to win a swimming medal in the Asian Games since Raymond Papa bagged bronzes in the men’s 100m and 200m backstroke in the 1998 edition in Thailand.
It was a disappointing outcome for the Filipina-Canadian, considering that she skipped the women’s 100m backstroke on Wednesday, September 23, to preserve her energy for the 50m freestyle.
Sanchez also came oh so close to a medal in the women’s 100m freestyle, where she ended up fourth as well on Tuesday, September 22.

An Olympic silver and bronze medalist back when she still represented Canada, Sanchez led the Philippines’ campaign in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games in Thailand, where she emerged as the most bemedalled Filipino athlete with three golds and five silvers. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Australia says OpenAI agent hacked government website
articles.summary: Australia said on Thursday an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining ‌unauthorized access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a…

image.caption: Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Richard Marles gestures during a press conference after it was revealed an AI agent developed by OpenAI infiltrated an Australian government website in June, in Sydney, Australia, September 24, 2026. (Hollie Adams/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Australia said on Thursday an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining ‌unauthorized access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.
The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the U.S.

The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the United States, coming on top of several recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents that have alarmed governments and companies.

items: OpenAI flags 6 new examples of 'concerning' AI behaviour

blocks.text: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to the medical ​statistics portal of Medicare, Australia's universal health insurance program, while conducting research on public medical ​spending.

"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the ... network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable," Albanese told reporters on Wednesday in New York, where he is attending the UN General Assembly.
OpenAI CEO tells world leaders to help guide AI's future

Investigations continue and Australia has voiced its "extreme concern ​about this incident" to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Albanese said, adding that he was deeply disappointed by the company's delay ⁠in notifying the government. "It took until September ⁠10 before there was any notification at all," Albanese said, adding that the ‌investigation would also examine why government systems had failed to detect the breach in the first place.
He also warned that three other government health-related websites may have been impacted by the OpenAI agent's activity, but did not confirm that had occurred.
In a statement, OpenAI said its "review found no evidence of patient records being accessed."

items: AI researchers 'earnestly believe' it could kill all humans within the next decade, Anthropic employee says

blocks.text: It added that it "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted ⁠to look up answers ... our models took actions we did not intend."

The AI agent breach adds to tensions between Australia and the largest U.S.-owned technology companies. Canberra has already drawn criticism from social media firms and Washington after introducing a world-first ban on social media for children under 16 and new rules that force tech ‌firms to let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.
The Australian government has set up a task force to investigate the breach and check whether existing network security is adequate for preventing similar incidents.
'AI models attempted to look up answers'

The breach was announced the same day the world's leading AI companies warned the United Nations Security Council of the risks AI posed to humanity, appealing for governments ​to work together to manage the increasingly powerful technology.
Australia has faced a series of hacking attempts on corporations and government-linked firms over the past four years.

Defence Minister Richard Marles said the Medicare portal that was breached ⁠did not contain individual medical claims, benefit payments, personal banking details, or patient medical histories of Australia's 27 million people.
Instead, the website holds only aggregated data ⁠on healthcare use across the country, he said. However Australia considered the breach serious.
"There were blocks clearly which were coming back telling the AI agent 'no'. ⁠The AI ⁠agent found a way around those blocks — didn't accept ​no for an answer," Albanese told reporters.

items: B.C. government suing OpenAI for alleged role in Tumbler Ridge mass shooting

blocks.text: The incident is the latest of several recent incidents in which ChatGPT maker OpenAI has disclosed hacks or unauthorized activity ​involving its AI agents well after they ⁠occurred.
Rivals Anthropic, Google's Gemini, and Meta have also disclosed incidents of their agents accessing external systems.

Maurice Chiodo, an Australian mathematician who works at Cambridge University's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, said the breach appeared to be "a significant escalation in seriousness from similar incidents we have seen in recent months."

He added that while there was a lot of talk of new laws around AI, policymakers needed to first consider enforcing existing ones, like those that criminalize unauthorized intrusions into computer systems.

articles.title: CICC lifts Discord ban, asks NTC to restore access
articles.summary: CICC Executive Director Renato Paraiso confirms the lifting of the ban against Discord after direct talks with Discord management on steps to enchance cooperation between the two parties

blocks.text: CICC Executive Director Renato Paraiso confirms the lifting of the ban against Discord after direct talks with Discord management on steps to enchance cooperation between the two parties

MANILA, Philippines – The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) announced it had lifted a ban blocking social communications platform Discord from properly working in the Philippines and had asked the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) to start the process of helping to unblock Discord accordingly.

During a streamed press conference on Thursday, September 24, CICC Executive Director Renato Paraiso confirmed the ban against Discord had been lifted after the CICC — a unit of the Department of Information and Communications Technology — had direct talks with Discord management.

The CICC had on Tuesday, September 22 given Discord and social discussion forum Reddit 24 hours to establish a presence in the Philippines. The government sought to enhance cooperation with the two companies to make response times faster in the event of emergencies requiring content or user-account takedowns.

According to Paraiso, concrete steps were outlined to improve the service for Filipinos. This will apparently include a “green lane” so the Philippine government can raise concerns and coordinate with Discord representatives on possible content takedowns or actions against threat actors. This included developing streamlined processes to make investigation requests from government agencies faster as well.

Paraiso said, “We empathize with the public,” as Discord users of all stripes were unduly affected by the blocking, including legitimate users. He added, however, that the blockage was meant to allow the Philippines to stand up against the rise of nihilistic violent extremism and protect children’s welfare.
According to Paraiso, preventing further violent events and the grooming of vulnerable people towards violence was sufficient reason for their swift actions.

Asked about what drove the 24-hour timeline for Discord and Reddit to establish a Philippine presence, Paraiso considered the forward movement with Discord a win for Filipino children, the Philippines, and the related platform as regards online child safety. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Judge blocks Trump's White House media ban, orders access to be restored
articles.summary: A federal judge temporarily blocked U.S. President Donald Trump's move to ban three news outlets from the White House grounds, saying early Thursday that CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their…

image.caption: President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he arrives at the White House on Marine One, Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026, in Washington, after greeting China's President Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A federal judge temporarily blocked U.S. President Donald Trump's move to ban three news outlets from the White House grounds, saying early Thursday that CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their access restored.
The legal battle has unfolded just weeks ‌before the November 3 midterm elections

It's the latest development in an escalating showdown between Trump and media outlets whose coverage he dislikes. Trump announced he was banning the outlets Friday, assailing what he called "fake news," and later arguing that their reporting was a risk to national security. The outlets argued they were singled out because of the content of their coverage, calling ban a blatant First Amendment violation.

In an order, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly said the media outlets had met the legal thresholds to obtain a temporary restraining order, in effect for 14 days. He said they were likely to succeed in showing that their White House press passes were revoked without due process.

items: MS NOW, CNN and Politico sue Trump administration over White House ban

blocks.text: "This is a high bar, but Plaintiffs have met it," he wrote.

Kelly said the government must have clear standards for conduct that would lead to revoking a press pass. He called the standard of objectionable reporting outlined in letters that the White House sent the outlets days after banning their reporters "so vague it hardly does the trick."
Kelly — whom Trump nominated in 2017 and who ordered a CNN journalist's access restored in a similar case in 2018 — heard arguments Wednesday and ended the hearing without ruling.
Temporary restraining orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo pending a closer review of the case by the court.

"This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law," Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, said in an emailed statement. "We greatly appreciate the court's swift action."
3 U.S. media outlets sue Trump administration
The White House did not immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment.

In an emergency hearing Wednesday, Kelly said his decision must be guided by prior rulings in comparable First Amendment cases, even if the government disagrees with them. His decision noted that the White House argued that previous cases cited had been wrongly decided.
"Maybe," Kelly wrote, "but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop."

Kelly also rejected the White House's claim that revoking the press passes was necessary for national security, saying officials did little to back up that notion. "Nothing in the record... suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns," he wrote.
"The Court is skeptical ... that Defendants' interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes."
Did Trump just silence himself? | About That
In arguments Wednesday, attorneys debated access to White House and any risk to national security

Boutrous argued about the urgent need for a change, saying there had been irreparable harm to the outlets at a time of momentous news events. "We're at war. We have world leaders coming to Washington."
Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik had reiterated the administration's point that the president had the right to choose who gets into the White House.
"Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Velchik said.

In arguing that Trump was not engaging in viewpoint discrimination, Velchik said the president had criticized other news organizations even more harshly -- such as calling ABC "the worst" -- but hadn't banned them.
"The president should be able to take immediate action to protect national security," Velchik told the court.
In response, Boutrous said, "Suddenly it's a national security case," arguing that the president brought up that point only after the lawsuit was filed.
Trump "keeps proving our point," Boutrous said, describing how the president has consistently used negative coverage of him as justification for the ban.

articles.title: Bill extending terms of barangay, SK officials sent to Malacañang
articles.summary: The bill extending the term of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials from four to five years is now up for the president's signature, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Thursday,…

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 4:43pm
President Marcos delivers a speech before departing for Cambodia for a State Visit, following the invitation of His Majesty King Norodom Sihamoni on Sept. 7, 2025.
Presidential Communications Office via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The bill extending the term of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials from four to five years is now up for the president's signature, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Thursday, September 4.
The bill is an amendment of Republic Act 12232 and reschedules the upcoming November 2026 polls to 2028.

"Pinadala na namin kay presidente, and sa pagkaalam ko walang balita na i-veto niya," Gatchalian told reporters on Sept. 24. (We've sent it to the president, and as far as I know, there's no word that he'll veto it.)
Senate Bill 2387 postpones the polls to November 2028 and schedules elections every five years after that.
The Senate approved the bill on September 14 by a 13-5 vote. The House adopted the Senate version on September 16, skipping the bicameral conference committee.
On Wednesday, Marcos said the bill had not yet reached his office and that he had not decided whether to postpone the polls.
In the meantime, the Commission on Elections has continued with the preparations for the polls. Filing of certificates of candidacy will start September 28.
If signed, the bill would be the second postponement in two years.
In August 2025, Marcos signed Republic Act 12232, which moved the elections from December 2025 to November 2026.
The last Barangay and SK polls were held in October 2023.
The president has 30 days from receiving a bill to sign or veto it. No action means the bill will lapse into law.

articles.title: Morocco: Center-right PAM leads in parliamentary election
articles.summary: PAM is part of Morocco's outgoing ruling coalition and was founded by an adviser to the king. The moderate Islamist Justice and Development Party surged amid increasing voter apathy.

image.caption: The PAM party gained 10 seats, according to provisional results, while its two coalition partners suffered lossesImage: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP

blocks.text: Morocco's center-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) took first place in Wednesday's parliamentary election, according to provisional results.
PAM is part of Morocco's outgoing ruling coalition.
The party won 97 out of 395 seats in parliament, 10 seats more than in 2021.
It was founded in 2008 by an adviser to the king and advocates social modernization and moderate secularist views. It is largely seen as close to the Moroccan monarchy.
The next coalition government will oversee preparations for the 2030 World Cup.

The vote is not expected to fundamentally alter the balance of power in the North African kingdom. As the country is a semi-constitutional monarchy, Morocco's King Mohammed VI retains substantial powers in both policy direction and foreign affairs.
How did other parties fare in Morocco's election?
The National Rally of Independents (RNI), the senior partner in the outgoing coalition, dropped from 102 to 66 seats, putting it at second place.
The smallest member of the governing coalition, the right-wing Istiqlal party also saw losses, taking 65 seats, 16 fewer than in 2021.
The moderate Islamist opposition Justice and Development Party surged to 54 seats, compared to just 13 in 2021.
Moroccans head to the polls amid rising voter apathy
Election marked by increasing voter apathy
The election saw turnout of 38%, marking the lowest level since 2007. Nearly 16 million people were registered to vote.
Only around 4% of registered voters were aged 18 to 24.
In 2025, Morocco was rocked by Gen Z-led protests, which were the largest in the country since the Arab Spring in the early 2010s.
Mistrust in politicians and issues regarding living conditions were widely blamed for the low turnout.
"I'm not going to vote because I have lost all faith in the political class," 50-year-old Majda Bakatir told the AFP news agency.
"We want our country to move forward, but politicians do not seem to care about our problems regarding healthcare, education, and purchasing power," she said.

articles.title: NBI arrests individual linked to South Cotabato school shooting
articles.summary: The NBI is seeking a P1 billion confidential funds for the procurement of tools and equipment that Matibag said should be considered as the agency’s “trade secret” in its efforts to…

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 4:40pm

Teachers raised the Philippine flag at half-mast at Banga National High School in Banga, South Cotabato, to express sympathy for the three students who died in a shooting incident on the school campus on Sept. 18, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) claimed on Thursday, September 24 that it had arrested an individual allegedly linked to the school shooting incident in South Cotabato.

During the Senate budget hearing of the Department of Justice (DOJ) and its attached agencies, NBI Director Melvin Matibag reported that they nabbed the individual in an operation on Wednesday, September 23.
“Yesterday we’re able to get hold of one of the individuals who is somehow related to what happened in South Cotabato,” Matibag said in mixed English and Filipino.
Matibag did not disclose other details regarding the arrest, but added that they also apprehended one suspected online groomer from Cebu.
“With the help of the NPS (National Prosecution Service) and DOJ (Department of Justice), we will be processing it today,” Matibag said.

Three students died and eight others were wounded in the school shooting incident in South Cotabato on September 18. Among the fatalities is the 16-year-old Grade 9 student who used his father’s handgun in the act.

Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Jonvic Remulla earlier said on Wednesday that authorities were already pursuing an individual who allegedly encouraged the shooter to commit violence.
According to Remulla, the suspected individual is telling students that their act of violence will be recognized and glorified.
Meanwhile, Matibag said going after the suspects who influence young people into nihilistic violent extremism (NVE) would be faster with the use of certain cybersecurity tools

The NBI is seeking P1 billion confidential funds for the procurement of tools and equipment that Matibag said should be considered as the agency’s “trade secret” in its efforts to resolve cybercrimes.

“Nand’yan naman po ‘yung tools na ‘yan. Ang sa akin lang po, it should not go to the ordinary procurement, because that is something that is somehow like a trade secret for law enforcement,” Matibag said.
(The tools are there. Just in my opinion, it should not go to the ordinary procurement, because that is something that is somehow like a trade secret for law enforcement.)

articles.title: ‘We shouldn't have to beg,’ says chief of First Nation facing decades of mercury poisoning in Ontario
articles.summary: Grassy Narrows First Nation and Wabaseemoong Independent Nations continue to seek justice from the provincial and federal governments over decades of mercury poisoning caused by contamination that…

image.caption: Thousands of people took to the streets of downtown Toronto on Wednesday for a River Run Rally led by Grassy Narrows First Nation and Wabaseemoong Independent Nations. They're demanding that the province and Ottawa address mercury poisoning dating back to the 1960s and '70s, when the Dryden Paper Mi

blocks.text: Thunder Bay

Grassy Narrows First Nation and Wabaseemoong Independent Nations continue to seek justice from the provincial and federal governments over decades of mercury poisoning caused by contamination that dates back to the 1960s and '70s. The First Nations' River Run Rally drew about 9,000 people to downtown Toronto on Wednesday. Here's what they want to see happen.
Grassy Narrows chief among 9,000 in rally at Queen's Park in Toronto to demand justice
Chrissy Isaacs says she physically struggles to open a water bottle some days, one of her many symptoms due to mercury poisoning.

The grandmother from Grassy Narrows First Nation (traditionally known as Asubpeeschoseewagong Netum Anishinabek) was among about 9,000 people who marched to Queen’s Park in Toronto on Wednesday, part of her community's River Run Rally to demand justice from the provincial and federal governments.

Mercury contamination in Grassy Narrows dates back to the 1960s and '70s, when the Dryden Paper Mill in northwestern Ontario dumped about nine tonnes of the toxin into the English-Wabigoon River System.

Since then, members of Grassy Narrows and Wabaseemoong Independent Nations have lived with health effects such as tremors, insomnia, memory loss, neuromuscular effects, headaches, and cognitive and motor dysfunction.
About 90 per cent of Grassy Narrows’s population has been affected.
Mercury in the community is mainly transmitted by consuming river fish, but it can also be passed on during pregnancy.

“Our people were river people, and our main food source was from the river and our livelihood was from the river,” Isaacs told CBC News ahead of Wednesday’s rally. “That was robbed from me from birth. I never got that chance to actually be able to really live that part of my life.”
LISTEN | River Run Rally calls for government action on mercury poisoning in the north:
8:48River Run Rally calls for action from government on mercury poisoning in the North
The First Nations are calling for the river system to be cleaned up, for all affected community members to receive compensation and for the Dryden Paper Mill to be shut down.
“We're losing our people so quickly, both communities,” said Grassy Narrows First Nation Chief Sherry Ackabee. “We shouldn't have to beg for this.”

items: First Nation demands Carney apology amid 60-year mercury crisis
Grassy Narrows residents demand Carney apologize for comments made about protest

blocks.text: Dryden Fibre Canada, owner of the paper mill, said the company “takes its responsibilities to the natural environment and greater community seriously.”

“We operate in a highly regulated sector with strict health and environmental standards; the Dryden Mill is compliant with all provincial and federal regulatory requirements and permits,” said an emailed statement sent to CBC News on Tuesday,
Ministry involved in river remediation process
The Ontario government under the then Liberal premier, Kathleen Wynne, announced $85 million in 2017 to support the river system's remediation.
Gary Wheeler, a spokesperson for the province’s Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks, provided an emailed statement on Monday about the status of the cleanup.
“Mercury contamination in the English and Wabigoon Rivers is a complex issue that requires detailed scientific work to determine options for remediation,” Wheeler wrote.

“The ministry is leading the next phase of the remediation process, which includes procuring a remediation firm to develop technically feasible remediation options, high-level costing, timelines and the development of a long-term monitoring plan.”

items: First Nations step up efforts to have Dryden, Ont., paper mill shut down over mercury contamination
He spent his career documenting collective trauma. Grassy Narrows was one of his toughest cases

blocks.text: A study released in May 2024 by Western University in London, Ont., suggests that the river system's contamination is getting worse due to industrial pollution.
It found that discharge of wastewater from the Dryden Paper Mill, combined with existing mercury, has created high levels of methylmercury — an even more toxic compound.
Paper mill accused of having 'no empathy'
Adrian Keejick, a drummer from Grassy Narrows who participated in Wednesday's march, told CBC Radio-Canada that it was important for him to stand in solidarity with his people.
“Many people have passed [away] and people have a lot of physical effects because of mercury,” Keejick said.
He feels the Dryden Paper Mill “has no empathy, no sympathy — just pure gain and profit, right?”
In a statement Wednesday, Glenn Cameron, a Wabaseemoong Independent Nations band councillor, said “the fact that we are still having this fight is obviously because of racism.”
“If you had any other two communities being poisoned like us in Canada, they would have already had the poison cleaned and the communities would have been compensated for all of the harm.”
CBC News reached out to Indigenous Services Canada for comment and will update the story with any response.
Mercury Care Home may open in November 2027

A Mercury Care Home that will provide in-patient services for 22 people and outpatient services for all affected community members was first promised in 2017 and delayed for several years. But Ackabee said it's expected to be completed by November 2027.
Grassy Narrows First Nation gets mercury poisoning treatment centre
The federal government said it's spending $82 million on the construction of the 6,500-square-foot home and $68.9 million on a community trust to support ongoing operations.
That means elders currently receiving care outside the First Nation can finally return home, said Ackabee.
“I can't wait for that day. We've lost quite a few [people] along the way waiting, and [the poisoning] should have stopped many, many years ago.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sarah Law is a CBC News reporter based in Thunder Bay, Ont., and has also worked for newspapers and online publications elsewhere in the province. Have a story tip? You can reach her at sarah.law@cbc.ca.
With files from Lounan Charpentier and Kirthana Sasitharan

articles.title: Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket
articles.summary: Explosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakers

blocks.text: Sales of Chinese hybrid cars have rocketed in the EU in the past four and a half years, new data shows, underlining growing concerns in Brussels over the future of the European car industry.

In 2022, just 659 Chinese-made fully hybrid cars (vehicles in which the petrol or diesel engine charge the motor and battery) were sold in the EU. However, after Brussels imposed anti-subsidy tariffs on fully electric cars from China in 2024, sales of hybrids have shot up to 160,662 in the first seven months of this year.

Eurostat figures show that sales of Chinese-made plug-in hybrid vehicles – models popular for longer driving distances which can recharge via both the fuel engine and an external power source – have also soared, rising from 56,706 sold in 2022 to 217,764 from January to July this year.

The volume of Chinese hybrids on the roads is now spooking the car industry and Brussels, which has asked China to voluntarily reduce its hybrid exports to the EU or face safeguards, likely to be quotas.

According to new figures released by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), hybrid cars now account for almost 37% of the overall market, with electric cars making up just over 21% of the market.
ACEA figures showed three Chinese manufacturers – BYD, Chery, and Leapmotor – making significant inroads with triple-digit growth in the EU.

A fourth firm, Geely, has had a steady 8% increase in the first eight months of the year, and remains the most popular Chinese brand in the EU with 205,000 cars sold in the first eight months of the year. Its brands include Sweden’s Volvo and Polestar, the EU’s only all-electric car manufacturer.
BYD is catching up with Geely with sales year-on-year rocketing 163% with 177,000 units sold.
Both firms, along with a fifth Chinese manufacturer, SAIC, are now firmly ahead of Elon Musk’s Tesla which sold 142,000 cars across the bloc in the first seven months of the year.
European car manufacturers still dominate with the Volkswagen group selling 2m cars in the first eight months of the year.

Sales of electric cars are also growing fast in parts of Europe including Germany, up 75% to 69,000 units in August, and in France, where sales are up by 112%. In Slovenia sales have increased by 266%. This compares with the UK, up 27% in August to 28,000 EVs sold and Ireland up just 7% to 2,200 units.

Earlier this month, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, described the now €1.18bn-a-day trade deficit between the bloc and China as having reached an unsustainable “tipping point”.
after newsletter promotion
The EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao will meet on 8 and 9 October to try to build a truce.
Also hoping for a trade truce are Donald Trump and Xi Jinping who meet in their third summit in 12 months in Washington on Thursday.

Trump agreed in South Korea last October to drop tariffs on certain Chinese imports in exchange for a suspension of China’s export restriction on rare earths, critical to the car industry across the US, EU and the UK.
Some believe a deal may not have been reached yet and the suspension may not be announced until the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference next month.

articles.title: Panelo: Excluding absent senators from impeachment vote violates Constitution
articles.summary: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte said Thursday the Senate impeachment court violated the Constitution when it voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict on the number of senators who are…

blocks.text: Published September 24, 2026 4:33pm

The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte said Thursday that the Senate impeachment court violated the Constitution when it voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."

“This is a clear violation of our Constitution because the Constitution states two-thirds of all members of the Senate are needed for conviction. They changed this yesterday,” Atty. Paolo Panelo said during an Unang Balita interview.
He further said it is not within the power of the Senate to make the change "so this is grave abuse of discretion."
“While the impeachment court is sui generis (a class of its own), it should still follow due process and the Constitution. It was clear to us the ruling did not follow the Constitution,” he added.
Panelo, however, could not say for sure if the Vice President’s camp will raise the issue before the Supreme Court.
Article 11, Section 6 of the Constitution states that “the Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment.”

The same provision also states that “No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate”, although it does not state a specific number for what constitutes two-thirds.
In a separate press conference, House prosecutor Terry Ridon of Bicol Saro party-list said the defense or those who disagree with the new threshold are free to go to the Supreme Court.
“If they think they have a case, they are free to go to the Supreme Court. We will wait for that petition and whatever the Supreme Court decides, we will abide by that,” he said.
Ridon, however, also said critics are free to lick their wounds over the decision of the Senate impeachment court on the threshold.
“Sa mga nagsasabi po na this is manipulated at kung ano ano pa ‘yung mga sinasabi nila, may tissue rito, punasan ninyo ang luha ninyo,” Ridon added.

The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."
Excluded members are those:

items: detained and/or suspended or otherwise legally restrained from exercising the functions of a senator,
persons sought by authorities and whose whereabouts are unknown,
suffering from a physical or medical incapacity,
beyond the coercive processes of the Senate, and
others similarly situated.

articles.title: Out on bail pending appeal, convicted businessman accused of new $17.5K scam
articles.summary: An Ontario woman says she was offered a financial lifeline after being duped by a controversial HVAC company — only for the proposed solution to sink her further into debt.

image.caption: Marcy Barbaro says she sent Raymond Kalonga a total of $17,500 in 2025 to free herself from a loan. (CBC News Graphics)

blocks.text: An Ontario woman says she was offered a financial lifeline after being duped by a controversial HVAC company — only for the proposed solution to sink her further into debt.

Marcy Barbaro has since learned troubling details about the man who she says promised to negotiate a way out of her costly contract: he did so while out on bail, awaiting appeal for his own alleged misdeeds in the industry.
Barbaro, of Midland, Ont., says she sent Raymond Kalonga — or as she knew him, “Ray Stephens” — $17,500.
“I do not understand how someone can be so duplicitous,” Barbaro said.

The latest development comes two years after Kalonga, 38, left a trail of unhappy customers and creditors in his wake during his time in St. John’s, where he operated his own company, Atlantic Standard HVAC.
He ran that business in Newfoundland while facing trouble in the courts in Ontario for his handling of a previous door-to-door sales company there.
Kalonga is currently out on bail while appealing a 525-day jail sentence and half-a-million dollar fine levied under Ontario consumer protection laws.
In that case, Kalonga claims he didn’t instruct his legal counsel to enter guilty pleas when they did, which he says nullifies the conviction and sentence.
Met on Facebook group for HVAC customers
Before connecting with Kalonga, Barbaro ran into problems with an unrelated company.

Customers of Provincial Smart Home Services say that company convinced them to buy expensive HVAC systems and other equipment they didn't need, by promising government rebates that never came and savings on energy bills that never materialized.

items: HVAC scams are still happening. Why is the government failing to act?
Watchdog: Investigating questionable HVAC contracts; how to buy Canadian

blocks.text: Barbaro was one of those customers, staring down a more than $27,000 bill.
Then, in early 2025, a saving grace.

Barbaro says a man named Ray Stephens began posting on a Facebook group for customers of Provincial Smart Home Services, saying his company had two decades of experience in the industry and could help them.
Barbaro says Kalonga — a.k.a. Stephens — offered to negotiate a buyout at half the cost, touting his experience and connections in the industry, and explaining how scammers work the system.
“He knows these contracts, he knows these scammers, and he may be able to offer a way out,” Barbaro told CBC News.
“He immediately sympathized with me. He explained to me how these scams worked.”

The two communicated through WhatsApp for months, often about their own lives and ambitions. Kalonga spoke of his deep faith, quoting scripture and espousing inspirational sentiments. Barbaro says they were becoming friends.
Barbaro provided the text, audio, and video messages to CBC News.
In those messages, Kalonga expressed distaste at Provincial Smart Home Services, calling it “more than just fraud. It is manipulation and physiological abuse.”
Barbaro says his apparent candidness about the industry helped build trust.

“I told you before, the finance companies honestly play this game where if they think [they] can strong arm an older person, unintelligent person or immigrant they do,” Kalonga wrote in a message to Barbaro in February 2025.
Messages show Kalonga offered to negotiate a buyout at a reduced rate for Barbaro — for a fee of $5,000.
An invoice and credit card statement provided by Barbaro show she paid one of Kalonga’s companies $2,500 on Feb. 11, 2025, for a loan consultation with a 30-day guarantee.
Thirty days came and went — without progress, she says.
Kalonga told Barbaro to be patient.
“You can see why I wanted to move forward with it,” Barbaro said.
“He'd already done me favours, he'd already taken time to explain to me how the contracts work, explained who the major players were … He was available at my beck and call through WhatsApp chat.”

Two months later, Barbaro sent $12,500 to another of Kalonga’s companies. She says that money was meant to go directly to Financeit, the lender behind Barbaro’s Provincial Smart Home Services contract.
“I don’t think you realize yet how much pull I have in this industry,” Kalonga wrote to Barbaro in April 2025. “Not tooting my own horn but I know my way around this game.”
She sent the remaining $2,500 for his services days later.
To date, the lender Financeit says it has not received the money and has no record of dealing with Kalonga. Barbaro still owes the lender.

Barbaro says she only understood the full extent of the deceit last September after learning Raymond Stephens is actually Raymond Kalonga. She Googled him, and found this 2024 article from CBC Investigates.
“That was a horrible moment,” she said. “While out on appeal he scammed me.”
Kalonga messages suggest links to warranty company
Not only that, Barbaro says Kalonga enlisted her to promote yet another company that’s been accused of targeting HVAC customers.

CBC News has spoken with several Provincial Smart Home customers who were unknowingly debited $33 monthly by Canada Home Protect — a company they were unfamiliar with. The company says it provides home warranty services.

Some customers told CBC News they were able to cancel the automatic payments by calling their bank. Others say they lost out on hundreds of dollars, before realizing they were being charged for services they never asked for.
“There is a clear pattern of repeated victimization,” said Bethanie Pascutto, lawyer at the Advocacy Centre for the Elderly (ACE).
“Once one of these unscrupulous actors is able to successfully take something from a vulnerable member of society, then that information tends to be shared.”
Pascutto says ACE has received thousands of phone calls from seniors in Ontario who believe they were scammed by door-to-door HVAC salespeople.
Then, last year, she began getting calls about Canada Home Protect.
“The concern that a lot of people had was that [the] protection plan was supposed to be included in the amount that they had already paid for Provincial Smart [Home Services],” she said.
“And also the fact that their banking information was being given to a different company without their consent and or even knowledge.”
Pascutto says she has contacted the company numerous times but has been unable to determine who is behind it.
However, the WhatsApp messages between Barbaro and Kalonga give a clue.
In April 2025, Barbaro told Kalonga she was apprehensive about writing a positive review for Canada Home Protect in the Facebook page for customers of Provincial Smart Home.
CBC Investigates: He offered to help save her from debt — then took $17.5K instead
She said customers there were complaining Canada Home Protect charged them for services they did not ask for, and that they were unable to reach the company.
“Unfortunately everyone is labeled a scam on this group. The only real scam is PSHS,” Kalonga replied.

CBC has been unable to locate business filings for the company to determine who is behind it. However, the address listed on Canada Home Protect’s website in downtown Toronto is actually a virtual office. That address is also used by one of Kalonga’s companies, Green Innovation Corp., according to wire transfer information between Barbaro and Kalonga.
Kalonga himself claimed to Barbaro in messages that he had links to Canada Home Protect.
“I stand by my businesses and none of my customers have ever been left to suffer unmet promises,” Kalonga wrote.
Kalonga wrote those messages while he was out on bail, pending his appeal in Ontario after he was convicted of doing just that.
On bail conditions to live in N.L., Kalonga registers business in U.S.
A CBC News investigation into Kalonga more than two years ago uncovered a trail of debts, frustrated customers and scathing commentary from an Ontario justice of the peace who called him “deceitful.”

items: CBC Investigates | Hot air and broken promises
Owner of HVAC company in N.L. files appeal in Ontario consumer affairs case

blocks.text: In February 2024, Kalonga was sentenced to more than 500 days in jail and fined half-a-million dollars for his conduct running a door-to-door sales company in Ontario from 2012 to 2013.
He is currently appealing on the grounds that the guilty plea wasn’t valid because the pleas were entered without Kalonga and his company’s consent.
A hearing date has not yet been set.
As part of his bail conditions, Kalonga is ordered to remain living in Portugal Cove-St. Philip’s, N.L.
However, it is clear in video messages to Barbaro, in public social media posts and through business filings that Kalonga has spent a significant amount of time in the United States.

Documents show Kalonga filed to incorporate a business called Astute Group Enterprises in December, in Fort Lauderdale. Florida business records list Kalonga's address at a residence in Massachusetts.
There is no one protecting the consumer from a criminal like Ray Kalonga.- Marcy Barbaro
A website under Kalonga’s name appears to have launched in July touting Kalonga’s services in business, investment, and speaking engagements.

During a court hearing on Feb. 10 in Newmarket, Ont., Kalonga’s lawyer for his appeal confirmed he is under an order to live in Newfoundland, and asked that he appear virtually for future court appearances.

“I presume he would be appearing from Newfoundland unless — I know sometimes he conducts business in other provinces so it's possible it would be another province,” said defence lawyer Mindy Caterina.
In an email to CBC News, Caterina said her client’s bail conditions do not restrict travel.
Offer to pay money back

Now, more than a year after Kalonga promised to help, Barbaro says she is left with few options and mountains of debt. She has filed a complaint with Ontario Provincial Police’s anti-rackets division and her local detachment.
Barbaro says going to small claims court would be a waste of time.
“I know I would win, but I won't get any money back — it doesn't matter,” Barbaro said.
“There is no one protecting the consumer from a criminal like Ray Kalonga.”
After CBC News contacted Kalonga for this story, a legal representative contacted Barbaro on Kalonga's behalf with an offer to pay the money back.
As of publishing time, Kalonga had agreed to pay back the $17,500 in full, plus interest.

articles.title: Why India's Election Commission is in the eye of a storm - again
articles.summary: India's polling monitor is facing yet another crisis of credibility with fresh allegations against its chief.

blocks.text: India's Election Commission (ECI) is facing yet another crisis of credibility after a series of fresh allegations of irregularities against its chief.

One of the most trusted public institutions in the world's largest democracy, the three-member commission is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and includes Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi as commissioners.

The latest row broke out after a report in the Indian Express newspaper, external said that in the past few months, CEC Kumar had been repeatedly questioned by his two colleagues over the integrity of the voter database, changes to the way new voters are enrolled and the security of the electoral rolls itself.

The report said that Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi objected to several decisions which were taken without their knowledge. There were at least 14 times in the past 10 months when Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi were kept in the dark, it added.
In one instance, the report says, the two commissioners even wrote a letter complaining to the chief secretary, the top bureaucrat in the Indian government.

The revelations have created a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation. Sandhu and Joshi have not publicly commented on the report but the ECI said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process".
The report comes at a time when the commission is carrying out a controversial country-wide revision of the electoral database.
The Election Commission says the aim of this Special Intensive Revision - better known by its acronym SIR - is to ensure that no ineligible name remains on the rolls.

It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address.

But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing CEC Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
But the latest revelations are being seen as much more serious as they are about questions being raised from within the Election Commission about the way its chief is functioning.
From the start, questions have lingered over the robustness of the revision, which has seen 130 million names from across India struck off the voters' list.

Millions of voters have also complained to the authorities that their names are missing, saying the new process set by SIR to register as voters is too cumbersome and involves furnishing documents that many don't have.
Former CEC SY Quraishi, who says he has "been a critic of the SIR from the beginning", told news agency PTI that he always wondered why Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi had been "keeping quiet".
"[Now] I realised that very silently and quietly they were protesting, they were writing notes. That is a good thing, they have gone up in my esteem," he said.

items: How a Brazilian woman became the face of India vote fraud row
New voters list in Indian state includes wrong photos and dead people
The row over 'vote theft' that has shaken Indian politics

blocks.text: The revelations have also provided fresh ammunition to the opposition parties and critics who have repeatedly claimed that SIR is being used to exclude their voters for the BJP's benefit and that elections in India are no longer free and fair.

On Wednesday, angry opposition politicians once again questioned the sanctity of India's election process and demanded that CEC Kumar resign, saying he had no right to continue in office, with some even calling for his arrest.

The charge was led by MP and senior Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi who has repeatedly accused the Commission of "stealing votes from the opposition". On Wednesday, he also accused the Commission and its officers of "treason".

"Vote chori [theft] is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on our constitution. The BJP, RSS [Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh] and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason. Justice will be served," he posted on X, external. He also shared a 15-second video telling the commission and its officers that "your time will come. You cannot get away".

Mamata Banerjee, leader of the regional Mamata All India Trinamool Congress, called for Kumar's arrest and demanded fresh polls with the pre-SIR voters' list in the state of West Bengal which she lost to the BJP in the recent elections. At least 2.7million voters were removed in the state during SIR - Banerjee and her supporters say that cost them dozens of seats and the election win.
Within hours of the Indian Express report and statements from opposition leaders, the Election Commission put out a statement, external defending its way of working.
"Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken.
"Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the statement said.

The note said that highlighting "certain specific internal notes and observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives" give only part of the picture.

And that in recent months, the commission has "introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full commission in the past one year".
The BJP has also defended CEC Kumar, calling the opposition criticism a "smear campaign" and that dissent was "a sign of a vibrant democracy".

Party spokesperson Sambit Patra told a press conference that "ever since the Modi government came to power in 2014, opposition parties have been collapsing one after the other". And because they cannot win elections, they are trying to "undermine the institutions of the country", he said.

items: Indian journalists condemn 'denial' of voting and passport rights of prominent editor
Why India's Election Commission is facing a test of credibility

blocks.text: But the row over the election database is likely to intensify. Banerjee has already said opposition parties will hold protests until Kumar remains CEC.
And India's influential Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which recently forced the education minister to resign, has also said it will protest against the "hijacking of India's democracy".

Analysts say the defence of the Election Commission is unlikely to satisfy many, with some pointing out that its statement doesn't address all the issues raised in the newspaper report and that "CEC Kumar needs to clear the air, external if we are to view the Commission as an impartial body".

articles.title: PAGCOR to fund 456 classrooms in 38 LGUs as shortage drags on
articles.summary: The Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation will fund the construction of 456 classrooms in public schools in 38 cities and municipalities, the Department of Education said, Thursday, September…

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 4:17pm
A teacher cleans a classroom at an elementary school in Manila on June 13, 2025, ahead of the opening of classes on June 16.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp. (PAGCOR) will fund the construction of 456 classrooms in public schools in 38 cities and municipalities, the Department of Education said on Thursday, September 24.

It is the second round of a program in which local governments can now take charge of the construction of school facilities, a mandate previously limited to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).
Each of the 38 local government units (LGUs) will get P55 million, or P2.09 billion in total, to build a three-story school building with 12 classrooms, DepEd said.
The buildings are due for completion by the end of 2027.
DepEd struggles to trim its classroom shortage to keep pace with the growing student population in basic education every year.
The department puts the backlog at 143,543 classrooms as of June 2026, down from 165,443 at the start of the Marcos administration.
Meanwhile, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), citing DepEd's own National School Building Inventory, told a House hearing in July that the gap is still more than 166,000.

"One of the biggest challenges that we face in the department is the shortage of classrooms," Education Secretary Sonny Angara said at the signing ceremony of DepEd's memorandum of agreement with PAGCOR.
Angara noted that the shortage will continue to grow as current school buildings are aging and disasters damage school facilities every year.
PAGCOR will release the money in three tranches, each subject to technical compliance and progress monitoring.
Meanwhile, the LGUs will run procurement and construction under government procurement laws and approved architectural plans. DepEd will own, run and maintain the buildings once they are completed.
This is the second batch of LGUs under the program. In March, PAGCOR signed agreements with 21 LGUs for each to construct a three-story building with 12 classrooms, or 252 classrooms in total.
The two batches bring the total to 708 classrooms in 59 LGUs.
DepEd this year has given LGUs the leeway to pursue their own school infrastructure projects after years of missed targets.
Since 2018, only the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) had been allowed to carry out DepEd-funded school building projects.
In 2023, the department finished the construction of only 192 classrooms out of a total of 6,379.
Under the 2026 national budget, LGUs can now act as primary implementers of school building projects, alongside the DPWH and the Armed Forces of the Philippines Corps of Engineers.

articles.title: Germany: Economic institutes double growth forecast for 2026
articles.summary: Experts predict German GDP will double to 1.3% this year but warn of structural difficulties ahead. The picture is complicated, they say, especially because of uncertainty in the energy sector.

image.caption: Economic experts see Germany's GDP slowly picking up steamImage: Hannes P. Albert/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Several leading German economic think tanks on Thursday announced they had increased their earlier GDP growth forecasts for the country.
New numbers now predict an uptick of 1.3% for 2026, more than double that of spring forecasts of 0.6% growth.

In their so-called "Autumn 2026 Joint Economic Forecast," this year titled "Recovery Under Structural Stress — Fiscal Policy on Slippery Ground," five institutes — the German Institute for Economic Research, the IfO Institute, the Kiel Institute for Global Economics, the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research Halle and the RWI-Leibniz Institute for Economic Research Essen also adjusted their economic outlook for 2027, predicting 1.1% growth.
The picture looks less rosy in 2028, when GDP is expected to slow to just 0.4% growth.
