articles.title: Man dead and multiple people injured after bus collides with two cars in Victoria
articles.summary: Four occupants of bus taken to hospital after multi-vehicle crash in Glenburn

blocks.text: A man has died and several other have been injured after a multi-vehicle collision in Victoria’s Yarra Ranges involving a bus carrying 18 people.
Emergency services responded to reports of a three-vehicle crash, including a commercial bus, on the Melba Highway at Glenburn at about 2.40pm.
The driver of one of the cars died at the scene, while the driver and passenger of the other car sustained minor injuries.
Police said they believed 18 people were inside the bus, including the driver. Paramedics assessed all 21 patients at the scene and transported several people from the bus to hospital.

A teenage boy was airlifted to hospital in a serious condition while a man in his 50s was taken to hospital with serious injuries. A teenage girl and teenage boy were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
A spokesperson for bus operator, Mee’s Bus Lines, described the incident as “pretty devastating” and said the team was “considerably upset by what’s occurred”.
The company said its understanding of the incident remained limited and that it was assisting authorities with their investigation.
The bus was a scheduled service travelling from Mansfield to Melbourne and departed at 1pm, according to the company.

articles.title: Benjamin Netanyahu to deliver defiant UN speech while facing protests and political isolation
articles.summary:
Prime minister will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ as he heads towards his toughest re-election challenge

When he takes the stage at the UN on Thursday, Benjamin Netanyahu will deliver a…
articles.byline: Andrew Roth and Alice Speri in New York

blocks.text: When he takes the stage at the UN on Thursday, Benjamin Netanyahu will deliver a familiar message of defiance even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader in growing isolation.

Netanyahu is facing his toughest re-election challenge in a political career spanning decades with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

Internationally, Israel is facing growing condemnation. The UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities.

And the US is in the midst of a historic shift in public opinion against Israel, with 62% of respondents telling Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hoping he is voted out in October.

Protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the streets of New York City, where mayor Zohran Mamdani has tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal to assure demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”.

Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, defended Netanyahu’s government in a telephone interview before this week’s speech seeking to cast criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias.

“We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” said Danon. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.”
“At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us,” he added.

Anger at Netanyahu will be on full display in New York City on Thursday, where several protests have been scheduled, including one from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”.
“Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here,” said Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action.

She described a “mainstreaming” of public opinion that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.”

And Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.

But in Danon’s telling, Israel’s problem was largely one of public relations rather than of policy, and he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the precipitous shift in polling. Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, he said, and to lay out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?”

He did not elaborate on those specific measures before the speech, but the White House and US policymakers will be listening as they calibrate their message to voters – as well as the backlash of public anger – ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.

Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders, but also to his own electorate in Israel ahead of the October elections. “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation,” said Miller. “And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.”

Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet with Netanyahu, however, during a visit expected to last less than 24 hours. Trump will be in Washington DC to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, and Netanyahu has cited Israel’s electoral campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reason to head home quickly after the speech.
A Trump administration official said Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit but none was organised. There are also no plans to meet congressional leaders, Danon said.

With criticism from top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading democratic presidential contenders, Israel could face a 2028 campaign with two candidates who no longer support arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic support that it has enjoyed in the past.
Even within the Maga base there are fractures, Miller noted, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”.

Danon said of a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.”

But there are multiple flashpoints now for anger from both US political parties, as well as the international community, including dire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank, and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices.

Asked if a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel is preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza, Danon said Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”, nodding to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace. But he said Israel “will do it ourselves” if that does not change, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.”

He was equally resolute on the West Bank, saying that Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism led by the UK over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction which would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank.

Senate Democrats are also introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement, and Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”.
The protests began even before Netanyahu arrived in New York.

Already on Wednesday, several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport in protest at weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft.

Aber Kawas, who in November is slated to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state, spoke at the event and later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers protesting Nethanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday.
“Thousands of people are against his presence in our city,” she said.

Even though some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.

articles.title: Will Eby's early election gamble pay off or backfire in B.C.? Here's what history tells us
articles.summary: On the whole, premiers and prime ministers have benefited from similar gambles in the past. But for others a decision to test the electorate ahead of schedule massively backfired. Here are some…

image.caption: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is seen heading to announce on Tuesday that voters in his province would be heading to the polls two years ahead of schedule. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: With the B.C. Conservatives in disarray, David Eby decided to roll the dice and call an election two years ahead of schedule in the hopes of extending his mandate.
The NDP leader cited the "existential" threat of U.S. President Donald Trump as his reasoning for sending voters to the polls on Oct. 24.
"We have big decisions to make as a province. And British Columbians, you deserve a say in the direction that we choose," he said in a news conference on Tuesday.

But opposition parties criticized Eby's decision. B.C. Conservative interim Leader Lorne Doerkson characterized it as a "cheap, opportunistic political move," while Green Party Leader Emily Lowan called it an unnecessary decision that would bring "yet more instability."
On the whole, premiers and prime ministers have benefited from similar gambles in the past. But for others, a decision to test the electorate ahead of schedule massively backfired.
Eby criticizes 'chaos' of B.C. opposition parties after calling snap election
The winners
When making his decision, Eby might have been considering his predecessor John Horgan.

Horgan and the B.C. NDP formed a minority government — thanks to a supply and confidence agreement with the Greens — after the 2017 election. The then premier rode a wave of popularity from his government's handling of the pandemic to a majority in a snap election in the fall of 2020.

Horgan wasn't the only premier to gamble with an early election call at the height of the pandemic. New Brunswick's Blaine Higgs took his Progressive Conservatives from a minority to a majority in the same year.
Higgs touted the importance of stability when he pitched himself to voters only two years after becoming premier.
Ford officially announces plan to call early Ontario election

Ontario Premier Doug Ford called an early election using a similar line to Eby in 2025, saying he needed a strong mandate to address Trump and his tariff war. Ford would win a historic third majority government, even though he called the election more than a year ahead of schedule.

Ford isn't the only premier to cite economic upheaval to call a snap election. Former Quebec premier Jean Charest cited the 2008 financial crisis as a reason for going to the polls just over a year after winning the 2007 election.
The gamble paid off for Charest, whose Liberals went from a minority to a majority government.
A '3-peat' for Chrétien and the Liberals in 2000 federal election
Former prime minister Jean Chrétien twice called early elections during his tenure, but it was his second gamble that was seen as a major payoff.

Chrétien called a vote in 2000 when polls indicated the Liberals had a sizable lead in Ontario. The Canadian Alliance, created out of the Reform Party in an effort to appeal to voters outside of Western Canada, had only selected Stockwell Day as its leader a few months before.
The Liberals would expand their majority government in the 2000 vote, winning 100 out of 103 seats in Ontario while making gains in Quebec. The Alliance only won two seats in Ontario.
A bust

Despite governing parties having the advantage of calling an election if they think they have a leg up on the opposition parties, there are examples of voters punishing politicians when they make such a move.
Former Ontario premier David Peterson was riding high in the polls in 1990 when he decided to call a summertime election, only three years after winning a majority.

But his popularity hit a downward spiral during the campaign. Although Peterson's Liberals came only five points behind the NDP in the popular vote, Bob Rae won a majority government, becoming the province's first (and only) New Democrat premier.
Astonishing victory for the Ontario NDP in 1990

Jim Prentice called an early vote when he was premier of Alberta in 2015. Prentice had taken over leadership of the governing Progressive Conservatives less than a year earlier and cited a need for a new mandate to pass his budgetary changes.

But there was also speculation that Prentice had an incentive to go to the polls early with the Official Opposition Wildrose Party in a bit of disarray. Prentice had coaxed eight Wildrose MLAs — including Wildrose leader Danielle Smith, now premier — near the end of 2014.
Like in Ontario in 1990, the NDP took advantage of the early vote and formed a majority government. The Wildrose became Official Opposition again and the PCs were relegated to third.
Quebec is in a bit of a unique position, having two different governments tossed out after two subsequent early election calls.
Pauline Marois' concession speech
After securing a majority in 2008, Charest legally could have governed until late 2013. (The province only passed a fixed election date law limiting votes to every four years in 2013.)
But the then-premier decided to send voters to the polls in the summer of 2012 on the heels of an emotional and divisive student tuition protests that shook the province that spring.
Pauline Marois and the Parti Québécois won a minority government, beating Charest's Liberals by just four seats.
Less than two years later, Marois called another election with her eyes set on a majority. Instead, voters backed the Liberals again, this time under Philippe Couillard.
A wash
There are a handful of examples of prime ministers calling early elections and holding on to government, with results short of a resounding endorsement.

Justin Trudeau led a minority government throughout the first year of the pandemic. But he decided to call an early election in 2021, potentially after seeing Higgs and Horgan winning majorities the year before.
Conservative Leader Erin O'Toole tried to punish Trudeau for calling the "unwanted and unnecessary election."

The polls showed the Conservatives had a chance of unseating the Liberals early in the campaign. But on election day the voters picked a House of Commons that looked nearly identical to the one from the 2019 vote.
Chrétien's razor thin majority in 1997 federal election

Stephen Harper refused to speak of a potential majority during the 2008 campaign, one that he decided to call after two years of governing in a minority. But he repeatedly asked Canadians to give his party a "strong mandate" to address what he described as an unworkable Parliament.
Harper's Conservatives won a stronger minority, although polls early in the campaign suggested they had a chance at forming a majority.
Chrétien's first early election call was in 1997, only three-and-a-half years after he first formed government. It was at the time the shortest turnaround for a majority government since 1911.

The Liberals held on to a majority, but only by a handful of seats. Chrétien won his own seat by fewer than 2,000 votes — the only time as prime minister that he failed to secure more than 50 per cent in his own riding.

articles.title: Will Alberta’s dual-practice model reduce surgery waits — or only for those who can pay?
articles.summary: As provinces grapple with how to decrease wait times for surgeries, Alberta is introducing a system in which doctors can simultaneously work in public hospitals and do private care on the side — a…

blocks.text: After nearly three years languishing on the public waitlist for a hip replacement, Cheryl Stewart will finally receive surgery this week.

Stewart told CBC’s The National that her pain wasn’t bad at first, but that as time went on, her hip “got 10 times worse,” until she could barely move beyond a short walk from her bed to her kitchen or bathroom.
She’s one of the Canadians caught in the crossfire as provinces search for ways to reduce wait times that have been a problem for more than a decade.

But in Alberta, where Stewart lives, the province's latest bid for a solution is introducing a controversial system where doctors can simultaneously work in public hospitals and do private care on the side, a model that health advocates say could not only increase public wait times, but may be in violation of the Canada Health Act.

The new model, which begins rolling out this month for eligible practitioners as part of a suite of changes brought in by Bill 11, is called dual practice. Proponents argue that with proper guardrails, it won’t siphon surgeons from the public care system, but will instead lower wait times for elective surgeries across the board by increasing surgical capacity.
Critics warn that the data doesn’t support this, and say dual practice promotes a system where money, and not medical need, determines who receives care.
Health-care groups rally against 2-tier health care
Those waiting for non-emergency procedures like hip and knee surgeries, which are often delayed, are feeling the brunt. Skipping the line wasn’t an option for Stewart.
"To have to go private and spend $35,000, of which I don't have a penny of, that would be an impossible thing for me to come up with," she said.
“It’s a two-tiered system. You certainly don’t feel like you’re in the upper tier, that’s for sure.”

items: Eligible doctors in Alberta can work in both public, private systems starting this fall

blocks.text: The 77-year-old added that “all of us have worked and all of us have paid our taxes,” and that it seems “unfair” for some people to be able to pay to get seen faster.
Comparing wait times
Data from both within Canada and from international jurisdictions throws cold water on the idea that private care investment frees up resources for the public sector.

Alberta’s proposed system is unique within Canada, but it bears similarities to a model already active in Quebec. There, doctors must notify the government before switching from public to private and, as of last year, receive approval first.

Quebec — where more than 800 doctors have opted out of the public system to operate privately — has the worst track record out of the four largest provinces on wait times for elective surgeries, according to data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI).

items: Health-care groups call on Ottawa to stop Alberta’s dual medical practice model
Federal health minister voices concern as Alberta implements dual-practice health-care model

blocks.text: Canadians are supposed to receive hip and knee surgeries within six months of the surgery being ordered, according to the national benchmark set by CIHI. But according to the latest national data on hip replacements, while 84 per cent of patients in Ontario, where the system remains almost entirely public, get their surgery within that national benchmark time, only 54 per cent of public patients in Quebec meet that benchmark.
Currently, Alberta falls below the Canadian average of 69 per cent, with 63 per cent of patients on the public side receiving their hip replacement surgeries within the benchmark.

Quebec introduced restrictions on the movement between public and private systems last year to curb the exodus of doctors, but the Montreal Gazette found last month that specialists are still pulling out of the public system.

A 2024 study looking at Australia found that when the government tried to push private care to relieve the burden on the public system, it yielded a “limited” real-world impact, only shaving off an average of less than half a day in wait times at public hospitals.

Private practice expansions in Australia, Ireland and the U.K. exacerbated inequalities and increased surgical wait times, a May article in The Lancet noted in reaction to Alberta’s dual-practice proposal.

Alberta insists it will maintain control by imposing strict rules on dual-practice doctors, including mandatory minimum hours in public operating rooms, if needed. Family physicians aren't eligible for dual practice under the new model.

“We’re going to make sure that doctors who do go into dual practice — and 400 have expressed an interest to do so — that they continue to provide the service to the public system that they historically have,” Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said in a news conference earlier this month, stressing that the intent is to allow surgeons to do more elective surgeries in total by being able to bill privately for extra work on top of their work in the public system.
Private incentives
But experts caution that government oversight of surgeons, who operate as independent contractors, is difficult to enforce.
Karen Palmer, a health policy professor at Simon Fraser University, said these systems simply don't work.
"There is no country in the world that allows dual practice ... that has found a way to eliminate its harmful effects even with regulation."

items: Alberta legislation could pave way for two-tiered health-care system, new report says

blocks.text: Dual-practice models can also create a built-in conflict of interest, she said.
"It incentivizes physicians to increase their public wait times so that patients feel that they sort of have no choice but to pay privately.”
Alberta premier insists dual practice health care won't threaten public system
Alberta physician Dr. Braden Manns said introducing more private options might allow those with funds to get quicker access, but warns it splits focus for doctors.
“If the surgeon can get four times as much to do surgery, private, for-pay surgery, they’re going to prioritize that,” he said.

Manns, who is also the senior associate dean of the Cumming School of Medicine at the University of Calgary, co-authored a recent commentary in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, arguing dual practice will worsen access to public health care.

“We have problems, but these changes are not going to fix them for the public system,” he said. “So the only ones benefiting are the chartered surgical facilities, investors and then the insurance industry.”
‘Literally killing me’
Those stuck in agony may feel they have no other choice.

In Prince Edward Island, wait times can be astronomical for elective surgeries. Charlottetown resident Neil Payne was told he’d be waiting 12 to 18 months for surgery on his deteriorating hip, but after six months of being off work, battling pain that sometimes kept him bed-ridden for hours, he couldn’t take it.
“It was literally killing me,” Payne, who is a father of seven, said.
So he went to a Montreal clinic to pay for surgery — placing him more than $20,000 in debt.
“It’s a big hit, really," he said. But he has no regrets. "It was life changing for me."

One physician who works in both the private and public systems in Quebec maintains that private clinics can help public care, while acknowledging that demand for private care spikes when public hospitals are underfunded.
“With guardrails, it absolutely can work as a complement to what’s available for patients,” Dr. John Antoniou said.
Critics say proven public solutions can do a better job.

Nova Scotia’s percentage of elective surgeries delivered within the benchmark has shot up in recent years following the introduction of a centralized waitlist for referrals, the expansion of operating room hours to include nights and weekends, and a push to make hospitals more efficient. Now, 77 per cent of hip replacements are delivered within the national benchmark, compared to 49 per cent in 2022.

items: Danielle Smith floats charging temporary residents $1,900 to access public health care

blocks.text: Health advocates say the choice shouldn’t be between pain and debt — and they’re calling on the federal government to step in to defend Canada’s public healthcare system from further erosion.

More than 20 Canadian health organizations issued a call to action for Prime Minister Mark Carney and Health Minister Marjorie Michel to review Bill 11 and step in if violations of the Canada Health Act are found.
Michel has previously flagged concerns with Alberta’s new model. But whether Ottawa will take action by clawing back public funds remains to be seen.
Does Alberta's dual-practice health-care model violate the Canada Health Act?

articles.title: Missed the debate? Key takeaways from Quebec party leaders’ final showdown
articles.summary: With less than two weeks until Quebec voters head to the polls on Oct. 5, the leaders of Quebec's five main parties faced off over the health-care system, the trade war and the possibility of a third…

image.caption: The five party leaders took part in Wednesday's debate at Maison Radio-Canada. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: With less than two weeks until Quebec voters head to the polls on Oct. 5, the leaders of Quebec's five main parties faced off over the health-care system, the trade war and the possibility of a referendum.
The third and final debate of this campaign was hosted by Radio-Canada.
While the leaders traded predictable jabs on the economy and immigration, several critical issues— namely Indigenous affairs and climate change— were left off the table.

And although issues pertaining specifically to English-speaking Quebecers were also not discussed during the debate, four of the five party leaders were given a chance to address anglophones while meeting with reporters afterwards.
Here are the key takeaways from Wednesday night.
On a referendum, PQ leader says he's an optimist
With the Parti Québécois (PQ) leading in the polls, the possibility of another referendum on Quebec independence is a very real possibility.

But it took more than half the debate for the topic to be raised — when Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) Leader Christine Fréchette took a jab at the PQ's leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, as she pumped up her own economic plan.

A little later, St-Pierre Plamondon was asked if he would hold a referendum after Trump leaves office even if the polls suggest the No side will win again. Although he didn't answer directly, he didn't walk back his promise — and stressed he remains an optimist.
"We shouldn't be afraid of democracy," he said, in response to the question. "Jacques Parizeau used to say: 'Don't be afraid of your democracy, of going to the polls, of reflecting on our future.'"
PLQ leader Charles Milliard professes love for ‘great country’ of Canada
Woman's struggle to find doctor sparks exchange
One Montrealer, Tania Lamoureux, asked a question to the leaders that sparked a heated exchange between the leaders about how to improve access to health care.
The woman said she’s been waiting for years to be assigned a doctor, and asked what concrete plans the leaders have to fix this problem shared by so many Quebecers.

"We still have a lot of work to do. I am very aware of this," Fréchette began, before citing improvements made by her party over the years. Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard cut in to say there are still significant waiting times at emergency rooms.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he would eliminate Santé Québec, the newly formed government agency that manages the province's health-care system, to cut down on bureaucracy, while Conservative Party of Quebec Leader Éric Duhaime said he would introduce more privatized care.
Québec Solidaire (QS) co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal championed more public care. Speaking more generally, she warned that cutting back on the state, as her counterparts propose, could impact services.
Duhaime and Milliard trade accusations around ideology amid discussion on private health care
Trump looms large
U.S. President Donald Trump and the trade war, not surprisingly, featured prominently in the debate.
We heard from the parties about how they would best manage the cost of living and Quebec's finances in tumultuous times.

items: Compare the promises of Quebec’s major parties in the 2026 election

blocks.text: Each tried to make the case they were the person best suited to defend Quebec's interests and protect its economy as Canada negotiates with Washington.
"We won't let you down," said St-Pierre Plamondon, speaking on behalf of the five party leaders. "There is a consensus on supporting you."
St-Pierre Plamondon again said he would cut back the bureaucracy to balance the budget — an ambition shared by the Conservatives.
Ruba Ghazal says Quebec’s hydroelectricity will make the province resistant to Trump’s attacks
Immigration a flash point, again
The topic of immigration generated some fiery debate, with each party outlining its well-entrenched position.

Three out of the five parties want to cut immigration levels compared to last year. The CAQ wants to reduce immigration levels to 45,000, down from 60,000 last year. The Conservatives set the same target, while the PQ would cut that further, to 35,000.
Only QS wants to raise the level of newcomers, targeting 70,000.

The Liberals, meanwhile, still didn't give a clear answer. The party has previously said it would accept anywhere between 45,000 and 70,000 permanent immigrants, depending on integration capacity and workforce needs.

items: Catch up on all of our live coverage on Thursday's debate

blocks.text: "I am not going to commit tonight," Milliard told reporters after the debate.
The business community has pushed for more immigrants to meet the demands of the labour market.
Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says Quebec needs to reduce its immigration numbers
What was left off the table
Beyond the many topics discussed during the debate, two issues were notably absent: Indigenous affairs and the environment.

During the election campaign, the Assembly of First Nations Quebec-Labrador (AFNQL) urged parties to commit to equitable public services, recognize First Nations police services as essential services, and support the revitalization of ancestral languages.

In a recent interview with CBC, Kebaowek First Nation Chief Lance Haymond said it has been "disappointing" that leaders of major parties have passed through his region of Témiscamingue without discussing plans to improve the lives of his constituents.

The leaders, as well, had little to say on the environment. On that front, much of the discussion centred around a proposal by Duhaime to suspend the gas tax. Duhaime took the opportunity to also outline his plan to withdraw Quebec from the cap-and-trade carbon market and eliminate the Electrification and Climate Change Fund, formerly the Fonds vert.
LISTEN | This is Montreal podcast episode on the anglophone vote:
This is Montreal23:03The 'Anglo' Vote: What place does it have, this Quebec election?
Post debate: leaders address English-speaking Quebec
The English-speaking community also received scant mention during the debate.
Afterward, St-Pierre Plamondon, who refused an invitation to take part, said he was "not closing the door" to taking part in such a debate in the future.
"Our conception of a country is in full respect of Quebecers whose mother tongue is English, so there's no reason not to talk together or make that change together," the PQ leader said.
Breaking down the key moments in Quebec’s final leaders’ debate

Duhaime once again urged English-speaking Quebecers to "stop being hostage of the Liberals," adding that if they want to hold more political weight as a community, "you need to show that there is some competition going on."
"When there's seats that have been Liberal for two centuries, it's very difficult to attract politicians because the Liberals take you for granted," he said.
Ghazal, whose Québec Solidaire party also seeks Quebec independence, said anglophone rights would be respected if Quebec became an independent country under her party.
"We will always respect their rights," she said.

Fréchette said she would be the premier of all Quebecers and that it is "essential for me to respect the English speaking community," while highlighting the fact that a CAQ government — contrary to the PQ and QS — would not seek a referendum.

articles.title: Why Canada's rolling out the red carpet for Vietnamese President Tô Lâm
articles.summary: Vietnam and Canada can deepen their relationships on trade, energy and academia, say experts — but some say the Southeast Asian country's track record on human rights shouldn't be ignored.

image.caption: Vietnamese President Tô Lâm, pictured here in May 2026, is paying a state visit to Canada in what could be a turning point for the two countries' relations. (REUTERS)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Vietnam and Canada can deepen their relationships on trade, energy and academia, say experts — but some say the Southeast Asian country's track record on human rights shouldn't be ignored.
In state visit, middle powers likely to deepen trade, energy, say experts
From a welcoming ceremony with military honours to a lavish state dinner — as far as diplomatic events go, a state visit is as formal as it gets: the ultimate symbol of friendly bilateral relations.

Today, Canada will be greeting Vietnamese Leader Tô Lâm with such a warm gesture. Lâm — who serves both as the president and the first general secretary of Vietnam's Communist Party — will be welcomed by Governor General Louise Arbour and Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a moment that could be a turning point for Canada-Vietnam relations.

The Southeast Asian country is a major trading partner, reaching $20.6 billion in two-way trade 2025. But it also has a checkered human rights record and keeps in good standing with adversaries like Russia and North Korea.
So why has Canada chosen its leader for its first state visit of 2026? CBC News spoke with several experts ahead of the occasion on what Canada stands to gain from closer ties to Vietnam.
Expanding trade
In some ways, Canada and Vietnam have much in common: Both countries are middle powers, sharing a border with juggernauts (the U.S. and China, respectively).
Both nations have also been steadily increasing their bilateral trade in recent years — Vietnam is now Canada's largest trading partner in Southeast Asia.

items: Carney's Davos speech draws reaction from around the world

blocks.text: "Canada and Vietnam have had a comprehensive partnership since 2017," said Julie Nguyen, chair of the Canada-ASEAN Initiatives at the York Centre for Asian Research, referencing industries like trade, defence, science and diplomacy.
"It is time for the two countries to elevate their partnership to the next level in order to ensure economic resiliency, security."
Vietnam is racing to become a high-income country by 2045. In order to reach that goal, it will have to move into advanced manufacturing, science, technology and AI development, Nguyen says.
Carney hosts investment summit amid trade war
"All of these products and services can be provided by Canada."

Canada is also working to finalize a free trade agreement with the Association of South East Nations (ASEAN). Vietnam could prove clutch in those efforts, since it is a prominent member of the intergovernmental regional organization, says Jeff Nankivell, president and CEO of the non-profit think-tank, the Asia Pacific Foundation.

And, Nankivell says, Canada is likely to find a willing partner in Vietnam, which has also faced punishing American tariffs, with the U.S. at one point slapping a 40 per cent levy on goods determined to have been transshipped through Vietnam.
"Everyone in the world is looking to diversify," he said.
"When we knock on the door of a country like Vietnam, it opens very quickly because they have a similar interest in diversifying."
Energy
Vietnam is also hungry for energy. It's one of the fastest-growing economies in the world and its population is relatively young and well educated.
That's of interest to Canada, because it could provide commodities like liquified natural gas (LNG), says Nankivell.
Could Canada fill the Iran war oil supply gaps?
"On conventional energy, LNG and crude oil, there could be statements of intention on the Vietnamese side to look to Canada for future supplies," he said.

items: How Carney's Davos speech holds up 3 months later

blocks.text: Canada could also respond to Vietnam's ambitious nuclear power program, says Nankivell.
"You might see announcements or memoranda of understanding related to closer co-operation to explore the deployment or acquisition of Canadian nuclear technology in Vietnam."
Human rights
But Canada and Vietnam also have key differences in values. Human Rights Watch highlighted this in an open letter addressed to Carney and Arbour about Vietnam's crackdown on political dissidents.
Amnesty International has accused Lâm's government of using a vague penal code to crack down on dissent and suppress freedom of expression.

He has also travelled to North Korea as recently as October of last year, a country with a dismal human rights record and from which Canada has suspended full diplomatic relations since 2010. Lâm has also held high-level talks earlier this month at the Kremlin with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Nankivell says it's an important reminder — and stronger trader relationships will only help Canada have more leverage in advancing liberal values.

items: Trump to hit more than 60 countries, including Canada, with new tariffs over 'forced labour'

blocks.text: "It is still very much in Canada's national interest to continue working towards a world where human rights are better respected than they are today, but you need channels for that," he said.
"Having a state visit with the leader of a country like Vietnam is an opportunity to deepen those ties."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jennifer Yoon covers the latest national and international news for CBC News on television, radio and digital. You can reach her at jennifer.yoon@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Labour likely to be biggest party in hung parliament, mega poll suggests – UK politics live
articles.summary:
The poll shows Reform UK ‘neck-and-neck’ with the Conservative party

Good morning. Andy Burnham and Kemi Badenoch are both preparing for their party conferences (next week, and the following…

blocks.text: Good morning. Andy Burnham and Kemi Badenoch are both preparing for their party conferences (next week, and the following week, respectively), and this morning YouGov has released a new MRP poll with encouraging news for both of them. Polling is very good at revealing electoral trends, but a lot less good at predicting electoral outcomes, and wise politicians don’t treat them as gospel. But they also find polling impossible to ignore, not least because it shapes the landscape within which parties operate. A leader expecting to win the next election acts differently from one expecting to lose it.
And would Burnham win an election held now? Not exactly, according to the YouGov figures, but Labour would be the largest party. Here is YouGov’s summary of its results.

double quotation mark-Labour would be the largest party in a hung parliament, were an election held tomorrow, winning 241 seats in our model’s central estimates -Such a result would be a net loss of 170 seats for Labour on the 2024 election, but is up from our MRP this time last year, which projected the party would be reduced to just 144 seats and showed Reform UK within touching distance of a majority -Reform UK are now neck-and-neck with the Conservatives, with the parties respectively on 123 and 130 seats in our median projection -Our central projection shows the Lib Dems on 71 seats, the SNP on 40, Plaid Cymru on 15, and the Greens on nine -37% of constituencies are decided by margins of five points or less in our central estimate, with this rising to 67% of seats projected to be won by Reform UK

blocks.caption: YouGov MRP poll results Photograph: YouGov

blocks.text: This is not a terrific result for Labour, but the party is in a much better position under Burnham than it was under Keir Starmer.

The YouGov figures suggest Badenoch has no chance of forming a government. But she may be even happier with these numbers than Burnham. A year ago polling suggested Nigel Farage was on course to be the next prime minister, and there was serious talk about the Conservative party being totally eclipsed by Reform UK. Not anymore. Today’s figures have the Tories narrowly ahead of Reform on the central estimate (the best guess – YouGov also has highest and lowest estimates for seat numbers). More importantly, the poll confirms that Farage’s hopes of forming a government are – for now at least – fading.

blocks.caption: YouGov MRP poll results Photograph: YouGov
YouGov MRP poll results Photograph: YouGov

blocks.text: YouGov surveyed almost 17,000 people for the poll, between 23 August to 18 September.
I will post more on the poll as the day goes on. There will be other news too, although there is not a lot in the diary.

articles.title: DOJ seeks more confidential funds in 2027 budget, cites 'more challenges'
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) and its attached agencies are seeking higher confidential funds for their operations in 2027, it was disclosed during the Senate budget hearing on Thursday.

blocks.text: Published September 24, 2026 3:43pm
The Department of Justice (DOJ) and its attached agencies are seeking higher confidential funds for their operations in 2027, it was disclosed during the Senate budget hearing on Thursday.
The DOJ has a P579.4 million budget for confidential funds, which is 47.3% lower than 2026's P1.1 billion budget.
Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida has sought the restoration of P500 million to the Office of the Secretary, noting that only P319.9 million was allocated under the NEP.
“Sa Inter-Agency Council Against Trafficking, napapansin po namin sa inter-agency na ang P10 million ay kulang at talaga kailangan pa naming dagdagan dahil may dagdag pong hamon,” Vida said.
(For the Inter-Agency Council Against Trafficking, we have observed that the P10 million allocation is insufficient, and we really need to increase it because we are facing additional challenges.)

He also hoped that Congress would grant DOJ’s budget of P475,000 to combat emerging cybercrime and P5 million for the National Coordination Center Against Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children and Child Sexual Abuse or Exploitation Materials (NCC-OSAEC-CSAEM).
Bureau of Immigration (BI) Commissioner Joel Viado also sought an additional P10 million to P20 million for his agency’s 2027 confidential funds.
He said the additional budget would help the agency in hiring more personnel.
“Nagre-request kami sa DBM ng additional positions. Ang aming fugitive search unit, ang humahabol o tumutugis sa mga pugante, wala pang 20 ’yan (nationwide),” Viado said.
(We are requesting additional positions from the Department of Budget and Management. Our Fugitive Search Unit, which tracks down and apprehends fugitives, has fewer than 20 personnel.)
Meanwhile, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is seeking a P1 billion budget for its confidential funds since the agency is planning to procure equipment to combat cybercrime.

“We are requesting sana about P1 billion divided into 12 months. Because more than the expenses on operations namin, we are intending to procure tools and equipment to fight cybercrime,” NBI Director Melvin Matibag said.

He shared that during its meetings with the United States Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and Thailand’s Central Investigation Bureau (CIB), the NBI found that many scams are linked to the Philippines.
“Nire-request naming increase sana dito for the confidential funds is for us to procure these tools to fight ang ganito mga criminal activities,” Matibag said.
(We are requesting an increase in the confidential funds so we can procure the necessary tools to combat these types of criminal activities.)
He added that since April, the NBI has been conducting around 200 to 220 investigative operations.
The BI and NBI are attached agencies under the Justice Dept.
For 2027, the DOJ proposed a budget of P46.435 billion, which is equivalent to 0.64% of the P7.2-trillion national budget.

Of DOJ’s total proposed budget, P31.723 billion (68.32%) was allotted for Personnel Services (PS), P11.340 billion (24.42%) for Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE), and P3.372 billion (7.26%) for Capital Outlay (CO). —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Cybersecurity body lifts ban on Discord
articles.summary: The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center has ordered the lifting of the ban on the online platform Discord.

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 3:25pm
Logo of online platform Discord.
Discord
MANILA, Philippines — The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) has ordered the lifting of the ban on the online platform Discord.
In a press conference on Thursday, September 24, Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda said the ban was lifted after "successful negotiations" with the platform.
"Inaalis na natin ang ban na ipinatupad ng ating pamahalaan simula kahapon sa online platform na Discord," he said.
(We are now lifting the ban that our government implemented yesterday on the online platform Discord.)
According to Aguda, Discord has outlined a commitment in response to the government's serious concerns regarding nihilistic violent extremism, grooming and other threats to online safety.
"Nakipag-ugnay po ang Discord sa atin sa DICT at CICC at nangakong magsasagawa sila immediately po ng mga hakbang upang higit na mapalakas ang proteksyon ng mga kabataan," he said.
(Discord reached out to us at the DICT and CICC, promising to take immediate steps to further strengthen child protection.)

The CICC, on September 22, issued an ultimatum to Discord and Reddit, another online platform, to establish Philippine offices within 24 hours so authorities could more effectively investigate and act on online harms tied to recent school shootings.
In the following days, internet service providers started blocking access to the online platform, which raised scrutiny from the public.

articles.title: Prosecution: Senate vote on Sara Duterte impeach threshold 'gives clarity'
articles.summary: Prosecution: Senate vote on Sara Duterte impeachment threshold 'gives clarity'

blocks.text: House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas on Thursday said that the Senate ruling for the threshold needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte before the Senate impeachment court provided clarity but did not guarantee victory.

Luistro was referring to the Senate impeachment court's decision which pegs the threshold for conviction at two-thirds of all members of the Senate who are "legally and factually participating" in the proceedings.

“Sa wakas, nagkaroon na ng kaliwanagan itong matagal ng discussion ng sambayanang Pilipino concerning the threshold vote. Ang kapangyarihan ng Senado o ng Impeachment Court na bigyan ng kaliwanagan ang threshold vote ay ayon din sa kanilang exclusive power to try and decide all impeachment cases,” Luistro said in a press conference.
(The action of the Honorable Impeachment Court yesterday was in line also with the constitutional mandate that they have the exclusive power to try and decide all cases of impeachment.)
She was referring to Article 11 Section 6 of the Constitution, which states that “the Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment.”
“I think this is very significant as we continue the impeachment trial. Kasi mas mahirap din po na hanggang sa oras na ito ay wala pang kaliwanagan,” Luistro said.
(It will be more difficult if the issue remains unresolved at this point.)

Article 11, Section 6 of the Constitution also reads, “No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate," although it does not state a specific number.
'Two-thirds is two-thirds'
Further, Luistro said that the impeachment court’s decision to exclude absent Senators remains in line with the abovementioned Constitutional provision

“I wish to make it clear that the two-thirds [threshold] to convict] does not change. And akin to the prosecution’s position, two-thirds is two-thirds. What the impeachment court made clear is the phrase all members of the Senate, whether the same pertains to all 24 or whether pertains to all who are legally and factually qualified only,” Luistro added.
It was Senator judge Erwin Tulfo who made the motion to change the threshold, given that four Senator judges have been absent from impeachment trial proceedings due to varying reasons.

Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained on plunder and other related charges due to their alleged involvement in flood control (P573 million) and undeclared campaign donations (P75 million), respectively.

Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, on the other hand, is in hiding amid a standing warrant of arrest issued against him by the International Criminal Court due to his alleged involvement in the drug war deaths during the Rodrigo Duterte administration.
Senator Loren Legarda, for her part, is on an extended medical leave abroad due to a lung ailment.
LIST: How senator-judges voted on threshold to convict Sara Duterte
Denominator
Luistro explained that while this allowed the reduction of votes needed for conviction, it also allowed the lowering of votes needed to acquit.

“By giving clarity to the denominator, what is lowered is not only the number for conviction but also the number for acquittal. That is a two-way consequence. If 20 is the denominator, conviction requires 14. But remember, acquittal needs only seven [votes with 20 as denominator],” Luistro said.

“So unlike when we have all the senators actively participating in the trial giving us a denominator of 24, the conviction would need 16 while the acquittal needs nine votes. With changes in threshold, and acquittal would only need seven votes. Mali pong sabihin na conviction vote lang ang bumaba sa pagkat kasabay pung bumaba ang acquital vote,” Luistro added.
(So it would be wrong to say that only the votes needed for conviction were lowered.)
In addition, Luistro said that the vote on threshold is no guarantee that the same result will be reflected in the final verdict.

“Their (Senator judges) position on the threshold vote does not necessarily show there would be position on the verdict of this impeachment trial. I believe the position of the Senator judges depends on the question confronting them,” she said.

“I have so much respect for all the members of the impeachment court and I know they are painstakingly evaluating the evidence to come up with their fair and impartial judgment come the time they cast their vote. Besides, this is far from over. We are not even done with [presentation of evidence for unexplained wealth. There’s still bribery, and the turn of the defense to present their evidence,” Luistro added.
Prosecutor Terry Ridon, for his part, said the burden of proof will always be on the prosecution, regardless of the threshold vote needed to convict.
“The burden continues for the prosecution to deliver on the evidence and we are committed to do that, regardless of the threshold,” Ridon said.

“The trial goes on, and we are very much confident with the strength of evidence that we are presenting in this impeachment trial. Whether it is 16, whether it is 14, regardless of the vote, the obligation of the prosecution remains the same,” Luistro said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Chiz Escudero after casting 'no' vote: Chair takes exception to decision but...
articles.summary: Senate impeachment court presiding officer Senator-Judge Francis Escudero indicated that he disagreed with the tribunal"s decision to change the base of the two-thirds vote needed to convict Vice…

blocks.text: Published September 24, 2026 2:50pm

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Senator-Judge Francis Escudero indicated that he disagreed with the tribunal’s decision to change the base of the two-thirds vote needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte, but added that its ruling reigned supreme over his preference for the threshold to remain at 16.

Escudero said this after the Senate impeachment court voted, 13-1, that the two-thirds vote shall be based on all the members who have legally and factually participated in the proceedings, and not on all 24 members of the Senate.
Six members, all belonging to the minority, chose not to participate.

“For the record, while the Chair takes exception to this decision, the Chair nonetheless accepts it as a judgment of this Court and is bound to give it effect,” Escudero said after saying the only "nay" in the proceedings regarding the threshold rule.

“The Presiding Officer, after all, is not the Court. He is merely the Custodian of the process not the proprietor of its outcome. This is the essence of democracy: that disagreement be preserved without obstruction and that a lawful result be obeyed without resentment,” he added.
Escudero said graceful acceptance of defeat is a tradition that “gives strength and legitimacy to the Senate” whether it sits as a legislative body or as an impeachment Court.

“We allow the fullest ventilation of views even if those views differ sharply from our own. But at the end of the day, we vote. We abide by the judgment of the majority even if we disagree with it,” Escudero said.
“Accordingly, the Chair accepts and declares the ruling adopted by the Court as the new controlling ruling upon further proceedings, and the Chair shall apply this ruling faithfully,” he added.
It was Senator-Judge Erwin Tulfo who made the motion to change the threshold, given that four senators have been absent from impeachment trial proceedings due to varying reasons.

Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained on plunder and other related charges due to their alleged involvement in flood control (P573 million) and undeclared campaign donations (P75 million), respectively.

Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, on the other hand, is in hiding amid a standing warrant of arrest issued against him by the International Criminal Court due to his alleged involvement in the drug war deaths during the Rodrigo Duterte administration.
Senator Loren Legarda, for her part, is on an extended medical leave abroad due to a lung ailment.
"This ruling and interpretation of the court shall operate pro hac vice, or for this occasion only. It shall not constitute a binding precedent in any future impeachment proceedings," Escudero said.

"This is a ruling, not an amendment of the rules. As such, it has no binding but merely persuasive effect on future impeachment proceedings, the hands of whom we cannot shackle as there is no stare decisis as between impeachment courts,” he added.
“Further, the circumstances that gave rise to this ruling are extraordinary... and the chair hopes that it shall never happen again,” Escudero said.

Escudero, after the vote on the threshold ruling, explained the basis for determining the number of votes needed for conviction, given that four of the 24 senator-judges have been unable to participate in the proceedings.
Escudero said that the following Senators will be excluded from the senator-judges qualified to vote:

items: detained and/or suspended or otherwise legally restrained from exercising the functions of a senator;
persons sought by authorities whose whereabouts are unknown;
those suffering from a physical or medical incapacity;
those beyond the coercive processes of the Senate; and
others similarly situated.

blocks.text: Escudero, however, said that such determination of who the senator-judges qualified to vote for the conviction or acquittal of Duterte will come at a later time. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: After SC nudge, Senate to seek urgent tag for anti-dynasty bill
articles.summary: The Senate will ask President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to tag the anti-political dynasty bill as urgent in the hopes of securing its passage before the end of the current session of the 20th Congress.

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 2:50pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate will ask President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to tag the anti-political dynasty bill as urgent in the hopes of securing its passage before the end of the current session of the 20th Congress.
Sen. Risa Hontiveros shared during the first hearing of the Senate ad hoc committee on the country's economic slowdown on Thursday, September 24.

Hontiveros was responding to former Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Deputy Governor Diwa Guinigundo, who blamed political dynasties for widespread corruption and a culture of "red tape" that stymies businesses.
"Our politics and institutions have a huge problem because of the dominance of political dynasties," Guinigundo said in mixed English and Filipino.
The Senate leadership has agreed to lobby for the swift passage of the anti-dynasty bill after the Supreme Court's recent and historic appeal for such a measure.

"Just last night — before we adjourned session — the Senate leadership requested that, in addition to being a LEDAC priority, the anti-political dynasty bill also be certified as urgent, so that we can attempt to pass it during the current session of the 20th Congress," Hontiveros said in mixed English and Filipino.
Marcos has made the anti-dynasty bill a priority of the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council (LEDAC).
But an urgent certification would compel Congress to fast-track its passage and bypass the three-day rule between readings.
The anti-dynasty bill cleared third and final reading at the House in June. The Senate version has hurdled the committee-level but has yet to reach the floor.
The current second regular session will end on October 9.
Economic slump partially attributed to dynasties
The special Senate committee on Reinvigorate Investment and Sustainable Economic Growth (RISE), chaired by Hontiveros, aims to reach a "unified diagnosis" of what ails the economy.
Gunigundo, one of the resource persons at the committee hearing today, argued that breaking the grip of political dynasties would help stamp out red tape and corruption in the bureaucracy.
To do this, the former BSP executive said both chambers of Congress needed to pass a "genuine" anti-political dynasty law.
The current House version of the bill, Gunigundo added, is riddled with loopholes as it does not address the core issues of dynasties.

Civil society groups have criticized House Bill 8289 for imposing kinship restrictions that are too narrow given it bans relatives only within the second degree of consanguinity (e.g. parents, children, and siblings).
Hontiveros thanked Gunigundo for bringing up the issue of political dynasties, given there are findings that localities long ruled by them lag behind in development.
"Thank you for mentioning the challenge posed to us in Congress ... concerning the anti-political dynasty bill, which we have been waiting on for 39 years now," Hontiveros said.
"I also wish to thank the Senate leadership, led by the Senate president, for responding to the Supreme Court's recent reminder to us," she added.
The Supreme Court last week issued a rare writ of mandamus that explicitly highlighted Congress' failure to pass an anti-political dynasty law for almost four decades.
Associate Justice Ramon Paul L. Hernando cited Article 2, Section 26 of the Constitution in the ruling to remind the government that it has a “constitutional duty” to prohibit dynasties.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian agreed with Gunigundo and said foreign chambers and ambassadors who visit the Senate often complain about dealing with the Bureau of Internal Revenue, the Bureau of Customs, and local government units.
"When they have a hard time, that is the image being portrayed about the Philippines in their country, that it's hard to do business here," he said.
Gatchalian opened the hearing by citing data that shows corruption and inflation have cost the economy an estimated P2.7 trillion in actual and opportunity losses since the second quarter of 2025.

articles.title: Teen rocker Nene Royal becomes first Thai to win America's Got Talent
articles.summary: Her heavy metal performance trumped nine other finalists, including magicians and even a robot crew.

blocks.text: Nene Royal, a 16-year-old rocker, has been crowned the latest winner of America's Got Talent - making her the first ever Thai winner of the long-running talent show.
For the show's finals on Tuesday in California, Nene, whose real name is Rattikarn Amloy, performed a rendition of Seven Nation Army by American rock duo The White Stripes.
Her heavy metal performances trumped nine other finalists, including magician acts, canine performers and even a robot dance crew.

Many in Thailand are celebrating her win, with some saying they were proud that she had made it to "one of the biggest stages in the world". The Thai government has called her an "inspiration to anyone who dares to dream big".

Nene emerged as a clear fan favourite early in the competition, after a viral clip of her audition, in which she belted out Zombie by The Cranberries to a stunned panel of judges. The video has racked up 20 million views.
On Wednesday night, ahead of the results being announced, Nene took the stage with Linkin Park to perform The Emptiness Machine, a 2024 rock song by the American band.
Later that night she broke down in tears, kneeling on the ground as she was crowned the winner of the show's 21st season - which comes with a prize of $1m (£755,000).
"I'm very happy and emotional right now," she said, thanking everyone for supporting her.
The results show was also eagerly followed by her legion of fans in Thailand, who were unable to watch the live broadcast on the television network NBC.
Many in Thailand had to resort to a YouTube livestream instead - and were thrown into distress when the livestream was abruptly cut in the middle of the results announcements.
But moments later came sighs of relief and exclamations of joy, as word got around that Nene had secured her historic victory.
"History made!" one Thai social media user wrote on Facebook.
"Let the world write it down that this Thai kid is incredibly talented," wrote another.
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul congratulated Nene Royal, saying in a statement that she had "brought honour to Thailand" and "instilled pride in the Thai people" with her win.

"What makes this win special is that Nene carried her Thai identity with confidence onto one of the world's biggest stages," the Thai government's public relations department said in another statement on Thursday.
"She showed that talent, hard work, and determination can come from anywhere, including a young girl from Phuket with a guitar and a big dream."
According to Nene, she started playing the guitar when she was seven years old and harboured dreams of becoming a touring musician.
In her hometown of Phuket, a tourist hub known for its beaches and seaside resorts, Nene was known to busk at Naka Weekend Market.
Piyarat Na Songkhla, 43, tour guide in Phuket, tells the BBC that he has seen Nene Royal perform since she was young.
"She's so adorable," he says. "I feel so elated and happy for her. It's unbelievable that she has gone this far. So proud of her."
The Facebook account of Naka Weekend Market posted a tribute to Nene after her victory.
"Everyone at Naka Market is so proud to see you shine on one of the biggest stages in the world," its post reads.
"Your talent, heart, and courage have inspired so many people, and this victory is a beautiful reminder of what can happen when someone truly gives everything to their dream."
Kajonkiet International School in Phuket, where Nene studies, also congratulated her on the win.
"We are so proud of you," reads a Facebook post from the school, which posted a video of its students and staff gathering to watch Nene's final performance, screaming and chanting her name.

articles.title: Gov’t to continue missing sabungeros probe despite families’ noncooperation
articles.summary: The government will pursue the case even without the cooperation of the victims' families.

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 2:41pm
MANILA, Philippines — The government will independently pursue the missing sabungeros cases despite the lack of active cooperation from the victims’ families, the Department of Justice (DOJ) said.

Justice Undersecretary Raul Vasquez said on Thursday, September 23 that the hearing on criminal cases against the accused individuals in the case will proceed in Quezon City courts despite reports that some families have withdrawn and stopped cooperating.

“The truth of the matter is, tuloy-tuloy ‘yung kaso. ‘Yung tatlong kaso na nasa Quezon City ngayon, nasa trial stage na ‘yan. Nagpe-presenta na ng ebidensya ang ating prosecutors,” Vasquez said in an interview with dzMM.
(The truth of the matter is, the cases will proceed. The three cases that are currently in Quezon City are already on the trial stage. The prosecutors are now presenting evidences.)

Cases of kidnapping, serious illegal detention and homicide are filed against business tycoon Atong Ang and several police officers for allegedly killing dozens of sabungeros, or cockfighting enthusiasts, who went missing between 2021 and 2022.
Families disappearing
On Wednesday, September 23, Prosecutor General Richard Anthony Fadullon said most of the families of the victims are disappearing one by one.
In the case filed in Santa Cruz, three family members were presented as witnesses, but two of them eventually stopped cooperating with the DOJ.
In Lipa and San Pablo, the victims’ families are no longer coordinating with their private counsel.

“Initially, nandoon ‘yung kagustuhan, pagpupursige, na ma-file ‘yung kaso, at akala nga namin, mabubuhayan ng loob na ipagpatuloy despite the fact na merong ibang naunang umatras. Napansin namin na unti-unti nawawala na ‘yung mga complainants, at totally hindi na nakikipag-usap at nakikipag-ugnayan sa amin,” Fadullon said.

(Initially, the desire and determination to file the case were there, and we thought they would be encouraged to proceed despite the fact that there are others who withdrew. We noticed that the complainants are gradually disappearing and they are totally not coordinating with us anymore.)
Public crimes
Vasquez explained that the cases filed against the accused individuals are public crimes that do not necessarily require the participation of the victims’ families as private complainants.

The justice undersecretary added that, unlike private crimes that require the cooperation from the victims for the case to proceed, public crimes like kidnapping and kidnapping with illegal detention can be pursued by the government independently.
“Those are crimes against the state, and therefore, they can be prosecuted even in the absence of private complainants,” Vasquez said.
The families’ noncooperation, however, might affect their ability to pursue civil damages or financial claims from the accused.
Vasquez said prosecutors are confident that they have sufficient evidence to pursue the cases.
Obstruction of justice
Vasquez mentioned that there is also an ongoing preliminary investigation into alleged obstruction of justice complaints against the legal team of Ang.
In late May, Ang’s lawyer Caroline Cruz was accused of bribing the families of some victims with monthly financial assistance in exchange for their absence during court hearings.
Cruz denied any wrongdoing, saying that the families of the victims reached out to her first.

Vasquez said that while families of the victims did not provide specific reasons behind their noncooperation, their sudden withdrawal could be attributed to the alleged obstruction of justice committed by Ang’s camp.

“‘Yung aspetong ‘yon ay inaaral pa base sa ebidensya kung meron bang obstruction of justice laban sa mga abogado na sinasabi nila ay gumawa ng paraan para hindi na tumuloy ‘yang mga pamilyang ‘yan,” Vasquez said.
(That aspect is being studied based on evidence, if there is any obstruction of justice against the lawyers who they accused of taking steps to discourage the family.)

articles.title: NBI eyes opening attache offices worldwide by 2027
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) plans to establish attaché offices at Philippine embassies worldwide to assist overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) who fall victim to cyber fraud.

blocks.text: AMID RISE IN CYBER FRAUD CASES
Published September 24, 2026 2:33pm
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) plans to establish attaché offices at Philippine embassies worldwide to assist overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) who fall victim to cyber fraud.

During the agency’s Senate budget hearing on Thursday, NBI Director Melvin Matibag said they would initially prioritize areas in the Middle East, Europe, South America, and Asia with large OFW populations.

“We intend to put NBI liaisons, attaché offices, in other countries, sa mga embassies na we have a strong presence of our OFWs kasi napansin namin na tumataas ang cases ng cyber fraud na nagbibiktima ang OFWs natin,” Matibag said.

(We intend to put NBI liaisons, or attaché offices, in other countries, particularly in embassies where we have a strong presence of OFWs, because we have noticed an increase in cyber fraud cases targeting our OFWs.)
“It will be good if we have an NBI attaché representing para doon matulungan natin ang ating kababayan na OFW,” he added.
(It would be beneficial to have an NBI attaché representing us there so we can assist our fellow Filipinos who are OFWs.)
The establishment of NBI attaché offices worldwide is part of the National Bureau of Investigation Reorganization and Modernization Act, which aims to improve the services of NBI.

Matibag said the plan has yet to be implemented due to budgetary constraints, but the NBI has formed a technical working group to coordinate with the Department of Foreign Affairs on its implementation.
He said eight out of the 10 cases handled by the NBI are related to cybercrime.
NBI is an attached agency of the Department of Justice (DOJ).
For 2027, the Department of Justice (DOJ) is seeking a budget of P46.435 billion, which is equivalent to 0.64% of the P7.2-trillion national budget.

Of DOJ’s total proposed budget, P31.723 billion (68.32%) was allotted for Personnel Services (PS), P11.340 billion (24.42%) for Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE), and P3.372 billion (7.26%) for Capital Outlay (CO). —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Discord ban lifted --CICC
articles.summary: Discord ban lifted --CICC

blocks.text: Published September 24, 2026 2:23pm

The ban order against media sharing and messaging platform Discord has been lifted, the Department of Information and Communications Technology’s (DICT) Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) said Thursday.
“Yup, we're ordering the lifting,” DICT Undersecretary Renato "Aboy" Paraiso, executive director of the CICC, told GMA News Online.
The lifting came after the CICC and Discord management’s meeting earlier to discuss compliance matters.
Paraiso earlier said, “we have a meeting with them (Discord) at 12 noon later.”

The ban took effect Wednesday evening after the CICC clarified that it did not extend the 24-hour period given to Discord to establish Philippine presence "pending direct discussions with the platform and concrete commitments on the CICC's requirements."
“Discord separately reached out to the CICC in a letter to express its willingness to engage with the agency on its existing teen safety measures," the CICC said.

The CICC on Tuesday gave both Reddit and Discord 24 hours to establish a Philippine presence within 24 hours to enhance collaboration with the government following the shooting at the Banga National High School in South Cotabato.
The agency earlier said it gave extensions to both Discord and Reddit, but issued a clarification that only Reddit was granted an extension.
Discord told the CICC that the newly rolled out Global Teen Experience would ensure that teenagers are placed in age-appropriate places on their platform.

Discord Senior Public Policy Advisor Vasundhara Singh said users who cannot be placed in a specific age group will have to confirm their age through facial age estimation, with biometric data not being stored in Discord.
The shooting in South Cotabato is the third school shooting incident in 2026.
In June, two students opened fire in a high school in Tacloban, killing three others.
Not more than two months later, in August, another student shot and killed a schoolmate in Ateneo de Zamboanga before turning the gun on himself. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Ex-DICT exec hits blocking of Discord, says it's unconstitutional
articles.summary: A former official of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) hit the blocking of Discord, an online communication platform, saying that such a move is unconstitutional.

blocks.text: Published September 24, 2026 2:02pm
A former official of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) hit the blocking of Discord, an online communication platform, saying that such a move is unconstitutional.
Former DICT undersecretary Jeffrey Ian Dy on Wednesday night noted that the blocking of any online platforms must be done with a court order.

“And this blocking (coordinated by DICT thru its agencies NTC and CICC) was done despite the Supreme Court ruling on Disini vs Secretary of Justice in GR no. 203335 explicitly stating that unilaterally taking down computer resources (including blocking) without a court order is unconstitutional,” said Dy in a Facebook post.

In separate letters dated Sept. 21, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC), an agency attached to the DICT, gave Reddit and Discord 24 hours to establish offices or designate local representatives in the Philippines, as the government moves to strengthen coordination with digital platforms following three school shooting incidents in recent months.
Reddit was given more time to put up an office in the Philippines after its officials met with CICC online within the prescribed 24-hour period.
Discord, on the other hand, has been banned from the Philippines since Wednesday night, according to DICT Secretary Henry Aguda.
He said the DICT's Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) and Discord management are meeting to discuss compliance matters.
Discord is popular among online gamers, especially with the rise of e-sports in the Philippines. Hence, the report of banning Discord led to a backlash from many users.
However, the former DICT official noted that Discord is not just benefiting online gamers but those in the virtual assistance industry as well.

“Have you heard of Discord’s Barangay VA Helpdesk group? It has 12,000+ members. It is a group dedicated to Filipinos working as freelance online Virtual Assistants. How about the Nexus server? Same thing. Jobcord? Same,” said Dy.
“Congratulations, DICT, because of our failure to apprehend criminals online, we sacrificed some 15,000 legitimate Filipino workers on Discord,” he added.
