articles.title: OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website, PM says
articles.summary: Albanese said he expressed "concern" to OpenAI founder Sam Altman, after authorities were informed three months after the breach in June.

blocks.text: An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI "infiltrated" an Australian government website in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said.
The agent gained unauthorised accessed to a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive Medicare information", Albanese told a news conference at the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Medicare refers to Australia's universal healthcare scheme. The breach is among the first publicly reported AI-led hacks of a government website in the world.
OpenAI said it only became aware of the incident in August "during an ongoing review of OpenAI misaligned model activity", and informed Australian officials on 10 September.
While the review is ongoing, a spokesperson for the AI firm said that it is not believed that any patient records were accessed.
Albanese said the breach occurred in June this year, but OpenAI only informed government officials via email on 10 September.
The prime minister said he spoke directly to CEO of OpenAI Sam Altman to say that it had taken "too long" to inform authorities and "to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident".
He said the agent accessed both public and non-public files and a "forensic investigation" is under way to find out if other government systems were affected.
The investigation will be led by the Australian Signals Directorate, the country's cybersecurity agency.
The public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal is administered by Services Australia, the main hub to redirect users to government services.
He told reporters: "No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing.
"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable."
Earlier this year, OpenAI revealed a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls and secretly worked together to hack another tech firm named Hugging Face.

articles.title: Trump greets Xi Jinping at plane as Chinese leader arrives for state visit
articles.summary: US president to give red-carpet treatment to Chinese counterpart despite tensions over AI development

blocks.text: Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping to the US on Wednesday evening at the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, an unusually generous meeting to kick off the Chinese president’s state visit.

For the world leaders’ second meeting this year, the US president is expected to roll out the red carpet for his Chinese counterpart as top issues such as the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability loom.

The Chinese president will receive a 21-gun salute on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events.
But tensions between the two countries, especially over AI development, will likely remain present during the two-day visit.
The White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to the state dinner on Thursday.

The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, but the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.
Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, instead promoting more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.
The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically – further raising the stakes for the US and China.
Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with pageantry, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.
Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to indulge Xi.
“He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect,” Melania Trump, the first lady, said of the visit to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning.

blocks.text: AI superpower ambitions take centre stage as Trump and Xi meet
Image source, Getty Images
The US and China are locked in a race to develop AI
ByJoe TidyCyber correspondent and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporter
"Whoever wins AI, WINS!"
US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China.
His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view.

"China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies.
You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not.
For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he has described as "a hoax".
China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all.
It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world.
Is the US in the lead?
There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured.
American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.

In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%", according to researchers at Stanford University, external.
Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models.

blocks.caption: Image caption, OpenAI boss Sam Altman called for a coordinated slowdown of advanced AI development

blocks.text: OpenAI boss Sam Altman called for a coordinated slowdown of advanced AI development
The stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies.
So that might partly explain why President Trump sees AI as key to US success.

Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models.
China's advantage
Despite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all.

Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans.
The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software.
This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms.
Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months.
Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable.
Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said.
"AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Yang Zhilin co-founded Moonshot, one of China's most successful AI models, in 2023

blocks.text: Image source, Future Publishing via Getty Images
Yang Zhilin co-founded Moonshot, one of China's most successful AI models, in 2023
AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesati told Tech Life on the BBC World Service.
"Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said.

In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become the world's biggest manufacturer of robots, with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated.

The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House.
Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said.
But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms.
China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit".
Safety concerns?
China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different.

While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war.
Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president.

"We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution".

Washington has prioritised innovation and sought to reduce regulation in an effort to "keep American labs ahead", said information security officer Jayant Dave from cybersecurity firm Check Point Software Technologies.

blocks.caption: Image caption, China is the world's biggest manufacturer of robots

blocks.text: Image source, VCG via Getty Images
China is the world's biggest manufacturer of robots
Beijing has taken a different strategy to the US hands-off approach.
Xi urged the country's leaders to keep a close eye on AI's risks and ensure the technology was always "under human control".

"China has taken a relatively cautious and centrally-coordinated approach," introducing guides on data usage and algorithms before many other countries, helping to address many underlying concerns, Dave said.
The use of guidelines, though not legally binding, sets expectations while giving developers room to innovate, said National University of Singapore AI ethics lecturer Jonathan Sim.
Will they cooperate?
Despite calls for international cooperation, it remains unclear how the AI superpowers plan to address the technology's potential dangers - if at all.

The two countries have previously cooperated on existential threats such as nuclear weapons, but that was based on a shared understanding of the threat, which is not currently the case with AI, Dave said.
"Washington worries about capability escaping control. Beijing worries about capability threatening domestic stability," he added.
Trump has dismissed proposals for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that it could allow Chinese developers to close the gap.
Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed establishing a notification mechanism for serious AI incidents.

While the messaging from Trump on China in recent weeks has been "more antagonistic", the fact that AI is expected to be on the agenda was a "good start", said policy analyst Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
What we don't want, he added, was for an "unhealthy version of the race narrative to perpetuate", potentially escalating an already fierce rivalry in AI.

articles.title: Watch: The arms race in space explained
articles.summary: The UK has jammed satellites to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been told.

blocks.text: The head of Britain's Royal Air Force has warned that we we now face an unprecedented threat in space, which could have a devastating effect on the satellites we rely on for communication, internet, bank transfers and satnav.
A defence source has told BBC defence correspondent Jonathon Beale, that Britain has already used a ground based system to jam or block the satellite communications of a hostile state.
Beale explains there is now a new arms race going on in space.

articles.title: UK survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair
articles.summary: Elisabeth Belien tells Kenneth Law's sentencing hearing she took the poison when she was just 23 years old.
articles.byline: Dan Sales, Christina McSorley, Sean Dilley

blocks.text: A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vulnerability.
Elisabeth Belien told the four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, Canada she had been at her lowest ebb when he sold her toxic chemicals when she was just 23.
Belien, who until Wednesday had not been known as one of his customers, said she had physically recovered after being successfully given an antidote by medics.
But as she faced him as he sat in the glass-panelled dock, she revealed she had suffered "survivor's guilt" after learning from police others had died.
Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in suicide forums online. But there are almost 80 deaths in the UK that have also been linked to him.
As part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.
But impact statements from their families are being read during the sentencing hearing this week.
Belien told the court: "I had struggled with my mental health for a long time before this. Kenneth Law made it a lot easier to act on that despair.
"I continue to struggle with intrusive thoughts and flashbacks of that day.
"I made a full recovery. However, emotionally and psychologically, the effects are far more long lasting.
"I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived It has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened.
"I felt like the purchasing from Kenneth Law, I enabled him to continue his business, supplying his products, to other people who might have been vulnerable, like I was. I felt guilty for surviving."
Belien, who said she took the poison in January 2023, said being in court reminded her "how easily" it could have been her own parents there talking about her.
"I'm learning that things can get better," she said.
"I'm learning to be excited to see what the future holds for me. But the gratitude I'm feeling for being alive today doesn't take away from the trauma of the experience."
Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.
He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US.
David Parfett, whose son Tom died in October 2021, said in a victim impact statement: "Since Tom died, I've struggled with my mental health.

"Initially, in the months after he died, I didn't properly mourn him, because my focus was on understanding, and then exposing the harm caused by the internet platforms that allowed Law to trade suicide to kids.

"I'm still, after five years, unable to fully process Tom's death. I'm a very different person to who I was before Tom took his own life, having previously been gregarious, outgoing. I find it difficult to enjoy life."
A statement was also read from the parents of Henry Tucker, a 14-year-old British boy who died in October 2021.
Kate and Henry Tucker said Henry had been diagnosed with autism but actually had a neurological condition that could have been treated with antibiotics.
"The realisation that his suffering and his death could have been prevented is a weight that is impossible to bear," they said.
"The death of a children under these circumstance is a heavy burden to carry for the rest of our lives.
"We will carry it however with Henry's blessings until we meet again. We love you Henry."
Norson Harris, the father of British victim Ashleigh Harris, read a statement in person on the agony of losing his daughter.
He said: "The circumstances of Ashleigh's death have been incredibly tough to bear.
"We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashleigh's death.
"Rather than offer the help needed that individual Kenneth Law sold her a chemical that Ashleigh took to end her life.
"I still hope over time Mr Law will recognise the answer to Ashleigh and the myriad of others who reached out to him should have been that they were loved and there was help available to them."
Earlier Stephen Mitchell Sr, the father of Canadian Stephen Mitchell Jr, told of the aftermath of his death on March 25 2023.
"He was ill, he needed help, and I tried my best to bring him that help," he said.
"Mr Law robbed my son of that chance to be well."
Mr Mitchel Sr, addressing Law in court, said: "I'm willing to accept that during Mr Law's time in incarceration, he might have had brief moments of regret, or even despair and helplessness.
"Perhaps he may have even thought during those moments: my life is meaningless, what is the point of living.
"That was the same thoughts that my son Stephen had before he took the chemicals that Mr Law sold him.
"When my son was well, he would have gladly helped Mr Law work out his depressive thoughts, if asked, because he believed in the value of people."
Sandra Scott, whose daughter, Amara Scott, died on February 9 2022 aged 25, said she and her family were trying to help her through a mental health crisis.
"Our efforts were cut short when, in her most vulnerable state, she made contact with the accused, she said.
"The day I and her friends found Amara, and the way that she died – it broke my heart.
"It was a blessing and an honour to be Amara's mother."
The hearing continues.
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

articles.title: Australia news live: Anthony Albanese says OpenAI agent hacked Medicare
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

  • Get our breaking news email, free app…

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese says OpenAI agent hacked Medicare
Anthony Albanese has revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June.
The prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York.

double quotation markThis incident occurred in June this year and involved an Open AI agent gaining unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia. The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files. A forensic investigation, aided by the Australian Signals Directorate, is now under way to ascertain more information, including what other government systems were affected. The Medicare statistics reporting portal is a public-facing statistics portal that contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending. No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage but investigations are ongoing. Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable. Today, I spoke with the CEO of Open AI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident. And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.
Key events

items: 2m agoWorld order no longer fit for purpose, says Albanese
19m agoAnthony Albanese says OpenAI agent hacked Medicare

blocks.text: PM to say Indo-Pacific ‘not a chessboard’ for superpowers

While Australia had ties with the US and China as its key security and trading partners respectively, Albanese will say the competition between the two powers should not be the only lens the Pacific should be dealt with.
“The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces,” he will say.
“Its countries are not spectators, they are shaping its future and writing their own script.”

The prime minister will make the speech after receiving the Atlantic Council’s Global Citizen award, where he is being recognised for his role in deepening alliances and promoting security and stability in the Indo-Pacific.
He will be among four award recipients at the event, including Formula One boss Stefano Domenicali, the president of Finland, Alexander Stubb, and actor Cynthia Erivo.
The speech comes a day after Albanese met briefly with Donald Trump at a gala dinner hosted by the American leader.
The prime minister and Trump have issued divergent calls on whether to rein in the use of AI after safety fears or, in the case of the US leader, accelerate its rollout.
World order no longer fit for purpose, says Albanese

The international world order set up following the second world war is no longer fit for the present-day environment, the prime minister will declare in a major foreign policy speech in New York today, Australian Associated Press reports.
In an address to the Atlantic Council, Anthony Albanese will say many of the institutions that were necessary post-1945 were not enough to meet present-day challenges.

The prime minister will use the speech on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York to argue partnerships with alliances remain crucial in a rapidly changing global environment.

double quotation markSince the end of the cold war, the prevailing assumptions of international affairs were clear: openness was security, efficiency mattered more than resilience and international rules would be observed. Those assumptions rested on the expectation that the influence of the major democratic powers would remain largely unchallenged. The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose. Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.
The prime minister will say Australia needed to shape a world order that will replace the old one, while preserving diplomatic rules.
Albanese will point to the strategic competition between the United States and China in the Indo-Pacific region as being the most consequential issue facing the region.

blocks.caption: Patrick Commins

blocks.text: Patrick Commins
OECD says Australia will struggle to get underlying inflation below 3%
The OECD says Australia will struggle to bring underlying inflation back below 3% in 2027, despite sub-par economic growth in this year and the next.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in its interim economic outlook flagged that the world economy had, once again, proved more resilient than expected to the global energy shock triggered by the ongoing Iran war.

The artificial intelligence boom had papered over many of the cracks, the report said, adding that “global economic prospects remain heavily dependent on whether a durable resolution to the Middle East conflict is achieved”.

With fuel costs here jumping over recent weeks and inflation proving more persistent than hoped, there is a strong consensus that the Reserve Bank will deliver another interest rate hike next Tuesday – the fourth this year.
The OECD projected Australia’s headline inflation would drop from 4.1% this year, to 2.8% in 2027.
But “core” inflation – which removes the effects of big price swings, like for fuel – would prove harder to shift back into the RBA’s 2-3% target range.
The OECD expected the underlying price growth measure to ease from 3.5% in 2026 to 3.1% in 2027.

“Faced with renewed energy price shocks and stronger than expected demand pressures, and at a time when inflation is already above target in many economies, central banks need to ensure that underlying inflation pressures are durably contained,” the OECD said.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Nick Visser with the main action.

articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn plan to begin Gaza's reconstruction
articles.summary: The figure was announced during a meeting of the group's board at the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45 billion (£1.85 billion) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs.

But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280 million handed over so far. The board estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4bn over the next decade.
Jared Kushner, Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded the project faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason".
"The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders.
He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said the group had made "real progress" over the past year.

"All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added.

In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinians officials.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate press conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that".
In August, a senior official on the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the Palestinian armed group Hamas.
In August, Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.

At least 1,381 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".
The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year.

Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats.
In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which will see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza.
But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.
The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide.

articles.title: Berlin Airport briefly suspends flights over drone sighting
articles.summary: Airspace over the German capital was temporarily closed after a drone was spotted on the runway. Flights have resumed but are experiencing delays.

image.caption: https://gadebate.un.org/enImage: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Berlin's airport briefly suspended flights on Wednesday evening after a drone sighting, Germany's DPA news agency cited airport and police officials as saying.

A drone was spotted on the Berlin Brandenburg Airport's northern runway at 8:00 p.m. (1800 GMT). Airspace above the airport was closed minutes later and operations were suspended for at least 45 minutes.
Several flights were diverted to Dresden.
As of 9:05 p.m., airspace was reopened but flights were experiencing delays.
Drone sightings on the rise
Drone sightings have become a common occurrence for airports in Europe, with Berlin's airport recording the highest number of sightings in Germany in the first part of the year.

Some 28 drone sightings were recorded during the first six months, as per figures by the German air traffic control (DFS). In seven of those cases, flight operations at the airport were temporarily suspended.
This is an jump from last year, when eight drones were detected at the airport and its surroundings in the whole of 2025, according to DFS.

articles.title: Save the Children officially warned by regulator over staff put at risk in Yemen
articles.summary:
Warning from Charity Commission for England and Wales concludes two-year investigation after death of Hisham al-Hakimi in October 2023

The international aid charity Save the Children has…

blocks.text: The international aid charity Save the Children has been issued with an official regulatory warning over management failures and misconduct that put staff at its Yemen office at serious risk.

The warning concluded a two-year investigation by the Charity Commission for England and Wales into the running of the office after the death of its safety and security director, Hisham al-Hakimi, in October 2023 after he was detained by the Yemeni authorities.

The commission said weak governance meant staff at the Yemen office were not properly safeguarded in response to what it called a “live security concern”, and incidents of poor conduct by staff were not addressed.

The warning letter refers to “substantial policy breaches and a lack of accountability” at the office, and said local charity bosses failed to adequately assess and escalate complaints and reports made by whistleblowers.
An internal Save the Children investigation in 2024 after the death of Al-Hakimi found a “negative working culture” in the Yemen office had left staff “disillusioned and marginalised”.
It apologised to staff after admitting it had let them down by failing to properly appreciate the risks facing them amid the deteriorating security situation in the country.

In a statement to the Guardian, Save the Children International said that since 2024 it had made significant changes under new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve support for staff and rebuild trust. The charity has closed its north Yemen office because of security concerns.

It said despite its best efforts to understand the circumstances around Al-Hakimi’s detention and his death the challenges in Yemen meant it may never know what happened and why. Another Save the Children member of staff is understood to currently be in detention.
The commission’s warning comes amid a growing humanitarian crisis in Yemen, where the charity has been providing emergency medical help, shelter and drinking water to displaced families.

Official warnings are relatively rare, and are issued when the commission decides breaches of trust or mismanagement in a charity put its staff or beneficiaries at risk. They can be issued where charity trustees are deemed to have acted recklessly or without proper care.
The commission ordered Save the Children International to ensure sufficient resources are in place to safeguard and protect staff and other individuals working with the charity.

Stephen Roake, assistant director for high-risk compliance at the commission, said: “It can be incredibly difficult for charities operating in high-risk, volatile environments and we know that circumstances can change rapidly. However, it is for this very reason that trustees must ensure they have sufficient oversight of their overseas operations.”

In a statement, Save the Children International said it had accepted the commission’s findings of serious shortcomings in governance, management, oversight and compliance with policies and procedures in the Yemen office at the time.

Since 2024, it had installed new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve staff support and rebuild trust. It had also introduced detention risk assessments, taken steps to improve incident management procedures, and strengthened crisis management.
It said: “We remain committed to learning from this tragedy and ensuring a safe, supportive environment for our colleagues.

“We will continue to work closely with the Charity Commission to address any outstanding matters, while continuing to support our colleagues in Yemen and deliver for children in extremely challenging contexts.”

Save the Children’s Yemen office warned last week that the country faced a “catastrophic humanitarian situation” as a result of escalating conflict, collapsing health services and outbreaks of disease.
More than 1,000 people have been killed or wounded, and tens of thousands displaced by fighting in recent weeks between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.

articles.title: Milei threatens at UN that Argentina will take ‘matters into our own hands’ on Falklands
articles.summary:
Argentinian president accuses United Nations of being filled with ‘parasites’ in bellicose general assembly speech

Javier Milei has condemned the UN as he warned that Argentina would take…

blocks.text: Javier Milei has condemned the UN as he warned that Argentina would take “matters into our own hands” in its dispute with Britain over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.

In a caustic speech at the general assembly in New York, the Argentinian president criticised the UN for being ineffective when it came to the long-running tensions over the British overseas territory in the south Atlantic known in Argentina as the Malvinas.

“An organisation that set out to defend the territorial sovereignty of its members decided to look the other way regarding the situation of the Falkland Islands,” Milei said of the UN, adding that Argentina was willing to act unilaterally over recent oil exploration near the territory.
The president criticised the Sea Lion project, a major offshore oil development located in the North Falkland Basin, describing exploitation of the territory’s resources as an “unlawful act”.
The president told the assembly that Argentina would “not remain indifferent to those who exploit resources under illegal foreign occupation”.
“Argentina is not going to sit around waiting for the UN and the international community to live up to their own mandate,” he said. “We’re going to take matters into our own hands.”

Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands. Milei’s government began sanctions proceedings this month against more than 60 companies and people linked to the oil drilling project.

The Falkland Islands government had approved the field development and production plans for the project, which is a joint venture between an Israel-based energy company and a London-listed oil and gas exploration company.

The UN does not officially recognise either British or Argentine sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentine forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and 3 Falkland Islanders.

“For us, the Malvinas are a national cause,” Milei told the general assembly. The UN, he said, was a “useless organisation whose only purpose is to sustain a cast of faintly arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”.
after newsletter promotion

“That’s why the Malvinas are not merely an issue between Argentina and the United Kingdom,” he said. “They also raise a question regarding the ability of this organisation to enforce its own resolutions.”
A referendum on the political status of the archipelago was held in the Falkland Islands in 2013. On a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.

Milei told the UN delegates that the principle of self-determination should not apply for the Falkland Islands as “the population was implanted by the occupying power on a territory whose sovereignty is in dispute”. “We call on the United Kingdom to resume negotiations with a view to finding a peaceful solution to the sovereignty dispute as required by international law,” he said.

Last month, Donald Trump said he was ​reviewing the US’s neutral position on ​the Falklands. The issue was a topic of discussion this week in a first meeting between Trump and the UK’s prime minister, Andy Burnham.

“The ‌clear ⁠position is: we will stand firm in the face of any threats,” Burnham said. “We will defend the ​right of ​the ⁠Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British. I just ​wanted ⁠the president to know directly from me, that’s the clear British ⁠position, ​and he very ​much understood what I was saying.”

articles.title: Harvey Weinstein resentenced to 15 years for sexual assault
articles.summary: The disgraced Hollywood mogul was found guilty of sexually assaulting former production assistant Miriam Haley. The man whose case spurred the #MeToo movement awaits a separate sentencing in a…

image.caption: A wheelchair-bound Weinstein appealed for leniency to the Manhattan courtImage: Dean Moses/amNewYork/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Disgraced movie mogul Harvey Weinstein was resentenced on Wednesday to 15 years in prison for sexually assaulting former production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006.

Once one of Hollywood's most powerful kingpins, churning out hits such as "Pulp Fiction", "Shakespeare in Love" and "Chocolat," Weinstein's fall from grace came when sexual assault allegations compounded against him in 2017, spiraling into Hollywood's #MeToo movement.

Accounts of several women who worked with him across the years showed a pattern of abusing his power in Hollywood and ability to make or break careers to extract sexual favors and sexually assault women.
What do we know about Haley's case?
Weinstein was found guilty of forcibly performing oral sex on Haley in 2006.

The former producer said she had accepted an invitation to his Manhattan apartment when he lunged to kiss her, and though she rebuffed him, he grabbed her and sexually assaulted her, ignoring her pleas to stop.
Weinstein was sentenced in 2020 to 23 years for the sexual assault of Haley, but the sentence was overturned in 2024 on appeal. A jury found him guilty again in 2025.
What happened in court?
On Wednesday, a 74-year-old, wheelchair-bound Weinstein made an appeal for leniency, apologizing to those he may have hurt.
"I do have remorse for Miriam Haley's pain, but I have to reiterate my innocence," he told the judge.
Haley stressed the assault was akin to "a life sentence."

"Having been sexually assaulted by Harvey Weinstein has had a devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away. Making the decision to speak up will have me looking over my shoulder for years to come," she said.
Prosecutors had sought a 20-year sentence for the disgraced producer, but his lawyers warned that a longer sentence would likely see him die in prison.
Is violence against women an epidemic no one cares about?
What other cases await Weinstein in court?

Weinstein also awaits a resentencing in a separate rape and assault case in California, where he is accused of assaulting an actress in a Los Angeles hotel room in 2013. In June, an appeals court upheld his conviction but scrapped his 16-year prison term.
Meanwhile, prosecutors said they will not pursue a fourth trial in the case of him sexually assaulting actor Jessica Mann.

In May, a New York judge declared a mistrial after the jury failed to reach a verdict. It was the third time Mann had taken the stand against Weinstein and she said she could not bear to testify again.
Another 2020 verdict for Weinstein in the Mann case was overturned due to mishandling of witnesses, and a 2025 case ended in mistrial.
Weinstein's lawyers have called for leniency, arguing their client is in failing health as he battles blood cancer, congestive heart failure and kidney issues.

articles.title: New fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region raises fears of a return to the country's civil war
articles.summary: Fighting in and around Tigray is testing Ethiopia's fragile 2022 peace deal. With old enemies forming new alliances, experts warn that the conflict could enter a dangerous new phase.

image.caption: Alula Aba Nega International Airport in Tigray: flights have been supendendedImage: Liu Fangqiang/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: The fighting reported in and around Ethiopia's northern Tigray region marks more than another episode of tension between the federal government in Addis Ababa and the region's leadership. It raises a fundamental question: What remains of the fragile peace established in 2022 — and where does the conflict go from here?

From 2020 to 2022, Ethiopia was devastated by a civil war between the federal government in Addis Ababa and Tigray's regional leadership. The conflict drew in neighboring regions and foreign troops from Eritrea, leading to a humanitarian crisis that displaced millions and left hundreds of thousands dead.
While a peace agreement halted the worst of the bloodshed in late 2022, it left many political and territorial disputes unresolved.

DW spoke to witnesses in the towns of Abala and Erebti on the border with Tigray who confirmed that new fighting had taken place there between Tigray forces and Ethiopian federal troops. Humanitarian sources also reported clashes in the area. Ethiopian Airlines has suspended flights to the cities of Mekelle, Shire and Axum, citing the "current situation in the Tigray region."
Reports that Tigray forces have taken control of airports in the region could not be independently verified by DW.
For Oslo-based peace researcher Kjetil Tronvoll, however, the latest developments represent a decisive escalation.
"I think the war has already begun," Tronvoll told DW.
German security analyst Gerrit Kurtz of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin also sees the developments as a serious escalation.
"This is a step towards a war," he told DW.
Two competing narratives
The two sides are presenting fundamentally different accounts of what triggered the latest escalation.

In a statement issued on September 23, the National Regional Government of Tigray said its forces had been responding defensively to an attack by the federal government. It accused Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of launching a new "genocidal invasion" and said Tigray forces had been ordered to defend the population.

The Tigray government also accused Addis Ababa of carrying out air and drone strikes and artillery attacks in recent months. It said it had previously refrained from responding to what it described as repeated provocations in an effort to de-escalate the situation.

The allegations could not independently be verified. The federal government, meanwhile, has portrayed the developments as part of a broader coordinated threat involving armed groups opposed to the prime minister.
The competing narratives illustrate one of the central problems facing any renewed peace effort: The parties do not even agree on the basic interpretation of the escalation.
A fragile peace under pressure

The current crisis cannot be separated from the shortcomings of the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. The deal ended two years of devastating war between the federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), but it did not resolve some of the conflict's underlying political and territorial disputes.

Western Tigray remains particularly contentious. The return of hundreds of thousands of displaced people remains unresolved, while questions over Tigray's political representation and its relationship with the federal government continue to fuel tensions.
"The Pretoria agreement stopped the fighting, but it did not resolve the underlying political conflict," Tronvoll says.

At the heart of that conflict is a fundamental disagreement over Ethiopia's political order. The TPLF has traditionally defended a strong federal structure and substantial regional autonomy. Abiy Ahmed's government has pursued a more centralized political model.
The issue is therefore not simply whether individual provisions of the peace agreement are implemented. It is also about competing visions of how Ethiopia should be governed.
Former enemies join forces
The emergence of an alliance of seven armed groups opposing Abiy adds another layer of complexity.

The grouping includes the TPLF, Fano forces from the state of Amhara and the Oromo Liberation Army from another regional state within Ethiopia. Some of these organizations were bitter enemies during the Tigray war. Their decision to cooperate therefore represents a significant political development — but not necessarily a durable alliance.
Kurtz says the alliance has been developing for some time and that some of its leaders have apparently already met.
"It was a very important development," he says. "The alliance has been in the making for a long time."
At the same time, he points to the fundamental differences between its members.
"All the political differences that they have are certainly there to resolve once their overall joint aim is achieved, which is overthrowing the government of Abiy."
Tronvoll similarly describes the cooperation as primarily tactical. The question is whether the groups can turn their shared opposition to Abiy into a lasting political and military strategy.
There is another complicating factor: Eritrea.

The Ethiopian government has accused neighboring Eritrea of supporting the alliance. Eritrea has rejected such allegations. Kurtz says there have been reports of contacts between the armed groups and Eritrea, but stresses that the new alliance itself appears to be a domestic grouping.

The geography of the alliance is another obstacle. Its members operate in different parts of Ethiopia and pursue different political objectives. Coordinating military operations across such distances would be difficult.

blocks.caption: Ethiopian security forces in 2021 after they took control of Amhara city from the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF)Image: Minasse Wondimu Hailu/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Can the escalation still be contained?
The most urgent question is whether the current fighting can still be contained before it develops into another full-scale war.
Kurtz argues that the immediate priority is straightforward: The forces involved in the fighting need to stop.
"Both the Ethiopian armed forces as well as the Tigray security forces are involved in active hostilities right now. So they should stop this," he says.

But bringing the fighting to an end will require more than a ceasefire on the ground. Ethiopia's conflict has become increasingly fragmented. Armed groups are operating not only in Tigray, but also in Amhara and Oromia, two other regional states within Ethiopia. Regional actors such as Eritrea are potentially also playing a role.
The new crisis facing Tigray’s families
Who can mediate?
International actors have repeatedly warned about the risk of renewed conflict. Yet sustained diplomatic engagement has so far failed to produce a new political process.

The United States remains an important actor, according to Kurtz, but he says Washington has not shown sufficient engagement. The African Union, the European Union and other international actors could also play a role.
The challenge is that there is no single actor with enough influence over all the parties.

"It will require a certain coalition of efforts," Kurtz says. He argues that preventing a wider war would require a broader diplomatic push, with international actors dividing responsibilities and coordinating their efforts.

The United Nations General Assembly in New York could provide an opportunity for international leaders to engage directly with the Ethiopian government, he says. But diplomacy would also have to address the armed groups involved in the new alliance.

Tronvoll is similarly critical of the international response so far. He argues that the warning signs had been visible for some time but that international efforts to bring the parties back to negotiations remained limited.
The political problem remains

For the people of Tigray, the stakes are particularly high. The region has yet to recover from the consequences of the 2020-2022 war. Many people remain displaced, infrastructure has been severely damaged and the economic recovery remains fragile.

A return to large-scale war would therefore not simply mean a resumption of an old conflict. It could open a new and potentially broader phase of Ethiopia's wider security crisis, particularly given the simultaneous conflicts in Amhara and Oromia.

The immediate priority is to prevent the latest fighting from developing into a wider war. But any sustainable settlement will have to address the political questions that the 2022 agreement left unresolved.
The key question is therefore not simply whether the war has returned.
It is whether Ethiopia and its international partners can still create enough diplomatic space to prevent the latest escalation from closing the door to a political solution.
Ethiopia's broken Tigray peace deal opens old wounds

articles.title: Eviction of 87-year-old woman sparks housing protests in Madrid
articles.summary: Police escorted Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had called home for more than seven decades. The case has reignited debate over Spain's housing crisis, rising rents and protections for…

image.caption: 'I have lived here for 71 years and I don't want to leave,' Maricarmen told reportersImage: Susana Vera/REUTERS

blocks.text: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman sparked protests in the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday.
Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her residence on Alcalde Sainz de Baranda Street, where she had lived for at least 70 years of her life.
"I have lived here for 71 years and I don't want to leave," Maricarmen told reporters as the eviction was being carried out.
Dozens of people protested behind the police cordon, chanting, "Maricarmen, you are not alone" and "Murderers!"

blocks.caption: Dozens of protesters gathered as Maricarmen Abascal was removed from her home.Image: Susana Vera/REUTERS

blocks.text: The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent.
With only 30 minutes to gather her belongings, Maricarmen was escorted by riot police officers. She was removed from her home on a stretcher and taken to an ambulance.
An 8-year-long battle
Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, when a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.
According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company has lasted eight years, and this was the fourth attempt to evict her from the home.
The elderly woman's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said that the real estate company had rejected proposals from the legal team as well as requests to postpone her removal from the property.
The company has not made any public statements on the matter.

blocks.caption: The case has highlighted the housing crisis in Spain's major citiesImage: Susana Vera/REUTERS

blocks.text: Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for Inquilinas de Madrid, a tenants' association that seeks to combat what it describes as the "rental bubble" in the Madrid region, said that Maricarmen was taken by ambulance to a local hospital.
She also announced that a writer, who wishes to remain anonymous, had offered to pay the elderly woman's rent, but the real estate company rejected the proposal.
Spain's housing crisis
Spain remains divided over how to address the worsening housing crisis.

The country's left-wing coalition government has pushed for stronger tenant protections and broader rent controls. However, it argues that as long as Parliament remains divided, it will be difficult to pass such measures.
Meanwhile, Madrid's regional government, led by the conservative People's Party, has favored a more market-oriented approach.
The president of the Community of Madrid, Isabel Diaz Ayuso, is currently embroiled in a controversy related to the purchase of luxury properties valued at €6.3 million ($7.2 million).

articles.title: Iran’s leader hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
articles.summary:
Masoud Pezeshkian says Tehran is ‘ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force’

Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump,…

blocks.text: Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing America as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while also insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table.

In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to America.

But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.”
On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators.

A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech.

The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on wining the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway which has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to spike.

He made it clear that Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests Iran will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently.

Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating Iran’s former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
He also insisted Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme but did not want to build nuclear weapons.

He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security.
“In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added.
Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war.

Insisting Iran was the victim of true terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.”
The leader’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa.
Ultimately Washington granted the permit, but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides, but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position.

He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.”
Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.

Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours said the crucial strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.

It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.

The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day.

The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iranian-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport chokepoint, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.

There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing.

Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.

Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace proposes $2.45B for reconstruction in Gaza
articles.summary: The board has noted that the Palestinian enclave needs roughly $35.2 billion for full, medium-term reconstruction. Trump's plan for peace in Gaza has largely stalled since an agreement was reached…

image.caption: Nearly a year after the ceasefire started, Gaza remains largely destroyed, with Israeli attacks still a nearly daily occurrenceImage: Ramadan Abed/REUTERS

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has proposed a six-month plan for the reconstruction and governance of the Palestinian Gaza Strip, costing some $2.45 billion (roughly €2.15 billion).
The plan was unveiled during a meeting on Wednesday.

It involves a 66-project blueprint to kick things off, but acknowledges the enormous hurdles that must be overcome to rebuild the devastated enclave, where last October's ceasefire has only slowed Israeli attacks.
What do we know about the Board of Peace Gaza reconstruction plans?
Former UK prime minister Tony Blair, who serves on the organization's executive board, said that Palestinians in Gaza "don't need a slogan; they need a solution."
The reconstruction and governance projects include estimated spending for:

items: Temporary housing
Rubble removal
Hospital repairs
Economic recovery
Deployment of a multinational security force

blocks.caption: Tony Blair outlined the proposal in a keynote speech in New York CityImage: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: The initiatives are all designed to support Trump's 20-point plan to end the war.
"The need is immense," the board said, estimating that full reconstruction will cost roughly $35.2 billion over the medium term and another $71.4 billion in the next decade.

The proposal also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects, as per an Axios report released ahead of the meeting.
Could Trump's Gaza plan cost Palestinians their property?
Where do things stand in Gaza now?
Trump's Gaza peace plan, which ushered in the October 10 ceasefire last year, included:

items: Additional Israeli military withdrawals from Gaza
The disarmament of the Palestinian militant group Hamas
The arrival of an international peacekeeping force
A new apolitical Palestinian government to administer the territory's day-to-day business

blocks.text: However, almost a year on, completion of the plan has remained elusive..

blocks.caption: Most Palestinians continue to live in tent camps or ruins of their former homesImage: Mohammed Skaik/TheNews2/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Israel still occupies roughly 60% of the territory and regularly carries out deadly attacks it says target Hamas militants. Gaza health authorities say over 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed since the ceasefire. The Israeli military says four of its soldiers have been killed.

Hamas, designated as a terrorist group by several countries, has thus far not given up its weapons, despite on some occasions expressing its readiness to do so. Israel has said it will not withdraw from areas it occupies until the group fully disarms and is removed from the enclave.
Meanwhile, most Palestinians continue to live in tent camps or ruins of their former homes, with no international military force or new government materializing.
The Board of Peace's high representative, Nikolay Mladenov, has said that progress relies heavily on Hamas disarming, but he has also called on Israel to scale back its military operations.

articles.title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
articles.summary: the disgraced Hollywood producer is already serving a sentence of 23 years for rape and sexual assault in another case.

blocks.text: Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.
In a victim impact statement in court, his accuser, Miriam Haley, said the assault had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".
Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions".

Weinstein has already spent six years in prison as the cases against him play out, and he has a separate conviction for sex crimes in Los Angeles. He has faced three trials in New York over rape and abuse allegations.

He was originally convicted and sentenced in the Miriam Haley case in 2020. But in 2024, New York's highest court overturned the conviction, ruling Weinstein did not get a fair trial. He was retried and convicted again in the case last year.

Weinstein was a high-flying Hollywood producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, before reports in 2017 detailed allegations of sexual assault against him stretching back decades, sparking the #MeToo movement.
